secs.t: Government of India Act 1935 - federation, provincial autonomy, central dyarchy, Federal Court, borrowed features

x: Exam angle: UPSC 2024 paired "All India Federation" (correct) with "Defence and Foreign Affairs under the federal legislature" (wrong).
The Government of India Act, 1935 was based on the
Third Round Table Conference and the White Paper
The Federation was never implemented because
joining was optional and the princely states refused to join
Although legislative subjects were divided into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists, residuary powers were placed with the
Governor-General
Provincial autonomy replaced provincial dyarchy with governments headed by ministers responsible to the provincial legislatures.
The six provinces with bicameral legislatures were
Bengal, Bombay, Madras, Bihar
, Assam and the United Provinces.
The Act extended communal representation to depressed classes, women and labour in addition to existing categories.
The Act provided for the Federal Court at Delhi, Federal/Provincial/Joint Public Service Commissions and the Reserve Bank of India.
The federal scheme
, office of Governor, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details were among the features carried into the Constitution.
Section 63 concerning the Governor's address became the basis of
Article 175
of the Constitution of India.

secs.t: Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892, 1909 - nomination, indirect election, budget, portfolios, separate electorate

x: Exam angle: "Indirect election launched in?" The answer is
Exam angle: "Which Act..." one-liners; the 2018 key: the Act that allowed some
elected representation
Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
attributed part of the crisis to the absence of Indian opinion in the council, a concern addressed through later expansion and nomination of Indian members.
The Act incorporated Indian nomination, recognised the portfolio system introduced in 1859 and retained emergency ordinance-making power with the Viceroy.
The Indian Councils Act, 1861 marked the beginning of representative institutions by enabling the Viceroy to nominate Indians such as the Raja of Benaras, Maharaja of Patiala and Sir Dinkar Rao.
The Indian Councils Act, 1861 empowered the Viceroy to promulgate ordinances, each of which could remain in force for
six months
The
Indian Councils Act, 1892
began the practice of indirect election through nominations made on the recommendation of bodies such as universities, municipalities and chambers of commerce.

The 1909 reforms raised the Central Council's additional membership to 60, retained an official majority at the Centre and provided non-official majorities in the provinces, subject to the practical effect of official control and veto.
The 1909 Act enlarged deliberative functions by allowing discussion of the budget, supplementary questions and the moving of resolutions.

secs.t: Act → what it introduced FIRST

x: The
Charter Act, 1853
created a functioning central Legislative Council, often referred to as a mini-parliament, by separating legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council.

The listed associations are correct: nomination of Indians began in 1861, indirect election in 1892, separate electorates in 1909 and a bicameral central legislature under the Government of India Act, 1919.

secs.t: Company-era Acts - Regulating Act 1773, Pitt's India Act 1784, Charter Acts 1793-1853

x: Exam angle: "Board of Control was set up by?" - Pitt's India Act 1784.
The Bengal famine, declining revenue and the Company's financial crisis compelled the British Parliament to intervene in 1772 and take control of Bengal away from the Company.
The Charter Acts were passed in 1793, 1813, 1833 and 1853, giving the sequence
B, D, A, C
The salaries of the Board of Control were charged to the
Indian exchequer
under the Charter Act of 1793.
The Act of 1786 gave the Governor-General, associated with Cornwallis, the power to override his Council and made him Commander-in-Chief.
Evangelical pressure, associated particularly with Charles Grant and William Wilberforce, contributed to the changes introduced by the Charter Act of 1813.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated legislative and executive functions, added six legislative members and introduced open competition for civil services.
The Regulating Act made Warren Hastings Governor-General in 1774, provided a four-member Executive Council and subordinated the Bombay and Madras presidencies.
The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s Council, marking an important step in the development of legislative institutions.
The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company’s trade monopoly except in tea and China trade and allowed missionaries to enter India.

The Regulating Act, 1773 provided for the Governor-General of Bengal and the Supreme Court at Calcutta; Pitt's India Act created the Board of Control; the 1909 Act introduced Muslim separate electorates; and the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy and central bicameralism.

secs.t: Governor-General's power to override his council → Act

x: The correct order is Pitt’s India Act, 1784; Charter Act of 1793; Act of 1786 is actually earlier than 1793, so the correct chronological sequence is A, B, C, D.
The Act of 1786 empowered the Governor-General to
override his Council in special circumstances
The Charter Act of 1793 extended the overriding power to all future Governors-General and Governors of the Presidencies.

secs.t: Indians' share in administration and open competition → Act and committee

x: Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian to clear the Indian Civil Service examination, in 1864.

secs.t: Dyarchy - which Act introduced it, at which level, which Act ended it

x: Provincial dyarchy was introduced by the Act of 1919, while provincial autonomy and proposed central dyarchy belonged to the Act of 1935.

secs.t: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission

x: Police, finance and land revenue
were reserved subjects administered by the Governor with the assistance of the Executive Council.
The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927, two years before the expected review, and was chaired by
Sir John Simon
The Simon Commission was boycotted in India under the slogan “
Simon Go Back
” because it had no Indian member.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Warren Hastings, William Bentinck and Canning respectively held the first offices of Governor-General of Bengal, Governor-General of India and Viceroy of India.

These enactments progressively transferred control from the Company to the British authorities in London, strengthened centralisation and laid foundations for codified law and India’s legal-administrative system.
Under the constitutional arrangements of 1919 and 1935, elected Indians occupied ministerial positions, and British officials had to function under Indian ministers.

secs.t: Sessions and dates - first meeting, Objectives Resolution, adoption, signing, final session, time taken

x: Exam angle: "adopted on?" The answer is
The provisions relating to citizenship, the oath of the President, elections, definitions and interpretation, including
, took effect on 26 November 1949.

The Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947, the Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947, the Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948, and the third reading began on 14 November 1949.

Rajendra Prasad was elected President on 11 December 1946; the Objectives Resolution was adopted on 22 January 1947; the Assembly met as Dominion Legislature on 17 November 1947; and the Draft Constitution was published on 21 February 1948.
Sachchidananda Sinha was the temporary President, Rajendra Prasad the permanent President, B.N. Rau the Constitutional Adviser and G.V. Mavalankar the Dominion Legislature Speaker.

secs.t: Other functions - flag, anthem, song, Dominion Legislature, interim government and portfolios

x: Vande Mataram was to be
honoured equally with Jana Gana Mana
and was given equal status.
From
17 November 1947
, the Constituent Assembly also sat as the Dominion Legislature.
G.V. Mavalankar
served as the Speaker of the Dominion Legislature.
The Munshi-Ayyangar formula was adopted on
14 September 1949
, a date now observed as Hindi Diwas.
The formula provided for a 15-year transition, continued English for Union and inter-provincial use meanwhile, and listed 14 other languages.
The Muslim League called Direct Action Day as a protest against Wavell inviting the Congress to form the Interim Government.
Jagjivan Ram held Labour; C. Rajagopalachari held Education and Arts; C.H. Bhabha held Works, Mines and Power; and Asaf Ali held Railways and Transport.
Nehru was Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council and held External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations.

secs.t: Committees of the Assembly → chairman

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2025 asked for the Linguistic Provinces Committee chairman; the answer is
S.K. Dar
Exam angle: Prasad - procedural committees; Nehru - Union ones; Patel - provincial and rights/minorities.
Exam angle: APPSC-G1 2004 wrong pair: "Steering Committee - Nehru" (it was
Prasad

J.B. Kripalani chaired the Fundamental Rights Sub-committee; H.C. Mukherjee the Minorities Sub-committee; Gopinath Bardoloi the North-East Frontier and Assam Sub-committee; and A.V. Thakkar the other Excluded Areas Sub-committee.
The Drafting Committee included Ambedkar, N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar, K.M. Munshi, Saadullah, N. Madhava Rau and T.T. Krishnamachari.

secs.t: Composition - Cabinet Mission scheme, method of election, seats

x: The Constituent Assembly was planned to have 389 members: 296 from British India and 93 from the princely states.
The 1946 results recorded 208 seats for the Congress, 73 for the Muslim League and 15 for independents.
The Cabinet Mission consisted of
Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander
and came to India in March 1946.

secs.t: Key persons - provisional president, president, constitutional adviser, vice-presidents

x: The original Preamble was illuminated by
Beohar Rammanohar Sinha
Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
, the eldest member, served as the temporary President at the first sitting on 9 December 1946.
Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha
served as the temporary President because he was the eldest member; the practice was associated with the French constitutional tradition.

secs.t: Remarks by framers and Constitution Day

x: Samvidhan Divas has been observed since 2015, the year of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's 125th birth anniversary.
Rajendra Prasad declared
Vande Mataram
the national song on 24 January 1950 and stated that it would be honoured equally with the National Anthem.
Ambedkar used the expression “grammar of anarchy” in his closing speech on
25 November 1949

secs.t: Criticisms of the Assembly - representativeness, composition, time taken

x: Naziruddin Ahmed
criticised the pace of the Drafting Committee by calling it a “Drifting Committee”.
Granville Austin
described the Assembly in these terms, highlighting its Congress dominance.
The Assembly lacked a direct adult-franchise basis, originated under British proposals, and took about three years.
Viscount Simon
used the phrase “a body of Hindus” while criticising the composition of the Assembly.

secs.t: British Crown's residual role - Governor-General, dominion status

x: C.
Rajagopalachari
served as Governor-General from June 1948 to January 1950 and was the last and only Indian to hold the office.
India's Dominion status ended on
26 January 1950
, when the Constitution came into force and India became a Republic.
C. Rajagopalachari assented to the
Madras Estates (Abolition) Act
on 2 April 1949, making it the first such law.

secs.t: Princely states - options, Instrument of Accession, Standstill Agreement

x: About 565 princely states were theoretically free after paramountcy lapsed, although in practice they were expected to join India or Pakistan.
An Instrument of Accession transferred
defence, external affairs and communications
to the concerned Dominion.
A Standstill Agreement continued existing administrative arrangements with the Dominion until final terms were settled.

secs.t: Constituent Assembly's dual role after the Act

x: The Act made the Constituent Assembly fully sovereign in its constitution-making role and also made it the Dominion legislature.
The representatives from the territories that went to Pakistan withdrew from the Constituent Assembly, reducing its strength from 389 to 299.
After the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, the Constituent Assembly functioned as the Provisional Parliament until the first general elections held in 1951–52.

secs.t: Time taken - years, sessions, sitting days

x: The Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, held 11 sessions and sat for 165 days.
The Draft Constitution was considered for
114 days
The Drafting Committee sat for
141 days
The Draft Constitution contained 315 Articles.
The original Constitution contained
395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Madras Assembly resolved to divide the Presidency into
Andhra, Tamil, Karnataka and Kerala
four months before independence.
The Dhar Commission and the JVP Committee rejected linguistic States at the time, but the Andhra demand continued and resulted in the Andhra State of 1953.
The debate has been connected with the Constituent Assembly’s statement of 24 January 1950 and the Supreme Court decision in Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986).

rows.title: Sources of the Indian Constitution - borrowed features and their origin countries
sub: Group-II M1-B-6: Sources of the Indian Constitution and borrowed features

secs.t: Rights and principles → source (FRs, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties, suspension of rights in emergency)

x: All four features are associated with the Canadian model: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre, centrally appointed Governors and advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court.

All four pairs are correct: Fundamental Rights came from the United States of America, Directive Principles from Ireland, suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency from Weimar Germany and the amendment procedure from South Africa.
The Emergency-related provision for suspension of Fundamental Rights was influenced by the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

secs.t: Federal features → source (strong centre, Concurrent List, residuary powers, governors)

x: Exam angle: the traps are residuary powers (Canada, not USA; in the US they rest with the states ) and the Concurrent List (Australia, not Canada).
The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143 was influenced by the Canadian Constitution.

secs.t: Government of India Act 1935 as source - features taken

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2023 matching key -
Emergency provisions → GoI Act 1935
Suspension of FRs → Weimar Germany
Concurrent List → Australia
Single citizenship → Britain
The Government of India Act, 1935
is regarded as the single largest source, particularly for the federal scheme, Governor's office, judiciary, Public Service Commissions, emergency provisions and administrative details.

secs.t: Parliamentary features → source (cabinet, single citizenship, bicameralism, rule of law, Speaker)

x: Exam angle: APPSC asked "bicameralism from?", "single citizenship from?" and "which borrowed feature is from Britain?" (cabinet system, GS 2019). The answer each time is
Britain
. Distractors are USA and Canada.
The institution of the Speaker and the role associated with that office were influenced by the British parliamentary system.
Britain has no single written Constitution, yet India borrowed its parliamentary system and conventions from the British model.

secs.t: Match-list sets: feature → source country

x: Exam angle: List I (feature) - List II (country) matching, and "which of these is from Britain?" (APPSC-GS 2019 key:
Cabinet system
The joint sitting of the two Houses came from Australia, Fundamental Duties from the USSR, the republican ideal from France and procedure established by law from Japan.
Australia influenced freedom of trade, commerce and intercourse and the provision for a joint sitting of both Houses.
Britain influenced all four listed features: Rule of Law, legislative procedure, parliamentary privileges and prerogative writs.
The nominal head represented by the President, analogous to the British Crown, reflects British influence.
The election of Rajya Sabha members was borrowed from South Africa, whereas the nomination of members to the Rajya Sabha was borrowed from Ireland.

secs.t: Election of Rajya Sabha members and amendment procedure → source

x: The procedure for constitutional amendment under Article 368 was borrowed from
South Africa
Residuary powers with the Centre
, along with a strong Centre, centrally appointed Governors and the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, were borrowed from Canada.
Residuary powers in India lie with Parliament, reflecting the Canadian model.

secs.t: Judicial and electoral features → source (judicial review, procedure established by law, impeachment, independence)

x: Judicial review and impeachment of the President came from the United States, ‘procedure established by law’ came from Japan, and the integrated judiciary and Federal Court model were influenced by the Government of India Act, 1935.
Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independence of the judiciary and impeachment of the President are among the features borrowed from the United States.
India follows ‘procedure established by law’ under Article 21, while the United States employs the broader expression ‘due process’; consequently, Indian review is narrower in this respect.

secs.t: Concurrent List, joint sitting, freedom of trade and commerce → source

x: The stated distribution is 98 subjects in the Union List, 59 in the State List and 52 in the Concurrent List.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Constitution was influenced by several foreign constitutions and the Government of India Act, 1935, but the framers adapted the borrowed features to Indian conditions rather than reproducing them mechanically.

The framers adapted borrowed provisions to Indian conditions and incorporated distinctive features, including the Directive Principles as a novel feature and the federal-unitary flexibility suited to India.

rows.title: Salient features of the Indian Constitution - lengthiest, blend of rigidity and flexibility, quasi-federal etc.
sub: Group-II M1-B-7: Salient features of the Indian Constitution

secs.t: Which is NOT a feature - odd-one-out sets

x: India is a secular state and has no state religion.
India has a parliamentary form of government, not a presidential form.
India is described as
a Union of States with a parliamentary system of government

secs.t: Parliamentary form of government - features, contrast with Britain and the presidential system

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2019 keyed "India's head of state is elected; Britain rests on parliamentary sovereignty; Indian Parliament is not sovereign" as correct, and "Britain's head is elected" as wrong.
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha and may be removed when it loses the House's confidence.

secs.t: Type of democracy and polity - representative democracy, supreme authority

x: India follows representative or indirect democracy: people elect representatives, and a parliamentary executive governs through them.
The expression signifies popular sovereignty:
ultimate authority rests with the people
of India.
The people are the ultimate source of authority, while the Constitution is the supreme legal authority governing Parliament and the Council of Ministers.

secs.t: Lengthiest written constitution - reasons for bulk and counts

x: Exam angle: "How many Articles in the original Constitution?" → 395.
Part VII was repealed by the Seventh Amendment in 1956; Part IVA was added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976; Part IXA by the 74th Amendment in 1992; and Part IXB by the 97th Amendment in 2011.

All four factors contributed to the Constitution's length: India's diversity, the 1935 Act's influence, the prominence of lawyers in the Assembly and the inclusion of detailed administrative provisions.
The Constitution originally had 22 Parts and presently has 25 Parts, after the insertion of Parts IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA and the repeal of Part VII.

secs.t: Other salient features - judicial supremacy synthesis, integrated judiciary, franchise, emergency, three tiers

x: The Indian Constitution combines the British idea of parliamentary government with the American principle of judicial supremacy.
Article 21 originally adopted the expression 'procedure established by law', whereas the American model is associated with the broader concept of due process of law.
The Right to Property ceased to be a Fundamental Right and is now protected by Article 300A as a constitutional legal right.
The DPSPs are conventionally classified as
socialist, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual principles
Part XVIII contains the emergency provisions, covering Articles 352 to 360.

secs.t: Constitutionalism and constitutional government - limited government vs absolute rule

x: Constitutionalism means that governmental power is limited by a supreme Constitution and exercised according to established rules rather than the personal will of the ruler.
India does not recognise
unrestricted parliamentary sovereignty in the British sense
Parliament's authority is subject to constitutional limitations and the basic structure doctrine.
Supremacy of the Constitution
is a basic-structure element.

secs.t: Supremacy of the Constitution - source of authority of Union and States

x: The Constitution is the supreme law and is the source from which both Union and State governments derive their powers.
The Constitution is supreme, and laws inconsistent with it are void to the extent of inconsistency.
The Preamble begins with '
We, the People of India
', signifying that the people are the ultimate source of constitutional authority.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All six features listed—supremacy of the Constitution, federalism, secularism, parliamentary government, judicial review and judicial independence—are identified as foundational features of the basic structure.
All five expressions—“borrowed constitution”, “carbon copy of the 1935 Act”, “un-Indian”, “elephantine” and “lawyers’ paradise”—are recorded criticisms of the Indian Constitution.
The associations are: written Constitution—United States; parliamentary government—Britain; strong Centre—Canada; Concurrent List—Australia; amendment procedure—South Africa.

rows.title: Preamble - text, keywords, 42nd Amendment; is the Preamble part of the Constitution (Berubari, Kesavananda)
sub: Group-II M1-B-8: Preamble - text, keywords, the 42nd Amendment and its amendability

secs.t: 42nd Amendment - words added to the Preamble, year, "Mini-Constitution"

x: Exam angle: APPSC asked "Secular added by?" in G2 2023 and G2 2025, and "Socialist and Secular added by?" in GS 2025. The answer is always the
42nd
. Distractors are the 44th, 43rd, 45th, 52nd and 86th.
In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the clauses of the 42nd Amendment that attempted to confer unlimited amending power on Parliament and exclude judicial review.
All four provisions listed—Fundamental Duties, new Directive Principles, the freeze on delimitation and curtailment of judicial review—were associated with the 42nd Constitutional Amendment.

secs.t: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution - Berubari, Kesavananda, LIC; enactment, legal effect, enforceability

x: Exam angle: APPSC GS 2025 asked "Preamble is an integral part - which case?" The answer is
Kesavananda Bharati
. Golaknath, Minerva Mills and Gopalan are the distractors.

In the Berubari Union case (1960), the Preamble was held not to be a part of the Constitution, although it was regarded as a key to the minds of the framers and an aid to interpretation in cases of ambiguity.
Kesavananda Bharati established the basic structure doctrine and recognised the Preamble as part of the Constitution, while Minerva Mills protected the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP.

secs.t: Preamble text - words present vs absent, order, original wording

x: The original 1949 Preamble described India as a “Sovereign Democratic Republic” and referred to the “unity of the Nation.”.
The Preamble does not contain the expression “
adult franchise
.” It does refer to unity and integrity of the Nation, dignity of the individual and economic justice.
The Preamble specifically mentions liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, and equality of status and opportunity.

secs.t: Keywords - meaning of Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic; status at commencement

x: ‘Sovereign’ means that India is internally and externally free, is not subject to external control and can determine its own foreign policy.
The term ‘Democratic’ denotes government responsible to the people through representative parliamentary institutions and covers political, social and economic democracy.
A republic has an elected head of State, excludes hereditary political office and keeps public offices open to all citizens subject to constitutional qualifications.
At commencement, the Preamble described India as a ‘
Sovereign Democratic Republic

secs.t: Source of authority - 'We, the people'; date of adoption

x: ‘We, the People of India’ declares popular sovereignty:
the Constitution derives its authority from the people
The enacting clause states that the people adopt, enact and give the Constitution to themselves.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and commenced on 26 January 1950.

secs.t: Descriptions of the Preamble → who said

x: N. A. Palkhivala
described the Preamble as the ‘Identity card of the Constitution’.
Ernest Barker
described the Preamble as the ‘Key-note’ or ‘key to the Constitution’.
Thakurdas Bhargava
described the Preamble as the ‘Soul of the Constitution’.
In the Berubari case, the Supreme Court referred to the Preamble as the ‘key to the minds of the makers’ of the Constitution.

secs.t: Objectives - justice, liberty, equality, fraternity; meaning of liberty

x: Liberty means the absence of unreasonable restraints on individual activity along with opportunities for the development of one’s personality; it does not mean absolute freedom from all restraints.
The idea of fraternity may be drawn from
Article 1
of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which refers to human beings being born free and equal in dignity and rights and acting towards one another in a spirit of brotherhood.

secs.t: Objectives Resolution → mover, source of the Preamble

x: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946; it was adopted on 22 January 1947; the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and commenced on 26 January 1950.
The Preamble is a modified version of the
Objectives Resolution
moved by Jawaharlal Nehru and adopted by the Constituent Assembly.

secs.t: Amendability of the Preamble - case and limits

x: Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament can amend the Preamble under Article 368, but cannot alter or destroy its basic features.
On 25 November 2024, the Supreme Court upheld ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to the 42nd Amendment insertions.
The constitutional position stated in the material is that secularism was part of the basic structure even before the word was inserted in 1976.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The counter-view is that secularism was inherent in the Constitution even before the insertion of the word, with Articles 25 to 28 cited in support.
The Supreme Court upheld the words and rejected challenges to the 42nd Amendment insertions in the context of the contemporary constitutional debate.
The Supreme Court upheld the words ‘Socialist’ and ‘Secular’ in the Preamble and rejected challenges to their insertion through the 42nd Amendment.

secs.t: Twelve Schedules → subject matter

x: Exam angle: "First Schedule contains?" The answer is the
states and UTs
. "Official languages schedule?" The answer is the
Eighth
The Ninth Schedule originally contained 13 Acts, presently contains 282 Acts, is connected with Article 31B, and laws added after 24 April 1973 may be examined by the Supreme Court.

secs.t: Parts I-XXV → subject and article range, including IVA, IXA, IXB, XIVA

x: Exam angle: "Part dealing with the Union Executive?" The answer is
Part V
Part VIII deals with
Union Territories
and covers Articles 239 to 242; Article 242 was repealed.
Part IX concerns Panchayats, Part IXA Municipalities, Part IXB co-operative societies and Part XVII the official language.
Part XIII covers Articles 301–307, Part XIV Articles 308–323, Part XIVA Articles 323A–323B, and Part XV Articles 324–329A.

secs.t: Third Schedule oaths - offices covered, oaths outside it

x: The Third Schedule prescribes the oath or affirmation for the
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
Union Ministers, Members of Parliament and Supreme Court judges are covered by the Third Schedule.
The Vice-President takes an oath under Article 69, not under the Third Schedule.
Article 60
prescribes the oath or affirmation of the President.

secs.t: Articles number game - key single articles

x: Article 1
declares that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
Article 280 deals with the Finance Commission.
Article 143
empowers the President to seek the advisory opinion of the Supreme Court.
Article 300A protects the right to property as a legal right, not as a Fundamental Right.

secs.t: Special provisions for states → Article (371 to 371J)

x: Article 371A relates to Nagaland, Article 371B to Assam, Article 371C to Manipur and Article 371F to Sikkim.
Articles 371D and 371E were inserted by the 32nd Amendment Act, 1973, in the context of the Six-Point Formula following the Jai Andhra and Telangana agitations.
Article 371J provides special provisions for
the Hyderabad-Karnataka region of Karnataka
and was introduced by the 98th Amendment Act, 2012.

secs.t: Deleted parts and articles - what was repealed and by which amendment

x: Article 2A was inserted by the 35th Amendment and omitted by the 36th Amendment when Sikkim became a full State.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gor Boli, also known as Lambadi, is the Banjara language of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana for which continuing demands for Eighth Schedule inclusion have been reported.
The Ninth Schedule was the first Schedule added, in 1951.

rows.title: Union and its territory - Articles 1-4; formation of new states, cession of territory

secs.t: New states - amending Act or amendment, and chronological order of formation

x: Exam angle: chronological ordering (Andhra State → Nagaland → Haryana → Sikkim → Goa → Telangana) and amendment-to-state matching.
The 1960 reorganisation divided Bombay into Maharashtra and Gujarat; 1963 saw Nagaland; 1966 saw Punjab and Haryana with Chandigarh as a Union Territory; and Sikkim became the 22nd State in 1975.

secs.t: Union Territories - number, administration, UTs with and without legislature

x: The merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu became effective on
26 January 2020
Article 239(2) permits
the Governor of an adjoining State
to be appointed as the administrator of a Union Territory; the Governor of Punjab administers Chandigarh as an example.
The proposed renaming was associated with
Article 3
of the Constitution, which concerns the formation and alteration of states and their areas, boundaries or names.

secs.t: Reorganisation Acts - Andhra State Act 1953, States Reorganisation Act 1956, J&K Reorganisation Act 2019

x: The Act created Jammu and Kashmir as a Union Territory with a legislature and Ladakh without one, abolished the Legislative Council and took effect on 31 October 2019.

secs.t: Cession of territory - Berubari reference, Land Boundary Agreement, enclaves

x: In the Berubari Reference, the Supreme Court held that Article 3 did not cover cession of Indian territory to a foreign country; an Article 368 amendment was necessary, resulting in the Ninth Amendment, 1960.
The Land Boundary Agreement was implemented through the 100th Constitutional Amendment, 2015, which amended the First Schedule entries relating to Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya and Tripura.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sequence is Andhra State in 1953, Andhra Pradesh in 1956, bifurcation in 2014, and the 2026 amendment making Amaravati the sole capital of Andhra Pradesh.
The Ministry of Home Affairs proposed a new Chapter K under Article 371 for
Ladakh
; the proposal is distinct from the existing Chapters A to J.
The demand to restore Jammu and Kashmir's Statehood continues

rows.title: Citizenship - Articles 5-11; Citizenship Act 1955, acquisition and loss, OCI, CAA 2019
sub: Group-II M1-B-9: Union and its territory (Articles 1-4) and citizenship (Articles 5-11)

secs.t: Modes of acquiring citizenship under the Citizenship Act 1955 - number, conditions, residence periods

x: Citizenship by descent applies to a person born outside India when either parent was an Indian citizen at the time of birth, subject to registration of the birth at an Indian consulate.
Birth relates to birth in India, descent to birth abroad with consular registration, naturalisation to residence and oath, and incorporation to a territory joining India.

Ordinary naturalisation requires twelve years in the statutory formulation: eleven years during the preceding fourteen years and the last twelve months immediately before the application, along with other conditions including the oath of allegiance.
The residence conditions for naturalisation may be waived for persons who have rendered distinguished service in fields such as science, art, literature or the cause of world peace.
The three modes of loss are renunciation, automatic termination on voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship, and deprivation by the Central Government in specified cases.
The CAA route covers Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014.
The 19 August 2026 MHA order transferred processing in the specified eight States and Union Territories to
District Collectors
instead of Empowered Committees.

secs.t: Articles 5-11 and Part II - citizens at commencement, Article 10, Article 11

x: Article 5 recognised citizenship at commencement for a person domiciled in India who fulfilled conditions such as birth in India, birth of either parent in India, or ordinary residence in India for five years.

Articles 6, 7 and 8 respectively concern migrants from Pakistan, certain returnees from Pakistan, and persons of Indian origin residing abroad who are registered by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
Part II deals primarily with persons who were citizens
at the commencement of the Constitution
; subsequent matters are left to Parliament under Article 11.

secs.t: Terms - NRI, PIO, OCI, Commonwealth citizen, single citizenship

x: Exam angle: NRI = citizen abroad; PIO and OCI = foreign citizens.
A PIO is a foreign citizen whose ancestors were Indian nationals, whereas an NRI remains an Indian citizen ordinarily residing outside India.
OCI cardholders are foreign nationals of Indian origin and enjoy a lifelong visa facility.
India follows single citizenship, meaning that citizens owe allegiance to the Union and do not possess separate citizenship of individual States.

secs.t: Sections of the Citizenship Act 1955 - provisions

x: Section 6
of the Citizenship Act, 1955, deals with acquisition of citizenship by naturalisation.
Section 14A provides for the National Register of Indian Citizens and the issue of a national identity card.
Deprivation by the Central Government applies only to citizens by naturalisation, registration or Article 5(c), and may be based on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty or helping an enemy during war.

secs.t: Citizenship (Amendment) Acts 1986, 2003, 2005, 2015, 2019 - change made by each

x: The 1986 amendment provided that citizenship by birth for persons born from 1 July 1987 required at least one parent to be an Indian citizen.
The 2003 amendment introduced OCI, added Section 14A, and from 3 December 2004 required the other parent not to be an illegal migrant for the relevant birth-based citizenship condition.

secs.t: CAA 2019 - passage, countries, communities, cut-off date, exempted areas

x: The Act gives citizenship effect from the date of entry, reduces the naturalisation residence requirement to five years and amends the Third Schedule.
The foreign passport must be surrendered within
15 days of approval
under the 2026 Rules.
The challenge principally invokes
Article 14
, particularly concerning classification based on religion and country.

secs.t: Competent authority to regulate citizenship - article and body

x: Article 11 empowers Parliament to make laws regarding acquisition and termination of citizenship and all other matters relating to citizenship.
The Union Home Ministry frames citizenship rules, whereas the Election Commission checks citizenship in relation to electoral rolls under Article 324.
The Union
Ministry of Home Affairs
frames the Citizenship Rules, including the Citizenship Rules, 2009.

secs.t: Single vs dual citizenship - Indian position, other countries, domicile

x: The United States and Switzerland recognise national as well as state or cantonal citizenship.
The Indian Constitution adopted the idea of single citizenship from
Britain
India has single citizenship and Article 9 deals with voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.

secs.t: OCI cardholder - eligibility, who is barred, rights not available

x: Foreign citizens of Indian origin, their spouses and children may be eligible for an Overseas Citizen of India card, subject to statutory conditions.
OCI cardholders are not Indian citizens and do not have voting rights, the right to contest elections, eligibility for constitutional offices or public employment as a general rule.

secs.t: Formation of states and UTs → year and Act/amendment, chronology

x: Mizoram attained Statehood on 20 February 1987 under the State of Mizoram Act, 1986 and the 53rd Constitutional Amendment.
The Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh came into existence on
31 October 2019
under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
Potti Sriramulu died in
December 1952
during his fast, after which Andhra State was created in 1953.

secs.t: Territory of India vs Union of India

x: As a sovereign State, India may acquire foreign territory through cession, treaty or conquest.

secs.t: States Reorganisation Commission and Act 1956

x: The Commission was constituted in 1953, Andhra State was formed in 1953, the Act was enacted in 1956 and Andhra Pradesh was formed on 1 November 1956 under that reorganisation.

secs.t: Territorial adjustments and UT administration

x: The Berubari reference held that territory could not be ceded under Article 3 and required an Article 368 amendment, resulting in the 9th Amendment Act, 1960.
Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged into a single Union Territory on
26 January 2020
The administrator is designated as a Lieutenant Governor in Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The challenge concerns the use of religion and country of origin in relation to Article 14; Article 239 is unrelated to this issue.
India has shifted from jus soli, citizenship based primarily on place of birth, towards jus sanguinis, citizenship based primarily on descent or blood relationship.
The Election Commission may check citizenship during revision of electoral rolls, while doubtful cases may go to the Central Government.

rows.title: Fundamental Rights - Article 12 (State), Article 13 and doctrines of eclipse, severability, waiver
sub: Group-II M1-B-10: Fundamental Rights - Article 12, Article 13 and related doctrines

secs.t: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

x: Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens.
Article 15 is among the Fundamental Rights available only to citizens.
Article 21
is available to all persons.
Articles 15 and 29 are available only to citizens, while Articles 20 and 27 are available to all persons.

secs.t: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

x: Exam angle: "How many FRs do citizens have?" →
Six
The sequence is right to equality (Articles 14–18), right against exploitation (23–24), right to freedom of religion (25–28), and cultural and educational rights (29–30).
Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d), voting is a statutory right connected with Article 326 and election laws, and property is protected under Article 300A.
The Right to Education Act, 2009 gives effect to
Article 21A
, which concerns free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years.

secs.t: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, and Article 32 permits an aggrieved person to move the Supreme Court directly for their enforcement.
Fundamental Rights are qualified rather than absolute, and courts review restrictions for constitutional validity and reasonableness.
Articles 21A, 29 and 30
confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights.
Although most Fundamental Rights operate against State action,
Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24
also impose obligations relevant to private persons.

secs.t: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

x: Article 33 concerns specified forces and security services, Article 34 concerns martial law, Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive legislative power on specified matters, and Article 359 concerns the President’s order suspending enforcement of named rights.
Fundamental Rights may be altered through the constitutional amendment procedure, but the amendment is subject to the basic-structure doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).

Article 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces, forces charged with maintaining public order, intelligence organisations and related services, including specified police and paramilitary personnel.

secs.t: Doctrines - meaning and case where applied (eclipse, severability, waiver)

x: Exam angle: doctrine-to-case matching; pith and substance is the doctrine for Union-State List encroachment.
Eclipse means dormancy and possible revival; Severability preserves the separable valid part; Waiver cannot operate against Fundamental Rights; Prospective overruling operates only in the future.
Ambica Mills (1974) clarified that the doctrine of eclipse applies to pre-Constitution laws, not generally to post-Constitution laws enacted in violation of Fundamental Rights.
The
eclipse
doctrine holds that a pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights becomes dormant rather than dead and may revive if the constitutional impediment is removed.
Pith and substance
is the relevant doctrine for examining Union-State List encroachment by looking at the true nature and character of the law.

Vellore concerned Palar River pollution by tanneries and applied precautionary and polluter pays principles; Bichhri concerned chemical-unit clean-up; Oleum gas leak established absolute liability; Kamal Nath applied public trust doctrine.

secs.t: Violation of Fundamental Rights - statement-based scenarios

x: Payment below the minimum wage may amount to forced labour under Article 23, as recognised in the PUDR/Asiad case of 1982.
Article 29(2)
prohibits denial of admission to a State-maintained or State-aided educational institution on these grounds.
Where the alleged violation is by a private individual and does not involve enforceable public-law action, the ordinary legal remedy is generally available rather than a writ.

secs.t: Article 13 - meaning of law, precedence of the Constitution, amendments as law

x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
Article 13(2) declares that the State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the Fundamental Rights conferred by Part III; such a law is void to that extent.
Article 13 is the constitutional basis of judicial review of laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights and establishes the supremacy of Fundamental Rights over ordinary law.

secs.t: Descriptions of Fundamental Rights - who said

x: Magna Carta of India
" - Fundamental Rights (Part III).

secs.t: Article 12 - meaning of State, other authorities, instrumentality cases

x: R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority
(1979) laid down the tests for identifying an instrumentality or agency of the State.
Pradeep Kumar Biswas
(2002) held that financial, functional and administrative domination by the Government is a significant basis for treating a body as ‘State’.
The cases were decided in 1967, 1979, 1981 and 2002 respectively: Rajasthan SEB, R.D. Shetty, Ajay Hasia and Pradeep Kumar Biswas.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fundamental Rights check governmental power, protect minorities, support liberty and the rule of law, and limit Parliament through Article 13.
Britain does not have codified Fundamental Rights in the Indian constitutional sense; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.
I.R. Coelho (2007) limited the absolute character of Ninth Schedule protection by permitting judicial scrutiny where basic-structure principles are affected.

rows.title: Right to Equality - Articles 14-18; reasonable classification, reservation jurisprudence
sub: Group-II M1-B-11: Right to Equality - Articles 14-18 and reservation jurisprudence

secs.t: Articles 14-18 - content and clause text

x: The listed places under Article 15(2) are shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks and bathing ghats.
Article 16(3) specifically empowers
Parliament
to prescribe residence requirements for certain classes of employment or appointment under a State or Union territory.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice and treats enforcement of any disability arising from it as an offence.

secs.t: Articles 15 and 16 special provisions - beneficiaries, groups not covered

x: Article 16(4A)
concerns reservation in promotion for SCs and STs, along with consequential seniority as reflected in the relevant amendments.
The 103rd Amendment inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6), providing for reservation for Economically Weaker Sections up to 10 per cent.
Article 16(5) permits offices connected with religious or denominational institutions to be kept for persons professing that particular religion or belonging to that denomination.

secs.t: Types of equality - article securing each

x: Articles 39(b), 39(c) and 39(d), which are Directive Principles, are associated with economic equality.
Articles 325 and 326 are associated with political equality through non-exclusion from electoral rolls and adult suffrage.
Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as
an inseparable trinity

secs.t: Article 18 - titles abolished, foreign titles, consent, national awards

x: Under Article 18(3), a non-citizen holding an office of profit or trust under the State requires
the President’s
consent to accept a foreign title.
The Bharat Ratna and Padma awards were discontinued in 1977 and revived in 1980.
Article 18 advances social equality by abolishing artificial distinctions arising from State-conferred titles, subject to the stated exceptions.

secs.t: Article 14 - equality before law vs equal protection, rule of law, arbitrariness, classification

x: Article 361 protects the President and Governors from civil proceedings during their term unless the prescribed
two months' notice
has been given.

The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.
The ruling held that the State cannot arbitrarily treat pensioners differently from serving employees in relation to dearness allowance.

secs.t: Reservation cases - ruling issue, creamy layer and 50% ceiling origin

x: Jarnail Singh (2018) held that separate data establishing backwardness of SCs and STs was not necessary, while applying the creamy-layer principle to SC/ST promotions.
Extraordinary situations, carry-forward vacancies under the 81st Amendment and the EWS reservation recognised in Janhit Abhiyan are stated qualifications or exceptions.
The nine-judge Bench decided Indra Sawhney by a
majority and upheld the 27 per cent OBC quota subject to exclusion of the creamy layer.
The 105th Amendment reversed the interpretation of the 102nd Amendment in the Maratha case and restored the States’ power to identify socially and educationally backward classes.

Champakam Dorairajan concerned the Communal Government Order; M.R. Balaji concerned caste and the 50 per cent principle; M. Nagaraj concerned promotional reservation conditions; Jarnail Singh concerned creamy layer in SC/ST promotions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court held that the State cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees in the matter of dearness allowance without satisfying Article 14's twin test.
The debate includes the relationship between the 50 per cent reservation ceiling and the EWS quota, along with the creamy layer for Scheduled Castes and sub-classification.

rows.title: Right to Freedom - Article 19 (six freedoms) and reasonable restrictions
sub: Group-II M1-B-12: Right to Freedom - Article 19 and reasonable restrictions

secs.t: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22

x: The
freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
was Article 19(1)(f), but it was deleted by the 44th Amendment in 1978.
Freedom of the press
is not separately listed in Article 19(1), but courts have read it into freedom of speech and expression.
The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(b), although peaceful protest is protected within constitutional limits.

secs.t: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts

x: Romesh Thappar was decided in 1950, Sakal Papers in 1962, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain in 1975, and Naveen Jindal in 2004.
Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) recognised the right to silence, including protection for those who respectfully declined to sing the national anthem.
Films may be subjected to pre-censorship in a manner in which the press cannot, because films are considered capable of reaching larger audiences.

secs.t: Article 19 availability - citizens only, foreigners, detained persons

x: Article 19 rights are available only to citizens; foreigners cannot claim them, and a company as a legal person cannot itself claim them, though citizen shareholders may bring a challenge in appropriate circumstances.
Article 19 primarily protects citizens against State action.
Imprisonment or detention curtails movement but does not by itself extinguish freedom of expression.

secs.t: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner

x: Exam angle: case-to-ruling matching; Romesh Thappar → 1st Amendment.
In
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
(1950), the ban on *Cross Roads* was struck down because public order was not then a ground under Article 19(2).
Criminal defamation is now covered by
Section 356
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita; Sections 499 and 500 were the corresponding IPC provisions.

secs.t: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness

x: The
First Amendment, 1951
added the State-trade clause in Article 19(6), thereby shielding nationalisation from challenge under the freedom of trade and business.
The reasonableness test, involving factors such as the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, and proportionality, is associated with V.G. Row (1952).
The court decides whether a restriction is reasonable by examining factors including purpose, extent, urgency and proportionality.

secs.t: Freedom of assembly and association - limits (gherao, strikes, arms), co-operatives

x: The notes identify
Section 163 of the BNSS
as the corresponding current provision for prohibitory orders earlier associated with Section 144 of the CrPC.
CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar
(1997–98) is cited for holding that bandhs are illegal because they interfere with the freedoms of others.
The Centre has invoked
Article 19(4)
, which concerns reasonable restrictions on the freedom to form associations or unions, in defending FCRA curbs.

secs.t: Freedom of movement and residence - restrictions for Scheduled Tribes

x: Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and for protecting the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
Restrictions on outsiders' entry and settlement in tribal or Inner Line areas may protect Scheduled Tribes' culture and land under Article 19(5).
The restriction may be used to protect the
culture and property
or land interests of Scheduled Tribes.

secs.t: Freedom of profession, trade - State monopoly and qualification limits

x: Article 19(6) permits the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens, thereby permitting State monopolies.
The relevant provisions of Article 19(6) were inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment.
There is no right to carry on dangerous or immoral trades, such as trafficking.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court recognised peaceful and lawful protest as everybody's right while emphasising that dissent must not occupy public space or trouble citizens.
The criticism characterised the prohibition of the NCERT chapter as censorship implicating freedom under
Article 19
Articles 14, 19 and 21
are collectively described as the golden triangle because of their interrelationship in protecting liberty and individual rights.

rows.title: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 - protection in conviction, life and liberty, education, preventive detention
sub: Group-II M1-B-13: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 - life, liberty, education and preventive detention

secs.t: Right to Education - Article 21A, inserting amendment and commencement, RTE Act 2009, earlier cases

x: Exam angle: amendment number (86th) and year (2002); Art. 21A vs Art. 45 vs Art. 51A(k) age groups.
Article 51A(k) imposes the duty on a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between 6 and 14 years.
The 86th Amendment made all three changes: it inserted Article 21A, changed Article 45 and added the parental duty under Article 51A(k).
Section 3 gives every child aged 6 to 14 years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education is completed.
Mohini Jain was decided in 1992, Unnikrishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment was enacted in 2002, and the RTE Act was enacted in 2009.

Article 41 concerns work, education and public assistance; Article 43 concerns living wage and decent living standards; Article 45 concerns early childhood care up to six years; and Article 47 concerns nutrition, public health and prohibition.

secs.t: Article 21 derived rights recognised by courts

x: Hussainara Khatoon dealt with speedy trial, Subhash Kumar with a clean environment, and Chameli Singh with shelter.
Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996) recognised the obligation to provide emergency medical care as part of Article 21.
M.H. Hoskot (1978) is associated with
free legal aid
as a component of fair procedure and personal liberty.
Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been expansively interpreted to include dignity, health, mental health, protection against solitary confinement and compensation for violations.
Maniyar Iliyaz v. P. Ayyappan
(2026) connected safe walking on footpaths with Articles 19(1)(d) and 21 and referred to restitutionary remedies.
The relevant years are Hussainara Khatoon (1979), Olga Tellis (1985), Subhash Kumar (1991) and K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

secs.t: Article 20 - ex post facto law, double jeopardy, self-incrimination, what it does not contain

x: Article 20(2) covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, but it does not extend to
departmental proceedings
Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961) distinguished physical evidence such as
fingerprints
from testimonial compulsion protected by Article 20(3).
Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
Section 337 of the BNSS contains the provision relating to double jeopardy; it corresponds to the earlier Section 300 of the CrPC.

secs.t: Right to die and euthanasia cases

x: Gian Kaur overruled P. Rathinam, but the material does not state that it overruled Maruti Shripati Dubal in the same formulation; the Bombay High Court decision preceded Rathinam.
Common Cause (2018)
recognised the right to die with dignity as part of Article 21 and upheld the validity of a living will or advance directive.
Section 226 BNS applies only to an attempt to compel or restrain a public servant from exercising lawful powers or discharging official duties; it is not a general offence of attempted suicide.

secs.t: Procedure established by law vs due process - A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi

x: ‘Procedure established by law’ requires compliance with a law enacted by the legislature. ‘Due process of law’ additionally requires the law and procedure to satisfy standards of fairness and reasonableness.
The Maneka Gandhi decision held that a procedure affecting life or personal liberty must be fair, just and reasonable and must not be arbitrary.
Maneka Gandhi established a close relationship among
Articles 14, 19 and 21
, commonly described as the golden triangle of fundamental rights.

secs.t: Article 22 - rights of arrested persons, preventive detention safeguards, period without Advisory Board

x: Article 22(1) and 22(2) provide all three safeguards in the case of an ordinary arrest: information about the grounds, legal representation, and production before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours excluding journey time.
Article 22(3) excludes
an enemy alien and a person detained under a preventive detention law
from the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2).
Preventive detention is detention without trial based on the apprehension that a person may commit specified harmful acts in the future.

Article 22(4) requires an Advisory Board, consisting of High Court judges or persons qualified to be High Court judges, to report sufficient cause before preventive detention continues beyond three months.
Regulation III of 1818 and the Rowlatt Act
are identified as important historical roots of preventive detention legislation in India.

secs.t: Preventive detention laws - names

x: The Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974, or COFEPOSA, targets suspected smugglers and foreign-exchange offenders.
The National Security Act, 1980 permits preventive detention for up to twelve months without charges, subject to constitutional and statutory safeguards.
The Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act and the Kerala Anti-Social Activities (Prevention) Act are state-level preventive detention laws.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana emphasised that
the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee
The letter was addressed to
Chief Justice Surya Kant
and cited the K.A. Najeeb precedent in relation to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam.
In the Harish Rana matter, his parents sought
withdrawal of life support before the Supreme Court
after he had remained in a persistent vegetative state for 13 years.

rows.title: Right against Exploitation - Articles 23-24; Right to Freedom of Religion - Articles 25-28
sub: Group-II M1-B-14: Right against Exploitation and Right to Freedom of Religion - Articles 23-28
Group-II S3-10: Religion in India - religious pluralism, secularism and the Indian model

secs.t: Article 25 - text of clause (1), conscience, profess, practise, propagate, limits

x: Exam angle: quoted text of 25(1) → identify the Article (asked 2018, 2023).
Freedom of conscience concerns the inner freedom to determine one's relationship with God or creatures and also includes the freedom to follow no religion.
To profess religion is to declare one's beliefs openly, either verbally or through visible symbols such as a turban, crucifix or kirpan.
Propagation means spreading one's beliefs, but it does not include a right to convert another person because that would impinge on the other person's freedom of conscience.

secs.t: Articles 23-24 - trafficking, begar, forced labour, child labour, link with 21A

x: Exam angle: clause-text matching; distractors are Arts 19(1), 26(1), 29(1).

Article 24 concerns child labour; Article 25 concerns freedom of conscience and religious practice; Article 26 concerns management of religious affairs; and Article 27 concerns freedom from taxes for promoting a particular religion.

The correct pairing is Article 24–child labour, Article 25–freedom of religion, Article 27–freedom from religious promotion taxes and Article 28–freedom concerning religious instruction or worship in certain institutions.
Article 24 protects children below 14 from employment in factories, mines or hazardous work, while Article 21’s life-with-dignity principle supports mandatory victim rehabilitation.

secs.t: Right to religion - nature, available to whom, public order, morality, health

x: The freedoms guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 constitute
Fundamental Right
s and are not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.
The Essential Religious Practice test is a court-made test for deciding whether a practice is integral to a religion and consequently protected.
Article 27 embodies the neutrality principle that no person can be compelled to pay a tax specifically appropriated for the promotion or maintenance of a particular religion.

secs.t: Religion cases → issue

x: Exam angle: case → religion/issue matching; ERP test origin.
The
Shirur Mutt case
, formally Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments v. Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar, in 1954 is associated with the origin of the Essential Religious Practice doctrine.
The Sabarimala judgment allowed women of all ages, rejected gender discrimination in devotion and reaffirmed secularism as part of the Basic Structure.
Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga
were reported as the first women of the barred age group to enter Sabarimala in January 2019.

The Centre argued that protection is not confined to essential practices and that every practice is protected unless it breaches public order, morality or health; it also placed the burden on the challenger.

secs.t: Explanations to Article 25 - kirpan; "Hindus"

x: Explanation II to Article 25(2)(b) provides that “Hindus” includes persons professing the Sikh, Jaina or Buddhist religion.
Explanation II states that the reference to Hindus includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists, and that Hindu religious institutions are construed accordingly.

secs.t: Laws under Articles 23-24 → year and scope

x: The
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956
penalises brothels, pimping and living off another person’s earnings from prostitution.
The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976 abolishes bonded labour, including
debt bondage
found in sectors such as brick kilns, agriculture and domestic work.
All three statements are correct: Section 143 addresses trafficking, the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, and victim consent does not validate trafficking.

secs.t: Articles 26-28 - religious affairs, taxes, religious instruction

x: Article 26 gives every religious denomination or section thereof
the right to manage its own affairs in matters of religion
, subject to public order, morality and health.
Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion, but a fee imposed for secular administration of a religious institution is permissible.

Article 26 concerns denominational religious affairs; Article 27 concerns taxes; Article 28(1) concerns State-funded religious instruction; and Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance.

secs.t: Conversion laws and the propagation debate

x: The Orissa Act was enacted in 1967, the Madhya Pradesh law in 1968, Stanislaus was decided in 1977, and the BNS replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024.
The later amendments widened the scope of the laws to cover conversions to
Islam
in addition to the earlier concern over Christian missionary activity.
Section 299 of the BNS corresponds to the earlier Section 295A, which was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds.

secs.t: Article 24 - child labour, age limit, nature of prohibition, linked laws

x: Article 24 is directed at employment of children below fourteen years in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered by the constitutional prohibition.
The amended law has the family-enterprise-after-school exception for children, prohibits hazardous work by adolescents, and the RTE Act covers children aged six to fourteen years.

secs.t: Secularism - meaning, components, Western vs Indian model, Arts. 25-28, 42nd Amendment

x: Indian secularism permits the State to regulate or reform religious practices under Article 25(2) and to provide assistance to minority institutions within the constitutional framework.
Equality provisions in Articles 14 to 16, freedom of religion in Articles 25 to 28, and cultural and educational rights in Articles 29 and 30 collectively reflect constitutional secularism.

secs.t: Theories of religion → sociologist

x: Emile Durkheim
associated religion with collective worship of society and distinguished the sacred from the profane.
Emile Durkheim
studied totemism in *The Elementary Forms of Religious Life*, published in 1912.
Max Weber
examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in *The Religion of India*.
*Homo Hierarchicus* and the analysis of caste through purity-pollution are associated with Louis Dumont, not B. Malinowski.

secs.t: Religious pluralism - coexistence, syncretic traditions (Bhakti, Sufi)

x: The Bhakti movement, spanning approximately the 6th to the 18th century, rejected ritualism and caste and interacted with Sufi traditions.
Bhakti-Sufi interaction helped build communal harmony and encouraged the development of regional literatures.
The Vijayanagara example illustrates coexistence through the employment of Muslim officers and protection of Jain communities.
Bammera Potana offered the *Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu* to
Lord Rama
, not to Krishnadevaraya.

secs.t: Secularism cases - Kesavananda Bharati, S.R. Bommai

x: The sequence is Ratilal (1954), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Church of God (2000) and S.R. Bommai (1994) only if ordered by the dates given in the material; therefore the correct chronological sequence is Ratilal (1954), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), S.R. Bommai (1994), Church of God (2000).
The Sabarimala ruling stated that the State cannot endorse a practice and that a claim of essential practice cannot be used to bar others' participation.

secs.t: Religious fundamentalism and revivalism - meaning, forms

x: Revivalism seeks to restore an idealised or golden past; Arya Samaj's “Back to the Vedas” is a cited example.
Communalism, separatism and fanaticism are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India, particularly in the context of religion becoming fused with politics since the 1970s.
Hate speech on social media and illegal conversions
have been identified as threats that erode the Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb.

secs.t: Terms from religions → meaning and religion

x: Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of good, and Angra Mainyu, the destructive or evil spirit, belong to
Zoroastrianism
, followed by Parsis in India.
Tirthankara means ‘Ford-maker’, and Jain tradition identifies 24 Tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha and ending with Mahavira.
Guru Granth Sahib is the scripture and eternal Guru of Sikhism

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt is at Tirupati; its dispute has involved interim management before the High Court and Supreme Court, while the 1987 Act regulates Hindu temples and mutts and the Department administers more than 42,000 temples.
The Punjab sacrilege-law debate refers to the Supreme Court’s upholding of Section 295A IPC in Ramji Lal Modi on public-order grounds; the provision is now reflected in the BNS framework.

rows.title: Cultural and Educational Rights - Articles 29-30; the right to property and the 44th Amendment

secs.t: Right to property - Article 31 journey, deleting amendment, Article 300A

x: Exam angle: A-R pairs "legal right under 300A in Part XII" + "44th Amendment, 1978".
Since Article 300A does not confer a Fundamental Right, a claim may be pursued under Article 226 or through an ordinary suit, rather than as an Article 32 Fundamental Rights petition.

The 2013 Act replaced the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and provides for mandatory Social Impact Assessment, 70 per cent consent for PPP projects, 80 per cent for private projects and return of unused land after five years.

secs.t: Article 30 - minority educational institutions, compensation clause

x: Article 30(1A) concerns compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution.
In Pramati, decided in 2014, the Supreme Court held that the RTE Act's 25 per cent quota does not apply to minority schools.
The cited NCPCR figure is
8.76 per cent
disadvantaged enrolment in minority schools.

secs.t: Fundamental vs constitutional/legal right - classification

x: Voting is based on adult suffrage under Article 326 and statutory provisions including Sections 62 of the RPA, 1951 and 19 of the RPA, 1950.

secs.t: Linguistic vs religious minority - determination

x: National notification brings a community within the National Commission for Minorities and makes it eligible under central minority schemes such as scholarships, PMJVK and PM VIKAS.
Article 350A directs States and local authorities to endeavour to provide adequate facilities for
instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Kerala Malayalam Bhasha Bill received assent in March 2026 and was contested on the ground that it could harm the Kannada linguistic minority in Kasaragod.
The stated concern is that FCRA amendments may pose a threat to minority-run civil society organisations.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court insisted on
strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A

rows.title: Right to Constitutional Remedies - Article 32; the five writs and their scope
sub: Group-II M1-B-15: Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30) and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32)

secs.t: Writ → literal meaning and purpose

x: Prohibition is issued by a higher court to prevent a lower court or tribunal with judicial or quasi-judicial functions from exceeding its jurisdiction.
Certiorari may be used to transfer a case from, or quash an order of, a lower court or authority.
The writs were borrowed from English law, where they were known as prerogative writs of the King, regarded as the fountain of justice.

secs.t: Writ → against whom it lies and does not lie

x: Mandamus may lie against public officials, public corporations, inferior courts, tribunals and government authorities, but not against the President or Governor for their official acts.
Quo Warranto may be sought by any interested person; personal aggrievement is not an essential requirement.
Quo Warranto examines the legality of a claim to a substantive public office created by the Constitution or a statute.

secs.t: Article 32 - right to move SC directly, "heart and soul", basic structure

x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
Dr. Ambedkar described
Article 32
as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower any other court to exercise powers within the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction, subject to constitutional conditions.

secs.t: Guardian of Fundamental Rights; number of writs

x: Before 1950, the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction.
Article 32(2) refers to
five
writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
Habeas Corpus
is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.

secs.t: Mandamus limits - making law, policy, private bodies

x: Mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies, for discretionary functions, legislative functions or non-statutory departmental instructions.
Habeas corpus
may be issued even against a private person who unlawfully detains another.
When a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, the same plea cannot ordinarily be raised before the Supreme Court under Article 32; the appropriate course is an appeal.

secs.t: Prohibition vs Certiorari

x: Prohibition is primarily preventive and stops a judicial or quasi-judicial body from continuing proceedings without or in excess of jurisdiction.
Certiorari is generally post-decision, but it may also be used to transfer a pending case.
Prohibition is a preventive writ issued during the pendency of proceedings.
Habeas corpus
safeguards personal liberty by requiring justification for a person's detention.

secs.t: Article 32 vs Article 226

x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
The Judiciary
is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has the constitutional role of protecting and guaranteeing those rights.
The 43rd Amendment repealed
Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A
, which had restricted the jurisdiction and powers of constitutional courts.

secs.t: Locus standi relaxation and PIL

x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.
Epistolary jurisdiction
refers to treating letters or postcards addressed to the court as writ petitions where they disclose a serious matter requiring judicial intervention.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 226 gives High Courts wider subject-matter jurisdiction by extending it to other purposes.
On 20 January 2026, a Supreme Court Bench comprising Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine the issue in appeals involving
Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling
The Supreme Court was examining an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings in matters involving threats to life and liberty, strengthening practical access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
