rows.title: Directive Principles of State Policy - Articles 36-51, classification, implementation
sub: Group-II M1-B-16: Directive Principles of State Policy - classification, content and implementation

secs.t: DPSP content → article

x: Exam angle: match directive → Article; "which is NOT a DPSP" statements (APPSC GS 2024 tested Art. 39A).
Article 38
directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.
Article 43A
directs the State to secure workers’ participation in the management of undertakings, establishments or other organisations engaged in industry.

After the 86th Amendment, Article 45 concerns early childhood care and education for children until they complete six years; education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
Article 48
directs the State to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines and provides the stated cattle-related objective.
Article 51
directs the State to promote international peace and security and to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.

secs.t: Justiciability - Article 37, guide to legislation

x: Article 37 expressly makes the Directive Principles non-enforceable by courts, while declaring them fundamental in governance and requiring the State to apply them in law-making.
However, non-enforceability arises from the express provision in Article 37; their role as a legislative guide does not explain the legal bar on enforcement.
Although DPSPs are not independently enforceable, courts use them as interpretive aids and have read several welfare-oriented principles into the scope of Article 21.

secs.t: Amendments adding or changing DPSP - chronological

x: Exam angle: APPSC G1 2024 asked two chronology questions on exactly these four changes.
The 42nd Amendment made the changes in C in 1976, the 44th Amendment made the change in D in 1978, the 86th Amendment changed Article 45 in 2002, and the 97th Amendment added Article 43B in 2011.
Article 43B was inserted as a Directive Principle to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of cooperative societies.

secs.t: Statements on DPSP → person

x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as a “novel feature” of the Indian Constitution.
K.C. Wheare
described the Directive Principles as a “manifesto of aims and aspirations.”.
Ivor Jennings
referred to the Directive Principles as “pious aspirations.”.

secs.t: Source country and antecedents

x: India borrowed the idea through the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution; it was not borrowed directly from Spain.
The Sapru Committee suggested dividing rights into justiciable and non-justiciable categories, an idea reflected later in the distinction between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.

secs.t: Article 39 clauses

x: Article 39(f)
directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment.
Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.

secs.t: Classification

x: Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under the Socialist principles.
Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46
are generally included among Gandhian principles.
Article 43B concerns the promotion of co-operative societies and is generally classified as a Gandhian principle.
The relevant Articles are 44 (Uniform Civil Code), 49 (monuments), 50 (separation of judiciary) and 51 (international peace), giving the order
B, D, A, C

secs.t: Common to DPSP and Fundamental Duties; directives outside Part IV

x: Article 351
directs the Union to promote the spread and development of Hindi so that it may serve as a medium of expression for all elements of the composite culture of India.

Several themes, including environmental protection, heritage, education and women’s dignity, appear in both the Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties, though the corresponding provisions are not always identical.

secs.t: Implementation - laws and programmes

x: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are implemented through land reforms and related laws; Article 40 through the 73rd Amendment; Article 39A through the Legal Services Authorities Act; and Article 41 through MGNREGA.
The Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B were used to protect land reform measures, including zamindari abolition and ceiling laws, from constitutional challenge.
Goa follows
the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867
, making it a distinctive example in discussions concerning a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.

All four statements correctly describe the features associated with the Gujarat UCC Bill, 2026: its position as the second State UCC, monogamy, equal inheritance, specified registration periods and exemption of Scheduled Tribes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court suggested a Uniform Civil Code as a means of addressing gender discrimination in personal laws in Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (2026).
The Supreme Court, while hearing a plea concerning Muslim inheritance law, considered whether to defer to Parliament on the implementation of
Article 44
relating to a Uniform Civil Code.
The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved
K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar

rows.title: Conflict and harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills
sub: Group-II M1-B-17: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and DPSP - Champakam, Golaknath, Kesavananda, Minerva Mills

secs.t: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down

x: The original Article 31C contained both protections: specified laws were protected from Articles 14, 19 and 31 challenges, and the declaration that they implemented the policy was placed beyond judicial questioning.
Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, which excluded judicial review.
The
Property Owners Association
decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.

secs.t: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology

x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.
Minerva Mills held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights in Part III and DPSPs in Part IV are part of the basic structure; absolute primacy to either would destroy that balance.
The correct sequence is A.K. Gopalan (1950), Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and Sanjeev Coke (1983).

secs.t: Amendments responding to courts

x: The First Amendment Act, 1951, followed Champakam and land-reform cases and inserted Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B, and the Ninth Schedule.
The Twenty-sixth Amendment responded to the Privy Purses case associated with Madhav Rao Scindia and abolished privy purses and the privileges of former rulers.
Minerva Mills struck down the extension because giving unlimited primacy to all DPSPs destroyed the constitutionally required harmony and balance between Parts III and IV.

secs.t: FR vs DPSP - differences

x: The source of Fundamental Rights is the Constitution of the United States of America, whereas the Directive Principles were inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.
Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and makes it the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.

secs.t: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

x: The Forty-Second Amendment, not the Forty-Fourth, attempted to extend Article 31C to all Directive Principles, and that extension was struck down.
Minerva Mills recognised that an Emergency proclamation is not wholly immune from judicial review.

secs.t: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

x: The validity of such a law is examined against the basic structure doctrine and, in particular, the constitutional guarantees represented by Articles 14, 19 and 21, known as the golden triangle.

The correct sequence is Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Waman Rao (1981), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007) only if arranged by the dates stated? Actually Minerva Mills was decided in 1980 and therefore precedes Waman Rao.

secs.t: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b).

The broad interpretation associated with Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy was followed in Sanjeev Coke, while the 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected its automatic application to every privately owned resource.

secs.t: Constitutional response to Champakam Dorairajan

x: Article 15(4)
was inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, to enable special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The amendment concerned Article 15, which deals with equality and non-discrimination, by inserting Article 15(4).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment belong to 1951, followed later by Minerva Mills and then I.R. Coelho in 2007.
Fundamental Rights were drawn from the United States, while the Directive Principles were inspired by Ireland.
Minerva Mills made the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles part of the Basic Structure.

rows.title: Fundamental Duties - Article 51A, Swaran Singh Committee, enforceability
sub: Group-II M1-B-18: Fundamental Duties - Article 51A, Swaran Singh Committee and enforceability

secs.t: Fundamental Duties list - Article 51A (a) to (k)

x: Exam angle: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" - check the list word for word.
Article 51A(a)
requires citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
Article 51A(k)
places this duty on a parent or guardian in respect of a child or ward aged six to fourteen years.
Article 51A(e) expressly refers to harmony and common brotherhood, whereas the Preamble uses the term fraternity.
Article 51A(a), concerning constitutional and national symbols, is classified as a civic duty, while Article 51A(b), concerning ideals of the freedom struggle, is classified as a moral duty.
Article 48A is a Directive Principle requiring the State to
protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife
Protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife are covered by Article 48A as a Directive Principle and Article 51A(g) as a Fundamental Duty.
Fraternity appears in the Preamble and is reflected in Article 51A(e), whereas Article 39 is not the listed DPSP location for fraternity.

secs.t: Swaran Singh Committee - year, members, duties suggested, suggestions dropped

x: The committee was set up by the Congress party in 1976, suggested eight duties, and the Forty-Second Amendment ultimately incorporated ten duties.
The proposal that laws imposing penalties for non-observance could not be challenged for violating Fundamental Rights or other constitutional provisions was not accepted.
The Constitution came into force first, followed by the Internal Emergency, the Forty-Second Amendment in 1976 and the Eighty-Sixth Amendment in 2002.

secs.t: Amendments → duty added and number; Part IVA

x: Exam angle: options mix 86th/96th and 2001/2002 - the answer is
The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added Article 51A(k), relating to educational opportunities for children or wards aged six to fourteen.
The Eighty-Sixth Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added the eleventh Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).

secs.t: Applicability - to whom; duty addressed to specific persons

x: Fundamental Duties are addressed to every citizen of India and do not extend to foreigners.
Article 51A(k) specifically addresses
parents or guardians
, requiring them to provide opportunities for education to children or wards within the constitutionally prescribed age group.
Corporations, being legal persons, have also been held capable of carrying the duty under Article 51A(g)
to protect and improve the natural environment

secs.t: Source country

x: The Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR.
Japan
's Constitution is identified as the only major democratic Constitution with a comparable list of citizens' duties.

secs.t: Enforceability - non-justiciable; legislation; Verma Committee

x: The
Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
gives statutory effect to aspects of Article 51A(a), concerning respect for the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
Imputations prejudicial to national integration are now dealt with under
Section 197
of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the corresponding earlier reference was Section 153B of the Indian Penal Code.
In Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Supreme Court held that Fundamental Duties cannot override Part III rights and that respectful conduct towards national symbols does not require compelled participation.

secs.t: Rights and duties - correlative

x: Rights and duties are treated as complementary.
Both statements are true, and the expectation that rights be exercised with restraint and respect for others explains why duties are regarded as the counterpart of rights.

secs.t: Criticism - vague, not exhaustive, placement

x: Direct judicial enforceability is not a criticism applicable to the list in that sense; it is a constitutional characteristic that the duties are non-justiciable.
Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and do not carry direct constitutional sanctions, they have been described as a code of moral precepts and, by critics, as superfluous.
The list is criticised as non-exhaustive because it does not expressly include duties such as
voting
, paying taxes and family planning.

secs.t: Duty inserted in which year → amendment (environment, forests, wildlife)

x: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the environmental duty in Article 51A(g), added DPSP Article 48A and moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List through Entries 17A and 17B.

The correct sequence is Stockholm Conference (1972), Wildlife (Protection) Act (1972), Forest (Conservation) Act (1980), and the 42nd Amendment (1976) would actually precede the 1980 Act; therefore the chronologically correct sequence among the listed events is D, A, B, C.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Fundamental Duties cannot be used to curtail the freedom of religion guaranteed under Articles 25 and 26; a Fundamental Duty does not automatically override a Fundamental Right.
The Vande Mataram debate concerns the relationship between religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26 and questions of participation or recitation in a national song.

rows.title: Amendment of the Constitution - Article 368, types of majorities, procedure, limitations
sub: Group-II M1-B-19: Amendment of the Constitution - Article 368, procedure and types of majority

secs.t: Amendment procedure - initiation, private member bill, no prior permission, no joint sitting, President's assent

x: Exam angle: "prior permission", "joint sitting" and "President may return" are all false for amendment bills.
Exam angle: statement sets on "private member needs prior permission" (false) and "joint sitting possible" (false).
India borrowed the amendment procedure from
South Africa
Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council
is provided for through a simple-majority procedure outside Article 368.
Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
The bill required 352 affirmative votes, representing two-thirds of 528 members present and voting, but received only 298.

secs.t: Article 368 and Part XX - addition, variation, repeal; who can amend Fundamental Rights

x: The correct sequence is Shankari Prasad (1951), Golaknath (1967), the 24th Amendment (1971), and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
Article 32 may be amended by special majority without ratification by the States, although the Supreme Court's power under it cannot be destroyed because it is part of the basic structure.
Creation of new States and alteration of the area, boundaries or names of States are dealt with under Articles 2, 3 and 4.

secs.t: Types of majority → provisions needing each (simple, special, special plus state ratification)

x: Different constitutional provisions are amended through different procedures: simple majority, special majority under Article 368, or special majority together with ratification by at least half of the States.
Laws made under Articles 2 to 4, including creation of new States, are passed by a simple majority and are not regarded as constitutional amendments for the purposes of Article 368.
The election of the President, the powers of the Supreme Court and High Courts, and the distribution of legislative powers require special majority plus ratification by at least half of the States.

secs.t: Provisions requiring state ratification - list, proportion, role of State Legislature

x: An amendment affecting specified federal provisions must be ratified by the Legislatures of not less than one-half of the States, using a simple majority in each Legislature.
In Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the provisions of Part IXB relating to State co-operative societies were struck down for want of ratification by the required number of States.

secs.t: Limitations - basic structure, 24th Amendment, judicial review of amendments

x: The 42nd Amendment inserted clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, declared the amending power unlimited and attempted to bar judicial review of constitutional amendments.
Golaknath was the first limitation of the amending power over Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the basic-structure doctrine; and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain first applied it.

secs.t: Amendments by simple majority outside Article 368 - which provisions

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT amended by special majority?" - official language, citizenship, Fifth/Sixth Schedule are simple-majority items.
Formation and alteration of States, Legislative Councils and official language provisions are among matters amendable by simple majority outside Article 368.
The relevant provisions are Article 11 for citizenship, Article 169 for Legislative Councils, Article 327 for elections and delimitation, and Article 343 for official language.

secs.t: Amendment procedure → source country and criticism

x: The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
Granville Austin
described the process as appearing complicated but being merely diverse.
The Constitution provides no joint sitting mechanism for resolving a deadlock between the Houses on an amendment Bill.

secs.t: Special majority - different meanings across Articles 368, 249, 312, 61

x: The Article 368 type of majority is used for removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, the CAG, the CEC and State Election Commissioners, constitutional amendment, and approval of a National Emergency.

The 131st Bill concerned women's reservation and delimitation, the Delimitation Bill was withdrawn, the 129th Bill was before a JPC, and the 130th Bill addressed continued detention of specified ministers for serious offences.

rows.title: Basic Structure doctrine - evolution and content; Kesavananda Bharati and after (Indira Gandhi, Minerva Mills, Waman Rao, I.R. Coelho)
sub: Group-II M1-B-21: Basic Structure of the Constitution - evolution, elements and later application

secs.t: Basic structure doctrine - meaning, absence of definition, judicial review and supremacy debate

x: Exam angle: statement sets testing "judge-made vs inserted by amendment" and "can Parliament amend FRs today" (yes, subject to basic structure).
The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
The doctrine is defended as a major contribution of the judiciary to constitutionalism because it checks the misuse of the amending power by a temporary majority.
Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable, but an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's basic structure.

secs.t: Case → contribution and chronological order

x: Exam angle: "In which case was basic structure first propounded?" - Kesavananda Bharati, not Golaknath or Shankari Prasad.

Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain was the first application; Minerva Mills invalidated clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368; Waman Rao fixed 24 April 1973; I.R. Coelho made post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws testable.
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain
(1975) marked the first application of the basic structure doctrine, and the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down; free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature.

secs.t: Ninth Schedule and basic structure - purpose, laws placed, Waman Rao cut-off, I.R. Coelho test

x: The Ninth Schedule has grown to more than 280 entries, but inclusion does not provide blanket immunity from judicial review, particularly after the decisions in Waman Rao and I.R. Coelho.
The Ninth Schedule was initially intended to protect
land-reform and zamindari-abolition laws
from challenges based on violation of Fundamental Rights.
Under the rights or direct-impact test, a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of the rights protected under
Articles 14, 19 and 21
I.R. Coelho (2007) held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are open to review if they damage the Basic Structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.

secs.t: Elements declared basic structure → case

x: Kesavananda Bharati recognised, among other elements, the
supremacy of the Constitution
as part of the basic structure.
Kesavananda Bharati associated
secularism, federalism and separation of powers
, among other constitutional principles, with the basic structure.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
(1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench, reaffirmed secularism and federalism as basic-structure principles.
In
Minerva Mills
(1980), the Supreme Court struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that sought to exclude judicial review.

secs.t: Amendments challenged or struck down on basic structure (39th, 42nd, 99th) → case

x: The 39th Amendment was challenged in
Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain
(1975), in which the provision placing the election of the Prime Minister beyond judicial scrutiny was struck down.

The First Judges Case recognised executive primacy; the Second created the two-senior-judge collegium; the Third enlarged it to four senior-most Judges; and the Fourth struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment.

secs.t: Kesavananda Bharati - bench strength, majority, overruled case

x: Kesavananda Bharati was decided by a 13-judge Constitution Bench, the largest bench constituted by the Supreme Court for this case.
The basic-structure doctrine was propounded in Kesavananda Bharati by a 7:6 majority.
The judgment in Kesavananda Bharati was delivered on
24 April 1973
, when S.M. Sikri was the Chief Justice of India.

secs.t: Origin of the doctrine idea - jurist and country

x: German jurist
Dietrich Conrad
argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.

secs.t: Doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court vs by Parliament

x: Pith and substance
is a judge-made interpretive doctrine evolved by the Supreme Court.
Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines.
The 42nd Amendment inserted Articles 368(4) and 368(5) to declare amendments non-justiciable and the amending power unlimited.
Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.

B.R. Gavai told the Joint Parliamentary Committee that the 129th Amendment Bill, 2024, did not violate the basic structure, whereas former Chief Justices U.U. Lalit and Sanjiv Khanna raised basic-structure doubts.

Articles 32, 141 and 142 provide the constitutional basis through which judicial decisions can fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts, as illustrated by Vishaka and Seema.

rows.title: Doctrines of constitutional interpretation - harmonious construction, colourable legislation, pith and substance, territorial nexus

secs.t: Doctrine → meaning in one line and field of application

x: Pith and substance examines the true nature and character of a law to determine legislative competence under the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
The doctrine of
pith and substance
is used to reconcile Central and Provincial, or Union and State, legislative powers by examining the true nature of the law.

secs.t: Doctrine → leading case (State of Bombay v Balsara, K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo, Venkataramana Devaru)

x: In State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara, the Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports.
State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. (1957)
concerned taxation of prize competitions run from outside the State and is associated with territorial nexus.
Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).

secs.t: Doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers, repugnancy - Article 254

x: R.D. Joshi v. Ajit Mills and the Calcutta Gas case are associated with the principle that an entry includes matters incidental and ancillary to it.
Article 254(2) permits a State law on a Concurrent List subject to prevail in that State when it has been reserved for and assented to by the President, subject to later Parliamentary override.

secs.t: Doctrines from judiciary and executive (prospective overruling, stare decisis, pleasure, separation of powers)

x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
Ram Jawaya Kapur was decided in 1955, State of Bombay v. R.M.D.C. in 1957, Golaknath in 1967 and Kesavananda Bharati in 1973.

secs.t: Doctrines borrowed from foreign law and origin country

x: The doctrine of pith and substance was borrowed from Canada.
Separation of powers is associated with Montesquieu of France, while the other three origins are Canada, the United States and England respectively.
The doctrine of public trust has its origin in
Roman law
The basic structure doctrine is identified with
Germany
as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.

secs.t: Constitutional morality and transformative constitutionalism as interpretive tools - case

x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality.
Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after
Grote
Constitutional morality was applied in
Navtej Johar
(2018), Sabarimala (2018) and NCT Delhi (2018).
Transformative constitutionalism treats the Constitution as an instrument for transforming an unequal society and advancing substantive constitutional values.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Critics argue that constitutional morality may be subjective and may provide a route to judicial overreach.
These doctrines make federal lawmaking workable and establish the manner in which Fundamental Rights operate in relation to legislation.
The current relevance assessment states that there is no 2025–26 ruling applying these doctrines by name.

rows.title: Structure of the Indian government - separation of powers and checks and balances
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-24

secs.t: Options against a judgment - override methods and their limits

x: Exam angle: "Parliament can overrule a judgment by a simple resolution" - false; it must change the law or the Constitution.
After I.R. Coelho, Ninth Schedule entries inserted after 24 April 1973 may be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
An ordinance is an executive law-making measure used when the legislature is not in session; it remains subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House.

secs.t: Constitutional government - definition and safeguards of liberty

x: Constitutional government is limited government: governmental power operates within the terms and limits of the Constitution.
Montesquieu held that
division of powers
was the most effective way to protect liberty.
Constitutionalism includes constitutional limits on power, rule of law, checks and balances, judicial review and protection of Fundamental Rights.

secs.t: Legislative checks on executive - subordination, responsibility, motions

x: The Council of Ministers is subordinate to the legislature and remains in office only while it enjoys the confidence of the
Lok Sabha
Question Hour, Zero Hour and discussions
enable day-to-day parliamentary scrutiny of administration.
A no-confidence motion concerns the Council of Ministers' collective responsibility and is moved only in the
Lok Sabha

secs.t: Separation of powers - Article 50 and the degree adopted

x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in
the public services of the State
India has legislature-executive fusion in the parliamentary system, while the judiciary is insulated through constitutional safeguards.
Articles 50, 121, 211 and 235 collectively reflect safeguards relating to judicial separation, discussion of judges and control of subordinate courts.

secs.t: Executive checks on legislature - summoning, dissolution, ordinances, veto

x: Article 85
deals with the summoning and prorogation of Parliament and the interval between its sessions.

Articles 86 and 87 concern presidential addresses and messages, Article 175 concerns the Governor's addresses and messages, Article 123 concerns Union ordinances, and Article 213 concerns State ordinances.
Article 111 concerns presidential assent, Article 200 concerns the Governor's assent, and Article 201 concerns Bills reserved for the President.

secs.t: Judicial checks - review, bar on discussing judges (Arts. 121, 211)

x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action; Articles 13, 32 and 226 provide important constitutional bases, and an ultra vires law is void.
Articles 122 and 212
prevent courts from inquiring into the validity of proceedings of Parliament or State Legislatures on the ground of irregular procedure.
The Vishaka guidelines, issued before the POSH Act, 2013, illustrate the use of Article 142 to fill a legal gap while pursuing complete justice.

secs.t: Separation of powers → case

x: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not provide for a rigid separation of powers.

Ram Jawaya Kapur dealt with the scope of executive power; Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain protected the judicial character of election disputes; Kesavananda Bharati recognised separation of powers among the basic features.

secs.t: Montesquieu - fusion vs separation in parliamentary and presidential systems

x: Montesquieu discussed the separation of powers in The Spirit of Laws, published in 1748.
The parliamentary system is characterised by fusion of powers, cooperation and coordination between the executive and legislature.
The presidential system is based on separation of powers and checks and balances among the three organs.
Ambedkar preferred
responsibility over stability

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed amendments concern Articles 83, 172 and 327, while the criticism relates to the possible weakening of collective responsibility under Articles 75 and 164.
Judicial overreach, frequent use of Article 142 and the ordinance route have been criticised as capable of eroding separation of powers.
The correct order is 1748, 1816, 1973 and 1975: The Spirit of Laws, separation of the Collector’s judicial powers, Kesavananda Bharati, and Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain.

rows.title: President of India - election, qualifications, term, impeachment; executive, legislative, financial, judicial powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-24: President of India - election, powers, veto and ordinance-making power

secs.t: Electoral college - who votes, who does not, value of vote

x: Article 55(3) prescribes proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote and voting by secret ballot.
The Presidential election method of proportional representation by single transferable vote was borrowed from
Ireland
Article 55(1) achieves these principles by assigning vote values to MLAs based on State population and distributing the aggregate MLA vote value among elected MPs.
The 1971 Census base remains frozen until
the first Census conducted after 2026
, as provided through the constitutional arrangement referred to in the 84th Amendment.
Article 71 protects acts done by the President in the performance of duties before the election is declared void; those acts do not become invalid merely because of the declaration.

secs.t: Articles 52-62 number game

x: Exam angle: "Removal of the President is under Article ___" - answer
Article 52 provides for the office of the President, Article 54 concerns the electoral college, Article 60 concerns the oath or affirmation, and Article 71 concerns election disputes.
The President can summon and prorogue Parliament, dissolve the Lok Sabha, summon a joint sitting, and send messages to either House.

Articles 54 and 55 concern the election of the President; Article 279A establishes the GST Council; the Fourth Schedule concerns representation of States in Parliament; Article 11 concerns citizenship.

secs.t: Qualifications, term, re-election, salary, oath, resignation

x: Article 58
prescribes the qualifications for election as President, including the condition that the person must not hold an office of profit under the Union, a State or a local or other authority.
The President swears
to preserve, protect and defend the Constitution and the law
, and to devote himself or herself to the service and well-being of the people of India.

secs.t: Impeachment - Article 61

x: Article 61 provides impeachment only for
violation of the Constitution
The notice of the impeachment charge must be signed by at least one-fourth of the members of the House in which the charge is initiated, and fourteen days' notice is required.
The Constitution specifically includes Delhi and Puducherry, while Union Territories without Assemblies do not participate.

secs.t: Powers of the President - statement based

x: Articles 72, 143 and 352 correspond respectively to the pardoning power, consultation with the Supreme Court and National Emergency.
The relevant articles are Article 72 for pardoning power, Article 123 for ordinances, Article 143 for consultation with the Supreme Court and Article 360 for Financial Emergency.
All four pairings are correct: Articles 148, 155, 76 and 324 respectively concern the CAG, Governors, Attorney General, and the Election Commission.

secs.t: Position - constitutional head, Article 74

x: Article 74
(1) provides that there shall be a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.
The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister, heading the Council of Ministers, functions as the real or de facto executive.
Article 74(2) provides that the question, if any, and what advice was tendered by Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.

secs.t: Vacancy - election time limit and acting President

x: While acting as President, the Vice-President ceases to perform the functions of the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; the Deputy Chairman presides.
Unlike a casual vacancy in the office of the President, Article 68 does not prescribe a six-month deadline for filling a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
When both offices are vacant,
the Chief Justice of India
acts as President; in the absence of the CJI, the senior-most Supreme Court judge performs the function.

secs.t: Presidents of India - order and FIRSTs

x: Zakir Husain
, who served from 1967 to 1969, was the first President of India to die in office.
After Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed died in office,
B.D. Jatti
acted as President.
N. Sanjiva Reddy assumed office in 1977, K.R. Narayanan in 1997, Pratibha Patil in 2007 and Droupadi Murmu in 2022.

secs.t: Pardoning power - Article 72 vs 161

x: Maru Ram (1980)
established that the President exercises the pardoning power on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
Kehar Singh and Epuru Sudhakar recognised limited judicial review where the exercise is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant grounds.
Commutation
substitutes a lighter form of punishment, such as changing death sentence to rigorous imprisonment.
In Kehar Singh (1989), the Supreme Court held that the President may examine the evidence afresh, but there is no right to an oral hearing.
Epuru Sudhakar held that clemency may be reviewed when it is mala fide, arbitrary or based on irrelevant or extraneous considerations.

secs.t: Veto types → Bills

x: The absolute veto involves withholding assent and is relevant to Private Members’ Bills and Government Bills when the Cabinet resigns before assent.
Pocket veto means keeping a Bill pending without taking a decision.
The Twenty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill duly passed by Parliament.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Articles 65 and 68
deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President.
The resignation of Jagdeep Dhankhar and the election of C. P. Radhakrishnan constituted the
third mid-term vacancy in the office of Vice-President
Article 87

provides for the President’s special address to both Houses assembled together at the commencement of the first session after each general election and the first session of each year, including the Budget Session context.

rows.title: Veto powers and the ordinance-making power (Article 123); pardoning power (Article 72)

secs.t: Ordinance - Article 123

x: The maximum possible life of an Ordinance is six months plus six weeks, linked to the interval between parliamentary sessions and the post-reassembly period.
The seven-judge Bench in Krishna Kumar Singh held that re-promulgation is unconstitutional, laying the Ordinance before the House is mandatory, and the satisfaction is justiciable.
In
D.C. Wadhwa
(1987), repeated re-promulgation without placing Ordinances before the legislature was characterised as a fraud on the Constitution.

secs.t: Pocket veto - meaning and use

x: A pocket veto consists of taking no action—neither assent, rejection nor return—thereby keeping the Bill pending indefinitely.
Article 111 does not prescribe a time limit for the President's action, unlike the ten-day rule referred to in the United States context.
The Supreme Court held in 2025 that indefinite inaction by the Governor under Article 200 is justiciable; therefore, the Governor does not possess a presidential-style pocket veto.

secs.t: Veto over money and constitutional amendment bills

x: In relation to a Money Bill, the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration.
The 24th Amendment, 1971 made presidential assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory; the President cannot reject or return it.
The return power is one-time and may apply to Financial Bills of Categories I and II.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
Frequent ordinances are criticised because
they bypass parliamentary deliberation
The US President has only a qualified veto, which can be overridden by a two-thirds majority of Congress.
A Governor's ordinance-making power for a State is exercised under
Article 213
; the Andhra Pradesh ordinance concerned organ-transplant committees.

rows.title: Vice-President; Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers - Articles 74, 75, 77, 78
sub: Group-II M1-B-25: Vice-President, Prime Minister and the Union Council of Ministers

secs.t: Vice-President - election, term, removal, ex-officio role, disputes

x: Exam angle: "Who elects the VP" (both Houses only) and "Where can the removal resolution first be moved" (Rajya Sabha).
Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with exclusive authority to decide doubts and disputes concerning Presidential and Vice-Presidential elections.
The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
Article 66 provides for proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and the election is conducted by secret ballot.
The Vice-President holds office for five years from the date of entering office and continues beyond that period until the successor enters office.
A minimum notice of
14 days
is required before moving the resolution for removal of the Vice-President in the Rajya Sabha.
When acting as President, the Vice-President ceases to function as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and draws the President’s salary rather than the Chairman’s salary.
The Chairman of the Rajya Sabha does not vote in the first instance but has a casting vote when the votes are equally divided.

secs.t: Size of the Council of Ministers - 91st Amendment and ranks

x: The 91st Amendment inserted Article 75(1A), limiting the Union Council of Ministers including the Prime Minister to
15 per cent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha
Article 75(1B), inserted by the 91st Amendment, prevents a member disqualified for defection from being appointed a minister until re-elected to Parliament.
The
91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003
inserted Article 164(1A), which prescribes the upper and lower limits for the State Council of Ministers.

secs.t: Article 75(5) - non-member minister

x: Article 75(5) requires a non-member Minister to become a member of either House of Parliament within six consecutive months; otherwise, the person ceases to be a Minister.
The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.
The six-month rule applies to the Prime Minister as well.

secs.t: Articles 74, 77, 78 - content

x: Exam angle: "All work of the GoI is done in the name of the President" - Art 77.

Article 74(2) concerns non-inquiry into ministerial advice; Article 77(1) concerns expression in the President's name; Article 77(2) concerns authentication; and Article 77(3) concerns transaction and allocation of business rules.
The provisions occur in the order Article 74(1), Article 75(3), Article 77(1) and Article 78: advice, collective responsibility, executive expression and Prime Ministerial duties.

secs.t: Prime Minister - appointment, qualifications, oath, real executive

x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
The President is the de jure head of the State, while the Prime Minister functions as the de facto head of government.
Article 75(2) provides that Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, which operates in practice on the advice of the Prime Minister.

secs.t: Prime Ministers - FIRSTs and unique facts

x: H.D. Deve Gowda, I.K. Gujral and Manmohan Singh were Prime Ministers from the Rajya Sabha.
A.B. Vajpayee
had the shortest tenure of a regular Prime Minister, lasting 13 days in 1996.
Narendra Modi was reported as the longest continuously serving elected Prime Minister on 10 June 2026, while Jawaharlal
Nehru retains the record for maximum aggregate days as Prime Minister
S. Radhakrishnan became President in 1962, Zakir Husain in 1967, V.V. Giri in 1969 and K.R. Narayanan in 1997.
C.P. Radhakrishnan
was elected Vice-President after the mid-term vacancy caused by Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation in July 2025.

secs.t: Deputy PM and Leader of the House - status

x: The office of Deputy Prime Minister is not mentioned in the Constitution; the Deputy Prime Minister takes oath as an ordinary Minister, Sardar Patel was the first, and the office has rank 5A in the Table of Precedence.
The Prime Minister’s Office is not mentioned in the Constitution; it is an extra-constitutional staff agency assisting the Prime Minister.

secs.t: Categories of ministers - Cabinet, MoS (independent charge), MoS, Deputy Minister

x: A Cabinet Minister heads an important ministry and attends Cabinet meetings; a Minister of State with independent charge heads a ministry independently; a Minister of State is attached to a Cabinet Minister; and a Deputy Minister assists a senior Minister.
The Constitution does not itself classify Ministers into these categories; the classification and ranking operate through convention, with the Prime Minister determining the arrangement.

secs.t: Executive power in practice - nominal vs real, Business Rules

x: The President is the nominal or de jure executive and Head of State, whereas the Prime Minister is the real or de facto executive and Head of Government.
Article 77(1) requires all executive action of the Government of India to be expressed in the name of the
President
Article 77(3) is implemented through the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 and the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ravneet Singh Bittu’s resignation on 24 July 2026 was associated with
Article 75(2)
, which concerns Ministers holding office during the pleasure of the President.
The proposal contemplated removal on the
31st day
after 30 consecutive days of detention for an offence punishable with imprisonment of five years or more.
The Bill dealt with prolonged detention of specified executive office-holders, a five-year punishment threshold, and referral to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

rows.title: Cabinet system, Cabinet committees, collective and individual responsibility; Attorney General of India
sub: Group-II M1-B-26: Cabinet system in India - functioning, committees and collective responsibility

secs.t: Parliamentary vs presidential system - features of India's form

x: Majority party rule, collective responsibility and the Prime Minister as the centre of power are necessary features of India’s parliamentary form.
Nominal and real executives, majority party rule and ministerial membership of the legislature characterise the parliamentary system.
Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers
to the elected House is the characteristic feature distinguishing the parliamentary system.

secs.t: Collective responsibility

x: The Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the
Lok Sabha
; therefore, a no-confidence motion is moved only in the Lok Sabha.
The
oath of secrecy
ensures confidentiality of Cabinet deliberations and supports the public presentation of a united government.
Even a minister who is a member of the Rajya Sabha is part of the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the
Lok Sabha
A resigned minister may make a personal statement in the House explaining the resignation with the
Speaker
’s consent.

secs.t: Cabinet - word in Constitution; cabinet vs council

x: The word ‘Cabinet’ appears only in
Article 352
, which deals with a Proclamation of Emergency and the written advice of the Union Cabinet.
The Cabinet is the smaller nucleus consisting of Cabinet Ministers; it takes policy decisions and directs and supervises the wider Council of Ministers.
Both statements are true, and the smaller composition and supervisory role of the Cabinet explain why it functions as the effective policy-making nucleus.

secs.t: Cabinet Secretariat and Cabinet Secretary

x: The Cabinet Secretariat has Civil, Military and Intelligence Wings and is associated with the Directorate of Public Grievances and the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser.
The National Authority CWC is listed among the wings or associated offices of the
Cabinet Secretariat
The Cabinet Secretary is first among equals among Secretaries, is placed eleventh in the Table of Precedence and heads the National Crisis Management Committee.

secs.t: Cabinet committees - chair and function

x: Cabinet Committees are
extra-constitutional bodies formed under the Transaction of Business Rules, 1961
, framed under Article 77(3).

The Appointments Committee deals with senior appointments; the Security Committee with defence and national security; the Economic Affairs Committee with economic and infrastructure projects; and the Parliamentary Affairs Committee with parliamentary business.
These two committees were set up in 2019 to
speed up investment and job creation
, including employment and skilling.

secs.t: Organisation of government - Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee, business rules

x: The N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar Committee submitted a 1949 report on the
reorganisation of the machinery of government
The 1949 report concerned reorganisation of the machinery of government, including grouping ministries and Cabinet Committees.
The First Schedule to the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 concerns the allocation of subjects to ministries.

secs.t: Kitchen cabinet - meaning and role

x: A kitchen cabinet is an informal inner circle consisting of trusted colleagues and friends of the Prime Minister, including some senior ministers and non-ministers.
The kitchen cabinet is criticised as an extra-constitutional power centre because it may shape decisions while bypassing the formal Cabinet.
The advisers around Indira Gandhi are cited as an example of a Prime Minister's
kitchen cabinet

secs.t: Attorney General - Article 76

x: Article 88 permits the Attorney General to speak and participate in either House, joint sittings and parliamentary committees, but does not confer a right to vote.
Article 105(4) extends parliamentary privileges and immunities to a person who has the right to speak or otherwise take part in parliamentary proceedings without being a member.
Article 88
confers the Attorney General's right to speak and take part in parliamentary proceedings without the right to vote.

secs.t: AG vs Solicitor General - legal status

x: The Constitution does not fix the Attorney General’s term.
The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet recommends the Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General, and the President appoints them.
Article 177
gives the Advocate General the right to speak and participate in the proceedings of the State Legislature, without a right to vote.

secs.t: Cabinet dominance - single-party vs coalition eras

x: During single-party majority eras, the Prime Minister and Cabinet generally dominate Parliament, leading to the criticism that the system may resemble a ‘cabinet dictatorship’.
The coalition era identified here is the period from 1989 to 2014.
Coalition governments had to accommodate coordination committees and the demands of alliance partners.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Excessive concentration of power in the PMO and Cabinet committees is criticised for diluting collective Cabinet decision-making.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs approved the third and fourth railway lines on the
Ballari–Guntakal section
at a cost of Rs 1,264 crore.
The Cabinet papers relating to the caste-census decision were held exempt under
Section 8(1)(i)
of the Right to Information Act.

rows.title: Types of legislatures - unicameral and bicameral; arguments for a second chamber
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-28

secs.t: Upper and lower house names in other countries

x: The United Kingdom has the House of Lords as its upper house and the House of Commons as its lower house.
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Russia's Parliament is the
Federal Assembly

secs.t: Unicameral vs bicameral - definitions and countries

x: India's Parliament is bicameral, comprising the Council of States or Rajya Sabha and the House of the People or Lok Sabha.
China, Israel, New Zealand, Sweden and Denmark are examples of countries with unicameral national legislatures.
Bicameralism is often preferred in large and diverse countries because two Houses can represent different sections, interests and regions.

secs.t: Arguments for and against a second chamber

x: A second chamber is argued to provide a double check, regional representation and expert participation.
The criticism of a second chamber expressed in these words is attributed to
Abbé Sieyès
Ayyangar regarded the Rajya Sabha as a forum for dignified debate that could delay legislation passed in the passion of the moment.
Nehru cautioned against the judiciary assuming the role of a “
third chamber

secs.t: Rajya Sabha as federal chamber - compared with the US Senate

x: Rajya Sabha seats are allocated broadly according to population under the Fourth Schedule, while every US State has two Senators, making 100 Senators in all.
The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill and must return it within 14 days.
A no-confidence motion is a device of the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Bicameralism in states - Art. 169 basis and practice

x: The Assembly resolution must be passed by a majority of the total membership and by a majority of not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
Article 169 empowers Parliament to create or abolish a State Legislative Council by law after the State Assembly passes the prescribed resolution.
Under Article 171, a Legislative Council cannot have more than one-third of the total membership of the Legislative Assembly and cannot have fewer than 40 members.

secs.t: Legislatures in UTs - Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir

x: Delhi's special constitutional arrangement, including its Legislative Assembly, is based on
Article 239AA, inserted by the 69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991
Delhi has 70 Assembly seats, Puducherry has 30 elected members and up to 3 nominated members, and Jammu and Kashmir has 90 elected seats.
Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir
are the three Union Territories having elected members in the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Bangladesh voted in the February 2026 referendum for a bicameral Parliament with a 100-member upper House elected according to party vote share.
Since a joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker and voting strength depends on the combined membership, a larger Lok Sabha would dilute the Rajya Sabha's relative weight.

rows.title: Parliament - composition of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, qualifications, terms, special powers of Rajya Sabha
sub: Group-II M1-B-27: Parliament - composition of the two Houses, qualifications and terms
Group-II M1-B-29: Functions and powers of Parliament; special powers of the Rajya Sabha

secs.t: Rajya Sabha - strength, election, retirement, Fourth Schedule, nominated members

x: Article 80 fixes the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250, comprising 238 representatives of States and Union Territories and 12 nominated members.
The present strength is 245:
225 representatives of States, 8 representatives of Union Territories and 12 nominated members
Twelve members may be nominated to the Rajya Sabha from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in the specified fields.
A nominated member may join a political party within
six months of taking the seat
Nominated Rajya Sabha members can participate fully in debates and vote in the election of the Vice-President, but they cannot vote in the election of the President.
Sachin Tendulkar was nominated in 2012 and Mary Kom in 2016.
The correct order is Uttar Pradesh (31), Maharashtra (19), West Bengal (16) and Tamil Nadu (18) — wait, numerically Tamil Nadu has 18 and therefore must precede West Bengal.
Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura each have one Rajya Sabha seat.

secs.t: Lok Sabha - maximum and present strength, seats by State, Anglo-Indians

x: Article 81 provides for a maximum of 550 members in the Lok Sabha: 530 from the States and 20 from the Union Territories.
The
104th Amendment Act, 2019
ended the provision for nomination of up to two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha, with effect from 25 January 2020.
Article 331 permitted the President to nominate up to
two
Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha if the community was not adequately represented.
The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 froze the allocation of Lok Sabha seats based on the 1971 Census until
the first Census after 2026

secs.t: Qualifications and disqualifications

x: A prospective Member of Parliament makes the prescribed oath or affirmation before
the Election Commission or a person authorised by it
, in the form given in the Third Schedule.
Article 102 includes office of profit, unsoundness of mind declared by a court, undischarged insolvency, loss or absence of Indian citizenship and disqualification under a parliamentary law.
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha or the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha decides such questions, subject to judicial review.
A vote or abstention contrary to the party whip may attract disqualification unless the action is permitted or condoned by the party within
15 days
A person elected to both Houses must intimate the choice within 10 days; otherwise, the Rajya Sabha seat falls vacant.
Under the Prohibition of Simultaneous Membership Rules, 1950, the State Legislature seat must be resigned within 14 days; otherwise the seat in Parliament becomes vacant.
Resignation is addressed to the Speaker or Chairman, may be rejected when it is not voluntary or genuine, and absence without permission for 60 days can lead the House to declare the seat vacant.

secs.t: Parliament's components - Article 79

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason - "Parliament consists of the President and two Houses" with the opening-address reason (both true, R explains A).
Article 86 enables the President to
address either House of Parliament or both Houses assembled together
and to send messages to them.
The President’s assent is necessary for a Bill to become law, and the President also summons, prorogues and addresses Parliament and may dissolve the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Equal and unequal status of Rajya Sabha

x: Under Article 67(b), a resolution for initiating the removal of the Vice-President can be moved only in the Rajya Sabha, though the Lok Sabha must agree to it.
Article 108 does not apply to constitutional amendment bills and no joint sitting can resolve a disagreement between the Houses.
There is no provision for a joint sitting in respect of a Constitutional Amendment Bill; therefore, rejection by either House causes failure.
The Bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 members present, but this was below the special majority required for a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

secs.t: Special powers of Rajya Sabha - Articles 249, 312, 67(b)

x: When the Lok Sabha is dissolved, the Rajya Sabha may approve the Emergency proclamation for the time being.
Article 312
enables Parliament to create new All-India Services on the basis of a Rajya Sabha resolution passed by the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
The numerical order is Article 67(b), Article 249, Article 250 and Article 312.
The prior recommendation of the
President
is necessary for introducing a Bill under Article 3.
Removal is initiated in the Rajya Sabha, requires a majority of all the then members of that House, and must be agreed to by the Lok Sabha by simple majority.

secs.t: Women representation in Lok Sabha

x: Women members crossed 10 per cent of the total strength of the House for the first time in the
15th Lok Sabha
, elected in 2009.
The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam is the
106th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2023
, providing for one-third reservation of seats for women in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies.
Women MPs declined from 78 in the 17th Lok Sabha in 2019 to 74 in the 18th Lok Sabha in 2024; the approximate share fell from 14.4 per cent to 13.6 per cent.

secs.t: Term of each House - early dissolution, emergency extension, permanence of RS

x: The
Fifth Lok Sabha
, constituted for the period 1971–1977, was extended during the 1975–1977 Emergency.
The Fourth, Sixth, Eleventh and Twelfth Lok Sabhas were dissolved prematurely in 1970, 1979, 1997 and 1999 respectively.
The six-year term of a Rajya Sabha member is fixed by the
Representation of the People Act, 1951
, and not directly by the Constitution.
To initiate the one-third retirement cycle, the terms of the initial members were curtailed and the members retiring first were decided by
lottery

secs.t: Sessions - summoning, number in a year, maximum gap

x: The Constitution does not prescribe a fixed calendar or exact number of sessions, though Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions are normally held.
An adjournment sine die is ordered by the Speaker in the Lok Sabha or the Chairman in the Rajya Sabha, without fixing a date for the next sitting.

secs.t: Parliamentary privileges - Art. 105, collective and individual, Art. 122

x: Exam angle: "only members enjoy privileges, not the House" is the
incorrect
statement.
The power to punish members and outsiders for breach of privilege or contempt is exercised by the House as a whole and is therefore collective.
Article 122 bars courts from questioning parliamentary proceedings on the ground of alleged
procedural irregularity
The seven-judge Bench in Sita Soren (2024) held that privilege does not protect bribery for voting or speaking and overruled the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao.
Freedom from arrest applies to civil cases during the prescribed period; it does not extend to criminal or preventive detention cases.
No arrest or legal process may be undertaken within the precincts of the House without the permission of its Presiding Officer.

secs.t: Session terminology

x: Adjournment
suspends a sitting for a specified period.
Prorogation ends a session, while dissolution ends the life of the Lok Sabha.
Normally, the Speaker or Chairman first adjourns the House sine die; the President then prorogues it, followed by a recess and later reassembly in a new session.

secs.t: Functions of Parliament

x: Questions, motions and a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha are instruments of parliamentary control over the executive.
The listed functions are included among the judicial or quasi-judicial functions of Parliament, though their procedures differ according to the office concerned.
The six-month limit prevents an excessively long interruption and helps maintain legislative business and executive accountability.

secs.t: Procedural provisions - Articles

x: Article 86
deals with the President's right to address and send messages to either House of Parliament.
Article 118
empowers each House to make rules for regulating its procedure and conduct of business.
Article 120 recognises Hindi and English for parliamentary business and permits the use of a member's mother tongue with the presiding officer's permission.

secs.t: Electoral functions

x: The Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses, including nominated members.
The Representation of the People Acts of 1950 and 1951 and the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 relate to election law.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed expansion has generated concern in southern States because the relative representation of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Rajasthan may increase after the 1971-based freeze is lifted.
The Bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against among 528 members present, falling short of the special majority required under Article 368.
The Tamil Nadu Assembly resolved to retain the Lok Sabha at 543 seats and preserve the approximate 2.2:1 Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio.
The resolution seeking removal of Speaker Om Birla was moved under
Article 94(c)
and was rejected by voice vote on 11 March 2026.
The inquiry report concerning former Allahabad High Court judge Yashwant Varma was to be tabled despite his resignation.

The Andhra State was created in 1953, the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act was enacted in 2014, the constitutional amendment Bill was introduced in April 2026, and the Rajya Sabha elections were held in June 2026.

rows.title: Presiding officers - Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman; Secretariat; sessions, adjournment, prorogation, dissolution

secs.t: Termination of sittings - adjournment, sine die, prorogation, dissolution

x: Adjournment sine die terminates a sitting without fixing a date for the next sitting.
The President prorogues Parliament and prorogation terminates the session.
A bill for which a joint sitting has been notified before dissolution does not lapse merely on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Sessions - Article 85, six-month rule, quorum

x: Article 85 requires that the gap between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next session must not exceed
six months
By convention, the Budget Session from February to May is generally the longest, the Monsoon Session is held from July to September, and the Winter Session from November to December.

secs.t: Speaker - election, removal, resignation, dissolution, casting vote

x: The salaries and allowances of the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are charged on the
Consolidated Fund of India
under Article 97.
Removal motions against G. V. Mavalankar in 1954, Hukum Singh in 1966 and Balram Jakhar in 1987 failed.
The motion against Om Birla was signed by
118 Opposition MPs
and was listed for debate on 9 March 2026.

secs.t: Speaker's powers

x: Article 110(3) gives
the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
the final authority to decide whether a bill is a Money Bill.
The Speaker’s decisions under the Tenth Schedule remain subject to judicial review, and the Speaker also performs the listed recognition, committee and ruling-related functions.
Recognition of the Leader of the Opposition requires the party to have at least one-tenth of the strength of the House, according to the Speaker’s direction.

secs.t: Chairman and Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha

x: The Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman and may be removed by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by an effective majority after fourteen days’ notice.
In January 2026, the Supreme Court upheld, in the
Justice Varma case
, the Deputy Chairman’s power under Article 91 to decide on a judge-removal motion when the Chairman’s office was vacant.

secs.t: Deputy Speaker and panel of chairpersons

x: The Speaker nominates a Panel of Chairpersons consisting of up to ten members.
A panel member may preside in the absence of both the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
The Lok Sabha Deputy Speaker post has been vacant since June 2019.
The office of Deputy Speaker was reported to have remained vacant in the Jharkhand Legislative Assembly for
21 years

secs.t: President's address - Articles 86 and 87

x: Article 86 empowers the President to address either House or both Houses together, require members' attendance and send messages to either House regarding pending Bills.
Article 87 provides for the President’s special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year.
The President’s address outlining Government policy is debated through a
Motion of Thanks
in Parliament.

secs.t: Parliament secretariats - Article 98

x: Article 98 provides for separate secretarial staff for each House, permits common posts, authorises Parliament to regulate recruitment by law and allows the President to make rules after consultation with the Speaker and Chairman until such a law is made.
In the absence of a law by Parliament, the President may make rules after consulting the Speaker of the Lok Sabha and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Only
two
oral answers were recorded in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon Session of 2026, a point cited in criticism concerning low scrutiny.
Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the Speaker, Kalluri Subbarao was the Deputy Speaker, and Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Council Chairman in the first Andhra Pradesh Assembly of 1956.

rows.title: Parliamentary devices - Question Hour, Zero Hour, motions (adjournment, no-confidence, censure, calling attention)
sub: Group-II M1-B-31: Parliamentary committees and parliamentary devices

secs.t: Zero Hour - timing, notice, duration, origin, Rules status

x: Exam angle: "time after Question Hour when members raise matters without prior notice" = Zero Hour.
Zero Hour has no fixed duration in the Rules and in the Lok Sabha lasts until the day's regular agenda is taken up.
The
Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
sends the relevant extract to the concerned Ministry when the Chair issues a direction or an assurance is given.

secs.t: No-confidence motion - constitutional status, support, reasons, Speaker's role, instances

x: A no-confidence motion is moved under
Rule 198
of the Rules of Procedure of the Lok Sabha.
The motion was moved in November 1954, the Prakasam ministry fell by one vote, President's Rule was imposed on 16 November 1954, and it ended on 27 March 1955.
A no-confidence motion directly
enforces the collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha

secs.t: Question Hour - timing, types of questions, answers, notice

x: Question Hour is held during
the first hour of every sitting
of the Lok Sabha, when Ministers answer questions.
A short-notice question is one for which notice is given
less than 10 days in advance
Question Hour
is regarded as the most effective method of day-to-day vigilance over the executive because Ministers are required to answer questions.

secs.t: Tools of parliamentary control over the executive

x: Judicial review is a constitutional function of the judiciary, not a parliamentary device listed among the tools of legislative control over the executive.
Question Hour, Calling Attention motion, the committee system, budget approval and the Motion of Thanks are all tools of parliamentary control over the executive.
State Legislatures use the same parliamentary devices for executive control and also use estimates and public accounts committees.

secs.t: Point of order, closure, guillotine, yielding the floor

x: Under closure by compartments, clauses are grouped into parts, with debate and voting taking place part by part.
Guillotine refers to putting all pending clauses to vote when the allotted time expires, including clauses that have not been discussed.
Yielding the floor
occurs when the member speaking gives way to another member or to the Chair.

secs.t: Office of Whip - basis, functions, types

x: A party Whip enforces party discipline regarding attendance and voting, and defiance in relevant circumstances may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
A one-line Whip is informative, a two-line Whip directs members to attend, and a three-line Whip gives a strict voting direction.
All three dates are correct: 4 March 1997 for the Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee, 16 May 2000 for the Lok Sabha Ethics Committee and 29 April 1997 for the Committee on Empowerment of Women.

secs.t: Motions - House, requirement; censure vs no-confidence

x: "reasons must be stated" = censure motion.
An Adjournment Motion sets aside the normal business of the House to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance.
An Adjournment Motion is a Lok Sabha device, requires 50 members' support, carries an element of censure and involves debate of at least two hours and thirty minutes.
Privilege matters are governed by Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha; cut motions relate to demands for grants, while Calling Attention is available in both Houses.
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
decides whether a No-confidence Motion is in order and admits or rejects it.
A policy cut reduces the demand to Re 1, an economy cut reduces it by a specified amount, and a token cut reduces it by Rs 100 to raise a specific grievance.

secs.t: Rules of Procedure devices - rule numbers

x: Zero Hour follows Question Hour, allows members to raise important matters without prior notice, does not bind Ministers to reply and is not included in the Rules of Procedure.
Rule 377 and Special Mentions serve corresponding purposes in the two Houses, while Rules 193 and 184 distinguish discussions without and with voting respectively.

secs.t: Resolutions - private member, government, statutory; AP equivalents

x: A resolution is a self-contained proposal and always takes the form of a substantive motion.
Private Members’ Resolutions are taken up on alternate Fridays during the afternoon.
The Andhra Pradesh Legislature uses the same broad parliamentary devices, including private member, government and statutory resolutions.
A Government Resolution may be moved by a minister for purposes such as approving treaties.

secs.t: Financial committees (PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings) - membership, chair, CAG reports

x: Exam angle: "which committee has no Rajya Sabha member" = Estimates; "examines CAG reports" = PAC (and CPU for PSUs).
The Public Accounts Committee has 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha members, elected annually by proportional representation through the single transferable vote.
The Public Accounts Committee checks whether money was spent within the scope of the relevant demand and highlights waste, loss and nugatory expenditure.
The Estimates Committee suggests economies, efficiency, administrative reforms, alternative policies and improvements in the form of estimates.

secs.t: Committee → nickname or role

x: The Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee, Committee on Public Undertakings, Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances and Department-related Standing Committees are described as watchdogs over the executive.
The
Committee on Government Assurances
tracks assurances and promises made by ministers until implementation.
The Committee on Papers Laid on the Table checks papers laid by ministers, other than statutory orders, for compliance.

secs.t: Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs

x: No minister can be a member of the Committee
on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

secs.t: Committee oversight linked to reform areas

x: Kasturirangan is linked with education and the 5+3+3+4 structure, Urjit Patel with inflation targeting at 4% plus or minus 2%, and Shanta Kumar with FCI/PDS reform including decentralised procurement and DBT for food.
Ashok Dalwai’s reform area concerns doubling farmers’ income, including value addition and land leasing.

secs.t: DRSCs, ad hoc, select and joint committees

x: The Speaker appoints the Chairpersons of Lok Sabha DRSCs, while the Chairman appoints the Chairpersons of Rajya Sabha DRSCs.
Inquiry committees may be created by a motion or by the Speaker or Chairman; the Committee on MPLADS is an example.
Business Advisory, Petitions, Privileges and Rules are examples of permanent Standing Committees.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The resolution/no-confidence motion against Speaker Om Birla was dismissed by
voice vote
Article 94(c), the fourteen-day notice requirement, support of fifty members and Lok Sabha Rules 200–203 govern the removal procedure.
The Calling Attention device dates to 1954, Zero Hour to 1962, the privilege notice to May 2026, and the PAC’s first meeting to 26 May 2026.
