rows.title: Legislative procedure - ordinary, money, financial and constitutional amendment bills; joint sitting
sub: Group-II M1-B-30: Legislative procedure - ordinary, money and financial bills; joint sitting

secs.t: Money Bill - Article 110 contents, introduction, Speaker's certificate, 14 days, Aadhaar case

x: A Money Bill may deal with the imposition, abolition, remission, alteration or regulation of a tax.
All three statements describe matters covered by Article 110(1), including Public Account custody, receipt or audit of Consolidated Fund money, and incidental matters.
The Speaker's decision is final under Article 110(3), and the certificate is endorsed on the Bill sent to the Rajya Sabha and presented to the President.
When the Rajya Sabha does not return a Money Bill within 14 days, it is
deemed to have been passed by both Houses in the form passed by the Lok Sabha

secs.t: Stages of an ordinary bill - readings, committee, transmission, assent

x: The committee stage forms part of the
Second Reading
, along with general discussion and consideration of the Bill clause by clause.
The second House may pass, amend or reject an ordinary Bill, or keep it pending for six months, potentially creating a deadlock.
Since no fixed time limit is prescribed for presidential action, the President may keep an ordinary Bill pending indefinitely, a situation known as a
pocket veto
A suspensive veto permits return of a non-money Bill; if Parliament repasses it, with or without amendment, the President must assent.

secs.t: Joint sitting - Article 108

x: Article 108
provides for a joint sitting to resolve specified deadlocks between the two Houses over an ordinary Bill.
Periods of prorogation and periods of adjournment over four consecutive days
are excluded while computing the relevant six-month period.
If the President does not summon the joint sitting, the Bill
comes to an end
The Bill is decided by a simple majority of the members of both Houses present and voting together at the joint sitting.
Joint sittings have been held only
three
times: for the Dowry Prohibition Bill, the Banking Service Commission (Repeal) Bill and the Prevention of Terrorism Bill.

secs.t: Lapsing of bills on dissolution of Lok Sabha

x: Exam angle: "passed by LS but not yet taken up in RS does not lapse" is
false
(APPSC-G1 2024 statement).

Adjournment or adjournment sine die does not cause Bills to lapse; prorogation causes pending notices to lapse except notices for introducing Bills; dissolution causes all pending business before the Lok Sabha to lapse.
Bills pending in the Rajya Sabha and not passed by the Lok Sabha, bills passed by both Houses awaiting assent, and bills returned for reconsideration do not lapse.

secs.t: Money Bill vs Financial Bills (I, II) vs Finance Bill

x: The Rajya Sabha may amend or reject a Financial Bill-I; its powers are not restricted to making recommendations.
A Financial Bill-II may be introduced in either House, by a Minister or a private member, but the President's recommendation is required when it is taken into consideration.
A Money Bill deals exclusively with Article 110 matters; a Financial Bill-I contains such matters partly along with other matters; a Financial Bill-II contains none of the Article 110 matters.
A Finance Bill gives effect to the Budget's tax proposals and is usually certified as a Money Bill.

secs.t: Bills by House of introduction; President's prior recommendation

x: For a Financial Bill-II involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India, the President's recommendation is required
before the Bill is taken into consideration
A Bill affecting taxation in which States are interested requires the President's prior recommendation before introduction.
Voting on Demands for Grants is confined to the Lok Sabha, requires the President’s recommendation, and is not subject to voting in the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Private member's bills vs government bills

x: Defeat of a Private Member's Bill does not affect the government's continuation in office.
The Lok Sabha committee examines constitutional amendment Bills introduced by Private Members before their introduction, besides classifying Bills and allotting time.
The Rajya Sabha has no separate Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions for this purpose; its Business Advisory Committee allots the time.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024 concerns simultaneous elections, or One Nation, One Election, and proposes a new Article 82A.
The first Union Budget was presented on 26 November 1947, the Andhra State Bill was introduced on 10 August 1953, assent was given on 14 September 1953, and Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
The Governor's options under Article 200 include assent, withholding assent, returning a non-Money Bill for reconsideration, and reserving a Bill for the President.
The Rajya Sabha passed the
NCDC (Amendment) Bill, 2026
during the Monsoon Session of 2026.

rows.title: Budget in Parliament - stages, cut motions, appropriation and finance bills, Consolidated/Contingency/Public Account

secs.t: Annual Financial Statement - Article 112, the word "budget", who lays and prepares it

x: ‘Budget’ is derived from the French word ‘bougette’, meaning ‘
little bag
The process begins with the Budget Circular, generally issued in September, and printing is traditionally marked by the Halwa ceremony.
The Halwa ceremony marking the commencement of Budget printing is held in the
North Block
R. K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on
26 November 1947

secs.t: Appropriation Bill - Article 114

x: The Appropriation Bill covers grants voted by the Lok Sabha as well as charged expenditure, and the amount cannot exceed that authorised in the Annual Financial Statement.
Article 114(3) requires
an appropriation made by law
before money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India.
An amendment cannot vary the amount or destination of a voted grant or vary charged expenditure.

secs.t: Vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional, supplementary and excess grants

x: A
vote of credit
under Article 116 is granted for an unexpected demand whose magnitude or character cannot be stated in detail.

A supplementary grant meets an insufficiency; an additional grant covers a new service; an excess grant relates to expenditure beyond the amount granted; and a vote of credit meets an unexpected indefinite demand.

secs.t: Cut motions - policy, economy, token

x: A policy cut proposes to reduce the demand to Re 1, thereby expressing disapproval of the policy underlying the demand.
A token cut reduces the demand by Rs 100 and is intended to ventilate a specific grievance.
Cut motions are moved only in the Lok Sabha during voting on Demands for Grants.

secs.t: Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund, Public Account

x: The Government acts as a banker or trustee in respect of money credited to the Public Account, such as provident funds, deposits and small savings.
The Contingency Fund is used for unforeseen expenditure when immediate action is necessary, pending authorisation by Parliament.
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account of both the Union and the States.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The budget-related provisions identified here are Articles 109 to 117 and Articles 265 to 267, covering financial legislation, public revenues and the principal government funds.
K. Atchannaidu presented the separate Agriculture Budget, Governor S. Abdul Nazeer addressed both Houses at the opening, and the State Budget was presented on 14 February 2026.

rows.title: Parliamentary committees - PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings, Departmentally Related Standing Committees, ad hoc

secs.t: Financial committees - PAC, Estimates, COPU: strength, RS membership, chairman

x: The Committee on Public Undertakings has 22 members, including 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha, and its chairman is appointed by the Speaker from the Lok Sabha members.
The Speaker appoints the chairperson of the Estimates Committee, who is invariably a member of
the ruling party

secs.t: Public Accounts Committee - reports, reporting, chairman

x: The PAC checks whether expenditure remained
within the scope of the demand for grant
approved by Parliament.
The PAC may take up matters on its own and examines efficiency, economy and propriety in addition to legality.
The Opposition chairpersonship of the PAC is a convention followed since 1967, not a constitutional or statutory rule applicable in every case.

secs.t: Committee nicknames and reform area

x: The
Committee on Petitions
is popularly described as the Ombudsman of Parliament because it considers petitions on bills and matters of public interest.
The PAC is described as a watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities, and the Estimates Committee suggests economies and alternative policies.
The watchdog group comprises the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Committee on Government Assurances, Estimates Committee, PAC, COPU and Departmentally Related Standing Committees.

secs.t: Origin years and recommending bodies

x: The Public Accounts Committee originated in 1921 under the
Government of India Act, 1919
All three statements are correct: DRSCs began in 1993 with 17 committees, expanded to 24 from 2004, and were introduced on the recommendation of the Rules Committee.

secs.t: Other standing committees - function, strength, date

x: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks how delegated rule-making powers are exercised.
The Rajya Sabha Ethics Committee dates from 4 March 1997, the Lok Sabha Ethics Committee from 16 May 2000, and their subject is the conduct of members.
The Speaker chairs the Lok Sabha
Business Advisory Committee
, which allots time for government and other business.

secs.t: Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs

x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs has 30 members, comprising 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
The committee examines commission reports, constitutional safeguards and welfare programmes.

secs.t: Departmentally Related Standing Committees

x: Each DRSC has 31 members, comprising 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
There are 24 DRSCs, with 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha; their quorum is 11.
DRSCs scrutinise demands for grants, referred Bills, annual reports and the long-term policy of the ministries under their jurisdiction.

secs.t: Ad hoc committees - select, joint committees, JPCs

x: The investigations occurred in the order Bofors (1987), Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992), Ketan Parekh (2001), soft-drink pesticides (2003) and 2G spectrum (2011).
The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, concerning simultaneous elections or ONOE, is currently before a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
The
Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025
is currently before a Joint Parliamentary Committee.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported average attendance at 16 DRSCs and the PAC was only
since their September reconstitution.
Jairam Ramesh issued a privilege notice against Education Minister
Dharmendra Pradhan
over remarks concerning a standing committee.
The PAC is criticised as a post-mortem mechanism because it examines expenditure after it occurs; frequent guillotine of demands can further weaken financial control.

rows.title: Parliamentary privileges; anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule) and the role of the Speaker
sub: Group-II M1-B-80: Anti-Defection Law - Tenth Schedule, grounds, exemptions and the Speaker's role
Group-II M1-B-81: Anti-Defection Law - judicial interpretation, working and suggested reforms

secs.t: Anti-defection law - Schedule, amendments, coverage

x: The 52nd Amendment amended
Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191
concerning vacation of seats and disqualification.
The expression became associated with rampant defections in
Haryana in 1967
, a phenomenon that contributed to the enactment of the anti-defection law.
The
52nd Amendment Act, 1985
inserted the Tenth Schedule and mentioned political parties in the Constitution for the first time, thereby giving them constitutional recognition.

secs.t: Merger exception and deletion of the split provision

x: The
91st Amendment Act, 2003
deleted the one-third split exception and brought splits within the scope of disqualification.
A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.
Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, caps the Union Council of Ministers at
15 per cent
of the Lok Sabha’s total strength.
Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B
impose these restrictions on a disqualified defector until re-election.

secs.t: Grounds of disqualification under the Tenth Schedule

x: Voting or abstaining against the party direction without permission attracts disqualification unless the party condones the conduct within
15 days
Voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct and does not require a formal resignation from the party.
Voting against the whip with permission is not a ground of disqualification.

secs.t: Speaker as deciding authority - finality and judicial review, time limit

x: Paragraph 6 vests the decision in the Speaker of the Lok Sabha or Legislative Assembly, and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha or Legislative Council, acting as a tribunal.
The Election Commission does not give an opinion in Tenth Schedule proceedings; that arrangement applies to certain other disqualifications under Articles 103 and 192.
Kihoto Hollohan preserved judicial review after the decision, but limited it to grounds such as mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice and constitutional mandate.

secs.t: Sources of privileges - Arts. 105, 194, 122; codification

x: Article 105 concerns Parliament's privileges, Article 122 concerns parliamentary proceedings, Article 194 concerns State Legislature privileges and Article 212 concerns State Legislature proceedings.
Article 122 applies to Parliament and Article 212 to State Legislatures; both concern non-interference by courts on the ground of
procedural irregularity
The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).

secs.t: Breach of privilege and contempt of the House

x: Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.
Contempt has a wider scope and includes acts that obstruct the House or its members in the discharge of their functions.
The recognised punishments include admonition, reprimand, imprisonment, suspension and expulsion.

secs.t: Anti-defection in states - cases

x: The Supreme Court gave the Telangana Speaker
three weeks
to decide the last two of the ten BRS MLA defection petitions and warned of contempt.
In June 2019, four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs were treated as having merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger.

secs.t: Applicability - MPs, MLAs, MLCs, independents, nominated members

x: Members of both Houses of Parliament and both Houses of State Legislatures, including MLCs, are covered.

secs.t: State anti-defection laws before the Tenth Schedule

x: The
Y.B. Chavan Committee on Defections
studied the problem during 1967–1969.
The anti-defection Bills introduced in 1973 and 1978 lapsed and did not become law.

secs.t: Keisham Meghachandra Singh case - time for the Speaker's decision

x: The Supreme Court indicated that the Speaker should decide disqualification petitions within
three months
, except in extraordinary circumstances.
The Supreme Court issued a time-bound direction in the Telangana matter and later gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.
The Supreme Court urged the Speaker to decide within
three months
and asked Parliament to consider establishing an independent tribunal for such matters.

secs.t: Voluntarily giving up membership - Ravi S. Naik, G. Viswanathan

x: Ravi S. Naik held that voluntarily giving up membership is not the same as resigning; it may be inferred from conduct, including publicly backing a rival party.
An expelled member continues to be regarded as belonging to the original party for the Tenth Schedule.

secs.t: Subhash Desai case - whip; legislature party vs political party

x: Ravi S. Naik concerned inference from conduct; G. Viswanathan concerned the status of an expelled member; Subhash Desai concerned the party’s authority over the whip and House leader.
The Supreme Court held that the
political party
, rather than merely the legislature party, appoints the whip and the leader in the House.

secs.t: Working of the law - resort politics, resignation route, Speaker delay

x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.
In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, thereby reducing the majority mark without being disqualified, and may later re-contest on the new party’s ticket.
The concern arises from the absence of a fixed time limit and the partisan context in which Speakers, who do not resign from their parties, decide petitions.

secs.t: Reform suggestions - Dinesh Goswami, Law Commission 170th, NCRWC, EC

x: The
Dinesh Goswami Committee
in 1990 recommended limiting disqualification to voluntarily giving up membership or voting against the whip on confidence or no-confidence motions.
The Law Commission’s 170th Report recommended
deleting the split and merger exceptions and treating pre-poll alliances as parties
Newer proposals include fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal, the latter having been suggested for consideration by the Supreme Court in 2020.

secs.t: Proposal to limit the law to confidence and money votes

x: Exam angle: match a case to its holding, or a committee to its remedy.
The proposal would retain party discipline for votes threatening government survival, such as confidence, no-confidence and money bills, while allowing dissent on other matters.
The sequence is Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Law Commission’s 170th Report (1999), Manish Tewari’s Bill (2010), and the Supreme Court’s independent-tribunal suggestion (2020).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Seven
of the ten AAP Rajya Sabha Members, including Raghav Chadha, claimed a merger with the BJP in April 2026.
The reform proposal is to limit the operation of whips mainly to
confidence votes and Money Bills
, thereby allowing greater legislative dissent on other matters.
All three statements reflect criticisms of the working of the anti-defection law, especially its effect on internal dissent and its perceived inability to prevent mass defections.

rows.title: Productivity and decline of Parliament - issues of debate quality, disruptions and reforms

secs.t: Sitting days - trend and comparison with early Lok Sabhas

x: The average sittings declined from about 135 days per year in the First Lok Sabha to about 55 days per year in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha.
The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days annually, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings.
Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.

secs.t: Disruptions - time lost, cost, suspension of members

x: PRS data placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
Rule 373 concerns withdrawal for the day, Rule 374 concerns suspension by House motion up to the remainder of the session, and Rule 374A provides automatic suspension for grave disorder.

secs.t: Bills passed without committee scrutiny

x: All three statements are correct: less than one-fifth went to committees, 58 per cent were passed within two weeks, and 35 per cent received less than one hour of debate.
Less than one-fifth of Indian Bills go to committees, while every Bill in the UK is examined by committees of both Houses.

secs.t: Ordinance and Money Bill routes as bypass

x: The increased use of ordinances under Article 123 and delegated legislation has grown as legislative engagement has fallen.
The proposals were to define immediate necessity, permit courts to test urgency, and publish reasons for ordinances.
The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110.

secs.t: Reform proposals - NCRWC, fixed calendar, minimum sittings

x: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended 120 sitting days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha.
The proposals include a fixed calendar, stronger Question Hour, mandatory committee scrutiny, and protection of opposition debate time.
The National Legislative Index covers sittings, business, disruptions, use of committees and grievance redressal.

secs.t: Role of opposition and Leader of Opposition

x: The Speaker recognises the Leader of the Opposition when the party has at least
one-tenth
of the House’s strength, equivalent to 55 members in the Lok Sabha.
The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the
Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
Question Hour, motions and committees are important opposition tools.

secs.t: PRS Legislative Research and Digital Sansad data

x: PRS Legislative Research compiles data on session productivity, Bill scrutiny and State-law reviews.
The official attendance and sitting data is available on the Lok Sabha website through
Digital Sansad
The cited average attendance at DRSC meetings was
53 per cent

secs.t: State legislatures - productivity, AP sittings

x: Many Assemblies met merely to comply with the six-month requirement; more than 600 Bills were passed, and about 33 per cent were passed in a single sitting.
The Business Advisory Committee fixing the agenda was chaired by
Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu
All three statements are correct: Odisha recorded 43 sitting days, Nagaland recorded 7, and the average for Assemblies was 24 days.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The guillotine refers to curtailing discussion and putting demands to vote without completing detailed debate, and is cited as an issue affecting parliamentary debate quality.
All four are cited issues: insufficient time or expertise, executive dominance, delegated legislation and hasty law-making, for which the Farm Laws of 2020 are given as an example.

rows.title: Parliamentary form of government - features, merits, demerits; comparison with the presidential system
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-36

secs.t: Features of parliamentary government

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason: "India is parliamentary because the executive is responsible to the legislature" - both true, R explains A.
A non-member may become a minister, but must become a member of either House of Parliament within
six months
The President’s constitutional role in completing the legislative process is a reason for treating the President as a component of Parliament under Article 79.

secs.t: Indian vs British parliamentary system

x: India's President is indirectly elected for a five-year term, whereas Britain's Head of State is a hereditary monarch.
Britain requires ministers to be members of Parliament and has legal ministerial responsibility and an institutionalised shadow cabinet.
In both countries, the growing centrality of the Prime Minister has led scholars to use the expression “
Prime Ministerial Government

secs.t: Presidential system - features

x: In a presidential system, cabinet members may or may not belong to the legislature; in the United States, Secretaries do not sit in Congress.
The parliamentary system is based on a fusion of executive and legislative powers, while the presidential system rests on separation of powers.
Executive responsibility and possible early dissolution are parliamentary features, while fixed tenure and removal only by impeachment are presidential features.

secs.t: Merits and demerits

x: Harmony between the executive and legislature can help resolve deadlock through fresh elections, and continuous accountability is a merit.
A stable fixed-term executive
is a merit of the presidential system, not a demerit of the parliamentary system.
Executive-legislature deadlock and the danger of a personality cult are recognised demerits of the presidential system.

secs.t: Origin countries

x: The parliamentary system originated in
Britain
and is commonly called the Westminster model.
The
United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India
are examples of parliamentary systems.

secs.t: India vs USA - common and different features

x: India and the United States share a written Constitution, a federal structure, an independent judiciary with judicial review, and constitutional rights protections.
India vests residuary powers in Parliament and distributes subjects through Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
The United States Supreme Court's
wide power of judicial review
has led to its description as a “third chamber.”.

secs.t: Constituent Assembly's choice of the parliamentary form

x: The Constituent Assembly preferred the parliamentary system partly to avoid executive-legislature conflict and to ensure accountability.
Experience with parliamentary institutions under the Government of India Acts of 1919 and 1935 was an important reason for adopting the parliamentary form.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility.

secs.t: Presidential system debate in India

x: Proposals for a presidential form were made in India during the 1970s and 1980s, including proposals associated with Vasant Sathe.
The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, chaired by Venkatachaliah and functioning during 2000–02, reviewed the issue and advised
retaining the parliamentary system
Critics argue that fixed tenures may introduce presidential features into the parliamentary system and weaken accountability; therefore; .

secs.t: Semi-presidential systems

x: France, Russia and Sri Lanka
are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.
France's Fifth Republic dates from 1958, and Sri Lanka's 1978 Constitution provides for a directly elected President with real powers alongside a legislature-responsible Prime Minister.
India's President is indirectly elected and nominal.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Narendra Modi completed
8,931 days
as head of an elected government on 22 March 2026, one day more than Pawan Kumar Chamling's 8,930 days.
The Governor's discretion is understood within the logic of
the parliamentary system
, in which constitutional offices operate in relation to the elected government and ministerial responsibility.

rows.title: Governor - appointment, powers, discretionary powers, position and controversies (Article 200/201, Article 356 reports)
sub: Group-II M1-B-33: State executive - Governor, Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers
Group-II M1-B-63: Role of the Governor as a source of Centre-State tension; Article 356 and S.R. Bommai

secs.t: Reservation of bills for President - Articles 200/201, mandatory cases, time limits (TN Governor case)

x: Exam angle: statements on the four options, the one mandatory reservation, and whether courts can fix timelines (current position: they cannot).
Exam angle: the April 2025 timelines and deemed assent do not survive the Nov 2025 Reference opinion.
Shamsher Singh (1974), decided by a seven-judge Bench, affirmed that the Governor ordinarily acts on
the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers

The sequence was withholding of assent to Tamil Nadu's anti-NEET Bill, the April 2025 Supreme Court order deeming ten repassed Bills assented using Article 142, and the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejecting deemed assent as impermissible.

Article 200 deals with the Governor's choices on a State Bill; Article 201 deals with Bills reserved for the President; Article 254(2) concerns Concurrent List repugnancy; and Article 360 concerns Financial Emergency.
The 2023 Punjab case held that the Governor
must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely
The April 2025 judgment read into Article 200 a one-month period for withholding assent on advice, three months for action against advice, and one month after re-presentation of a re-passed Bill.
The current position rejects general court-imposed timelines and deemed assent, while allowing limited judicial intervention where inaction is prolonged and unexplained.
Article 288
concerns taxes on water or electricity in relation to certain inter-State river projects, and Bills imposing such taxes must be reserved as specified.
Article 304(b)
requires the previous sanction of the President before introduction of a State Bill imposing reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade, commerce or intercourse.
The opinion held that Article 142 cannot substitute the Governor or President, merits are not generally justiciable, and only limited mandamus may be issued for prolonged unexplained inaction.
The Governor invited C. Joseph Vijay on the basis of 120 letters of support, following the Sarkaria-Punchhi order and requiring an early floor test.

secs.t: Governor's discretionary powers - Article 163, judicial review, constitutional vs situational discretion

x: Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision final on the question of discretion, but his acts cannot be questioned on that ground; Article 163(3) protects ministerial advice from judicial inquiry.

Article 200 concerns reservation of Bills, Article 356 concerns the President's Rule report, Article 167 concerns information from the Chief Minister and Article 239 concerns administration of Union Territories.
Nabam Rebia held that the powers under Article 174 and the address under Articles 175–176 are exercised on aid and advice.
The Perarivalan judgment of 2022 held that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice on pardon or remission under Article 161; this position was reaffirmed subsequently.
Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision final on whether a matter is discretionary, but it does not create complete immunity from judicial review.

secs.t: Commission recommendations on the Governor - Sarkaria, Punchhi, Rajamannar, Venkatachaliah, First ARC

x: The Sarkaria Commission recommended a politically neutral outsider, consultation with the Chief Minister, use of Article 356 as a last resort, mandatory floor tests and time-bound decisions on Bills.

The First ARC stressed public experience and non-partisanship; Rajamannar dealt with Centre-State relations; Sarkaria recommended a neutral outsider and consultation; Punchhi recommended fixed tenure.
Rameshwar Prasad cited Sarkaria regarding misuse of Article 356 reports and urged a cooling-off period before politicians are appointed as Governors.

secs.t: Appointment and office - Articles 153-158, same Governor for two states, qualifications, pleasure (B.P. Singhal)

x: Exam angle: minimum age of 35; "pleasure of the President" makes the office structurally dependent on the Centre.
Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State, while the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 enables one person to serve as Governor of two or more States.
The normal term is five years, but the Governor continues in office until the successor enters office.
In the absence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, the oath is administered by
the senior-most judge of that High Court
The emoluments of a Governor are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State under Article 202(3).
Where one Governor serves two or more States, the
President
determines the allocation of the cost of emoluments among those States.
The pleasure doctrine is not unfettered: removal cannot be arbitrary or based merely on a change in the Government at the Centre.
Reservation is mandatory for a Bill that, in the Governor's opinion, endangers the position of the High Court.

secs.t: Legislative powers - address, dissolution, ordinance (Article 213) vs President's

x: Under Article 171, the Governor nominates
one-sixth
of the members of a State Legislative Council from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in specified fields.
The Governor places the CAG report relating to the State, the report of the State Public Service Commission and the State Finance Commission report before the State Legislature.

Article 166 concerns executive action in the Governor's name; Article 164 concerns the Chief Minister and ministers; Article 165 concerns the Advocate-General; and Article 316 concerns the State Public Service Commission.
A Governor's ordinance lapses six weeks after the State Legislature reassembles, unless it is replaced or otherwise ceases earlier according to the constitutional procedure.
The relevant Articles are 161 for pardoning power, 174 for summoning and dissolution, 213 for ordinances and 356 for recommendation of President's Rule.

secs.t: Governor as administrator of an adjoining UT - on whose advice

x: If appointed administrator of an adjoining UT under
, the Governor acts
independently of his own state Council of Ministers

secs.t: Immunities and appointments - Article 361, salary fund, whom he appoints

x: Article 166 concerns executive action in the Governor's name, Article 164 concerns the Chief Minister and ministers, Article 165 concerns the Advocate-General, and Article 161 concerns the Governor's pardoning power.
Article 361 protects the Governor from being answerable to any court for official acts and bars criminal proceedings during the term of office.

secs.t: Governors of AP - FIRST, and the common Governor for AP and Telangana

x: Biswabhusan Harichandan
became the separate Governor of Andhra Pradesh in 2019 after the common-governorship arrangement under E.S.L. Narasimhan.
S. Abdul Nazeer
was the Governor of Andhra Pradesh in August 2026 and notified the Monsoon Session from 17 August 2026 under Article 174(1).
Section 8 assigned special responsibility to the Governor for law and order and allocation of government buildings, mainly in Hyderabad as the common capital.
K.V. Ranga Reddy
served as Deputy Chief Minister in united Andhra Pradesh in 1956, alongside Chief Minister Neelam Sanjiva Reddy.

secs.t: Article 153 - one Governor for two or more states

x: Art. 153
: there shall be a Governor for each state.
The
7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956
allows the
same person to be Governor of two or more states

secs.t: Chief Minister and Council of Ministers - Arts 163, 164, 167

x: Article 164(4) requires a non-member minister to become a member of the State Legislature within
six months
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 limits the Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, to 15% of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly.
The 91st Amendment provides that the Council of Ministers in a State, including the Chief Minister, shall not consist of fewer than
12 members

secs.t: FIRST women Governors and Chief Ministers

x: Sarojini Naidu
became the first woman Governor of an Indian State, serving as Governor of Uttar Pradesh in 1947.

secs.t: Article 356 - grounds, Governor's report, approval, duration, extension, Assembly, Art 365

x: President's Rule continues for
six months
at a time after approval, subject to the constitutional conditions for further extension.
President's Rule may continue for a maximum of
three years
, with parliamentary approval required at six-month intervals.
The 68th Constitutional Amendment extended the 1987 proclamation of President's Rule in Punjab to five years.

secs.t: Frequency of President's Rule - FIRST, recent, never/most, AP instance

x: Kerala in 1959
witnessed the first dismissal of an elected State Government under President's Rule.
Manipur
has experienced President's Rule most often; 2025 marked its eleventh instance.
President's Rule began in Manipur on
13 February 2025
and was revoked on 4 February 2026.
President's Rule in Manipur was revoked on 4 February 2026 when Y. Khemchand Singh became Chief Minister.

secs.t: Judicial scrutiny of Art 356 - Bommai guidelines, AP High Court episode

x: The nine-judge Bench in S.R. Bommai held that an Article 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review and that the Centre must show relevant material supporting it.
Bommai protected the Assembly pending parliamentary approval, permitted restoration of a displaced ministry, and treated secularism as a basic feature.
Rameshwar Prasad held that an Assembly could not be dissolved merely on the basis of unproven fears of horse-trading.

secs.t: Special cases - J&K Governor's Rule, post-Ayodhya dissolutions

x: In the former Jammu and Kashmir constitutional arrangement, Governor’s Rule was imposed under Section 92 of the J&K Constitution for six months, after which Article 356 could apply.
The BJP governments of
Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh
were removed after the December 1992 Ayodhya events.
The Supreme Court upheld the dismissals of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh on the ground that
secularism
had been violated.

secs.t: Commissions' views - Sarkaria, Punchhi

x: Sarkaria favoured a Governor from outside the State, who was not a recent active politician, and whose selection followed consultation with the Chief Minister.
The Punchhi Commission recommended a localised emergency for a district for up to three months, codification of Bommai guidelines in Article 356 and fixed tenure for Governors.

secs.t: Governor's discretion flashpoints - hung House, withholding assent, recommending PR

x: Under Article 163(2), the Governor’s decision on whether a matter falls within his discretion is
final
, subject to the constitutional scheme and judicial interpretation.
The stated order is pre-poll alliance, largest party with support, post-poll coalition, and post-poll alliance with outside support.
The stated practice is that
an early floor test
should follow the Governor’s invitation, so that majority support is demonstrated in the House.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: C. Joseph Vijay was sworn in after letters of support from
120 MLAs
were presented, while TVK itself had won 108 seats.
The controversy concerned Governors walking out of or skipping the mandatory Article 176 address in Opposition-ruled States.
The 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill proposes automatic removal after detention for 30 consecutive days on charges carrying a possible sentence of five or more years.
Rameshwar Prasad’s call for a cooling-off period before a politician becomes Governor was reported as being revisited in 2026.
The Andhra Pradesh references are President’s Rule in 1973 during the Jai Andhra movement and the 2020 Andhra Pradesh High Court episode concerning constitutional breakdown.

rows.title: Chief Minister and the State Council of Ministers; Advocate General of the State

secs.t: Chief Minister - appointment (Article 164), floor test, oath, non-member time limit, collective responsibility, salaries

x: Under Article 164(3), the Governor administers the oath of office and secrecy to the Chief Minister and other ministers.
Article 164(4) permits a non-member to remain a minister, including Chief Minister, for
six months
Under Article 164(5), the salaries and allowances of State ministers are determined by the
State Legislature
by law.

secs.t: Duties of CM towards the Governor - Article 167

x: Administering the Governor's oath is not a duty of the Chief Minister under Article 167.
All three statements correctly describe the Chief Minister's duties and intermediary role under Article 167.
The
Governor
may call for information from the Chief Minister regarding administration and legislative proposals under Article 167.

secs.t: Chief Ministers - FIRST woman CM and AP FIRSTs

x: The first cabinet of united Andhra Pradesh, formed in 1956 under Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy, had 13 ministers.
Nallapati Venkata Ramaiah
was the first Speaker of the united Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.

secs.t: Deputy Chief Minister - constitutional status, AP instances

x: The Constitution does not specifically mention the office of Deputy Chief Minister.
A Deputy Chief Minister ranks with Union Ministers of State and occupies position No. 10 in the order of precedence.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed provision applies when the offence is punishable with imprisonment of
five years or more
and the person remains in custody for 30 consecutive days.
The Bill proposes removal on the 31st day when the Prime Minister, Chief Minister or Minister has been held in custody for 30 consecutive days in the specified circumstances.
The 11th NITI Aayog Governing Council saw the presence of all 28 Chief Ministers for the first time.

rows.title: State legislature - Assembly and Legislative Council; creation and abolition of the Council (Article 169)
sub: Group-II M1-B-34: State legislature - Assembly and Legislative Council; creation and abolition of the Council

secs.t: Legislative Council composition - elected fractions, nominated, size, tenure

x: One-twelfth of a State Legislative Council is elected by registered graduates having at least
three years
' standing.
One-twelfth of the Council is elected by teachers with at least three years' teaching experience in institutions not lower than the secondary-school level.
The Governor nominates one-sixth of the Council from the specified fields, and the nominations are made on Cabinet advice.
Members of a State Legislative Council are elected indirectly through
proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote

secs.t: Assembly vs Council - money bills, ordinary bills, delaying power, no joint sitting

x: Under Article 199(3), the
Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
certifies whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
A Bill originating in the Council ends when rejected by the Assembly, and there is no second chance for the Council.
The State Legislative Council can delay legislation but cannot permanently veto an Assembly Bill.
The Governor requires the President's instructions where a Bill containing the same provisions would require prior sanction of the President or would have to be reserved for his consideration.

secs.t: Speaker of the Legislative Assembly - powers, casting vote, Money Bill, resignation, vacating

x: Under Article 181, the Speaker does not preside while a resolution for removal is under consideration, but may speak and vote in the first instance.
Under Article 189, the Speaker does not vote in the first instance but exercises a casting vote in the event of an equality of votes.
The Speaker continues after dissolution until immediately before the first meeting of the new Assembly.
The Deputy Speaker
acts with the full powers of the Speaker
when the office is vacant or the Speaker is absent.
The casting vote on a tie is a separate rule and does not explain why the Speaker abstains from voting in the first instance.

secs.t: Articles 168-212 - content

x: Article 169 concerns Legislative Councils, Article 173 qualifications, Article 194 privileges, and Article 202 the Annual Financial Statement.
Article 172
deals with the duration of State Legislatures; the normal duration of the Legislative Assembly is five years unless sooner dissolved.
Articles 174, 175 and 176 respectively concern sessions and dissolution, the Governor's address and messages, and the special address.
Article 174 requires that not more than
six months
intervene between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next.
Articles 178 to 187 deal with the Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman, Deputy Chairman and related legislative offices.

secs.t: Article 169 - resolution majority, Parliament's role, Governor's role

x: Parliament uses a simple majority and determines the Council's strength within the constitutional limits.

The constitutional process is initiated by a special-majority resolution of the Legislative Assembly and completed through a law of Parliament; the Governor has no role in initiating or approving that resolution.
The Assembly may pass the required special-majority resolution, after which Parliament may enact the law.

secs.t: Legislative Assembly - quorum, term, strength, non-Tenth Schedule disqualification, order of proceedings

x: Under Article 172, the normal term of a State Legislative Assembly is
five years from the date appointed for its first meeting
, unless dissolved earlier.
Parliament may extend the Assembly's term by one year at a time during a National Emergency, but the extension cannot continue beyond six months after the Emergency has ceased.
Under Articles 191 and 192, the Governor decides such questions, but must act according to the opinion of the Election Commission.
The
104th Constitutional Amendment Act
, 2020 discontinued the provision for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Legislative Assemblies of States.

secs.t: States with Legislative Councils - present list and recent changes

x: Tamil Nadu abolished its Legislative Council in 1986.
Saleem Ahmed was elected Chairperson of the Karnataka Legislative Council by a vote of 38 to 30.
G.S. Patil became the
18th
Speaker of the Karnataka Legislative Assembly.
The six States with Legislative Councils are
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh

secs.t: Disqualification of state legislators - Arts 191-192

x: Article 190(4) provides for vacation of the seat when a member remains absent without permission for 60 days, subject to the constitutional exclusions relating to periods when the House is prorogued or adjourned for more than four consecutive days.
Article 190
provides, among other matters concerning vacation of seats, that a person cannot be a member of both Houses of a State Legislature at the same time.

secs.t: MLAs in indirect elections

x: Elected MLAs participate in the Presidential election, elect Rajya Sabha members by PR-STV, and elect one-third of the members of the State Legislative Council.
Elected MLAs are part of the electoral college for the President under Article 54.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Gaddam Prasad Kumar is the Speaker, whereas Gutha Sukender Reddy is the Chairman of the Telangana Legislative Council.
A Legislative Council acts as a revising chamber that can check hasty legislation and provide a place for experts who may not be able to secure election.
Critics describe the Council as a costly delaying chamber because its political significance and continued existence may fluctuate with the ruling party’s position in the Assembly.

rows.title: Legislature of Andhra Pradesh - structure and functioning
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-39

secs.t: AP Legislative Council - strength, Governor's nominees, AP-Telangana sharing, composition

x: Section 22(2) provided for the allotment of existing Members of the Legislative Council between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana under the Fourth Schedule.
The Council comprises 20 members elected by local authorities, 20 elected by MLAs, 5 by graduates, 5 by teachers and 8 nominated by the Governor.
Sections 22(1) and 22(2), read with the Fourth Schedule, dealt with the initial Council strength and allocation of existing MLCs.

secs.t: AP Legislative Assembly - strength then and now, reserved seats, Speakers

x: The Anglo-Indian nomination provision under Article 333 ended with the
104th Constitutional Amendment
Madapati Hanumantha Rao was the first Chairman of the Legislative Council, while Puchalapalli Sundarayya was the first Leader of Opposition.
K. Raghu Ramakrishna Raju
is the Deputy Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly as stated for 2026.

secs.t: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 - legislature provisions

x: Section 18 provided for one Anglo-Indian nominee each in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana under Article 333, although the provision has since lapsed.
The present Andhra Pradesh has 175 Assembly constituencies and 25 Lok Sabha constituencies under the Delimitation Order, 2008 after the 2014 reorganisation.
Section 26 contemplated 225 seats for Andhra Pradesh and 153 for Telangana, subject to Article 170, but the increase has not yet been implemented.

secs.t: District → Assembly constituencies (13 districts, 2008 delimitation)

x: East Godavari
has 19 Assembly constituencies, the highest among the districts listed.
All four pairs are correct under the 2008 delimitation: Srikakulam 10, Vizianagaram 9, West Godavari 15 and Chittoor 14.
Kadapa has 10 seats, whereas Kurnool and Anantapur each have 14 seats.
The district-wise figures together total 175 Assembly constituencies.

secs.t: AP Legislative Assemblies by number - notable features

x: In the 2024 election, the NDA won 164 of 175 seats and the YSRCP won 11 seats.
The NDA total consisted of 135 TDP seats, 21 JSP seats and 8 BJP seats.
The YSRCP won 11 of the 175 seats, which was below the one-tenth threshold required for official Opposition status.

secs.t: AP Legislative Council - abolition, revival, later resolutions

x: The Council was created in 1958, abolished in 1985, revived in 2007, and the Assembly passed an abolition resolution in January 2020.
The Andhra Pradesh Assembly withdrew its abolition resolution in November 2021; consequently, the Legislative Council continued.
The 2015 amendment raised the maximum permissible strength of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council from the reorganisation limit of 50 to 58 members.

secs.t: Bills passed in the AP Assembly → subject

x: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966 provided for
Telugu
as the official language.
The November 2021 Repeal Act withdrew the three-capitals law and the CRDA repeal, thereby restoring Amaravati.
The united Assembly rejected the Draft Reorganisation Bill by a resolution through voice vote; nevertheless, the law enacted by Parliament prevailed.

secs.t: AP Assembly seat - present and earlier

x: The interim Assembly building at Velagapudi has hosted sessions since 2017.
The new Assembly building at Amaravati is designed by
Norman Foster + Partners
Before 1956 the Andhra State Assembly met at Kurnool.
The sequence is Kurnool before 1956, Hyderabad thereafter as the common capital, Velagapudi from 2017, and the present seat at Amaravati.

secs.t: Committees of the AP Legislature - PAC, Estimates, Public Undertakings

x: Andhra Pradesh has the Committee on Public Undertakings in addition to, not instead of, the Estimates and Public Accounts Committees.
The Public Accounts Committee, along with the Estimates Committee, helps ensure that grants are properly used.
Both statements are true, but appointment of committee chairpersons by the Speaker does not explain the separate convention that the Public Accounts Committee chairperson belongs to the Opposition.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Governor S. Abdul Nazeer summoned the Monsoon Session from 17 August 2026 under
Article 174(1)
The Bill proposed fresh delimitation and an increase of Lok Sabha seats to 850, with consequential effects on State Assemblies, but it was negatived in the Lok Sabha.
Since the Bill was negatived in the Lok Sabha,
the freeze on seats under the 84th Amendment continues

rows.title: Supreme Court - composition, appointment, collegium and NJAC, jurisdictions (original, appellate, advisory, writ)
sub: Group-II M1-B-36: Supreme Court - composition, appointment, jurisdiction and powers
Group-II M1-B-38: Independence of the judiciary - constitutional safeguards; collegium and the NJAC judgment

secs.t: Appointment - collegium and Judges cases, NJAC, 99th Amendment, CJI appointment

x: Exam angle: "Which amendment was declared void in 2015?" - 99th; "who upheld NJAC?" - Chelameswar.
The First Judges Case, decided in 1981 and reported in 1982, held that consultation did not mean concurrence and recognised executive primacy in judicial appointments.
The Second Judges Case held that consultation means concurrence, established judicial primacy and gave rise to the collegium consisting initially of the CJI and two senior-most judges.
The Supreme Court collegium in June 2026 comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh and P.S. Narasimha.
The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted
Article 124A
, among related provisions, to provide for the National Judicial Appointments Commission.
The Venkatachaliah Commission was appointed in 2000 during the Prime Ministership of
Atal Bihari Vajpayee
and recommended an NJAC.
The five-judge Bench in the Fourth Judges Case was led by
Justice J.S. Khehar
and struck down the NJAC and the 99th Amendment by a 4:1 majority.
Justice J. Chelameswar
was the lone dissenter and upheld the NJAC, whereas the majority declared the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act unconstitutional.
The Government conducts background checks, may return a recommendation once, but is bound to appoint the candidate if the collegium reiterates it.

secs.t: Number of judges - who can increase it, present strength, Acts

x: Article 124(1)
provides the constitutional basis for determining the number of judges of the Supreme Court.

The 2026 Ordinance was promulgated under Article 123, notified on 16 May, raised the number from 33 to 37 additional judges apart from the CJI, and was proposed to be replaced by a Bill in the Monsoon Session.
The chronological sequence is 1950 (8), 1977 (18), 1986 (26) and 2009 (31).

secs.t: Retired and ad hoc judges - Articles 127, 128; additional judges

x: Article 127 applies when there is no quorum of permanent judges available to hold or continue a sitting of the Supreme Court.
A retired judge sitting under Article 128 has the powers of a Supreme Court judge but is not deemed to be a regular judge of the Court.
Article 224 deals with additional and acting judges of High Courts.

secs.t: Original jurisdiction - Article 131

x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original writ jurisdiction, but it is not exclusive because High Courts may issue writs under Article 226.
Election disputes concerning Parliament and State Legislatures are outside the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction and ordinarily go to the High Courts.
The Supreme Court evolved the curative petition in
Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra
(2002), permitting a limited remedy after dismissal of a review petition in exceptional circumstances.

secs.t: Independence safeguards - statement-based

x: A Supreme Court Judge can be removed by the President only after both Houses of Parliament pass an address supported by the prescribed special majority.
Salaries cannot be varied to a judge’s disadvantage except as permitted during a Financial Emergency; the safeguard is that ordinary executive action cannot reduce them.
Under Article 121, the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge cannot be discussed in Parliament except upon a motion for the Judge’s removal.
Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court Judge from practice in India, while Article 220 permits a retired High Court Judge to practise only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts.

secs.t: Supreme Court FIRSTs - persons, inauguration

x: The Federal Court was established in 1937, Privy Council appeals were abolished in 1949, the Supreme Court was inaugurated in 1950, and it shifted to Tilak Marg in 1958.
The Supreme Court is dealt with in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147, and performs the role of final constitutional interpreter and guardian of Fundamental Rights.

secs.t: Jurisdictions - appellate, SLP, advisory, Article 142, court of record

x: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from judgments or orders of any court or tribunal in India, except those relating to the armed forces.
Article 145 requires at least
five
Judges for hearing a case involving a substantial question of interpretation of the Constitution.
Article 129 recognises the Supreme Court as a Court of Record and expressly gives it the power to punish contempt of itself.

secs.t: Qualifications, resignation and removal - Article 124, Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968

x: Article 124(4) deals with removal of a Supreme Court judge, while Article 218 applies the relevant provisions to High Court judges.
Removal of a Supreme Court or High Court judge is permitted only for
proved misbehaviour or incapacity
, through the constitutionally prescribed procedure.
Under Articles 148 and 324(5), the CAG and the CEC have removal protection comparable to that of
a Supreme Court judge
Under Article 67(b), the Rajya Sabha passes the removal resolution by an effective majority and the Lok Sabha agrees to it.
Article 124(3) requires Indian citizenship and either five years as a High Court Judge, ten years as a High Court advocate, or being a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.
Article 124(7) prohibits a retired Supreme Court Judge from pleading or acting before any court or authority within India.
The in-house procedure of 1999 handles complaints of lesser misconduct against higher judiciary members without invoking the formal constitutional removal process.
The
Memorandum of Procedure
governs the process of appointment of Judges to the higher judiciary.

secs.t: Chief Justices and judges - FIRST, longest-serving, present, from AP

x: Justice
Y.V. Chandrachud
served as Chief Justice of India from 1978 to 1985 and was the longest-serving CJI.
K. Subba Rao served as CJI in 1966–67 and N.V. Ramana served in 2021–22; both were from Andhra Pradesh.
Justice B.R. Gavai retired in
November 2025
and was succeeded by Justice Surya Kant as Chief Justice of India.

secs.t: Supreme Court of India vs US Supreme Court

x: India's appellate scope is broader and includes special leave under Article 136, whereas the US Supreme Court mainly considers constitutional and federal questions.
The Indian formulation is associated with a narrower review standard, while due process in the United States permits substantive as well as procedural review.
Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right in India and enables the Supreme Court to issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

secs.t: Appointment reform proposals → body

x: The 2023 Parliamentary Standing Committee recommended amending the Memorandum of Procedure so that the Collegium recommends adequate numbers of
women and marginalised candidates
The listed reform ideas include judicial standards and accountability legislation, a permanent disciplinary authority, asset disclosure, RTI on the administrative side and transparent appointments.
“Imperium in imperio” literally conveys the criticism that the Collegium functions like an authority within an authority, reflecting concerns about opacity and judges selecting judges.

secs.t: Transfer of judges and Memorandum of Procedure

x: Appointment is linked with Article 217(1), transfer with Article 222, and the Memorandum of Procedure provides for recommendation by the CJI and two senior-most judges, generally from outside the candidate's parent High Court.

The sequence is recommendation by the CJI and two senior-most judges, consideration by the Union Law Minister, consultation with the concerned State, and appointment by the President after consultation with the CJI and Governor.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Article 130 permits the Supreme Court to sit at places other than its principal seat, subject to the decision of the Chief Justice of India with the approval of the Central Government.
The sanctioned judge strength was raised to 38 through an ordinance in May 2026, when the case backlog was nearing six figures.
The debate includes criticism of Collegium opacity, concerns regarding executive delays in notifying names, and demands for diversity and regional benches.
The Collegium named Chief Justices for the
Patna, Calcutta, Bombay, and Punjab and Haryana
High Courts in August 2026.

rows.title: High Courts and subordinate judiciary; judicial review, judicial activism, PIL and judicial overreach debate
sub: Group-II M1-B-37: High Courts and subordinate courts; the High Court of Andhra Pradesh
Group-II M1-B-39: Judicial review - meaning, scope, constitutional basis and limits
Group-II M1-B-40: Judicial activism - meaning, causes, instruments (PIL) and the judicial overreach debate

secs.t: High Court of AP - Andhra State HC, united AP HC, separate HC at Amaravati, first Chief Justice, AP Reorganisation Act 2014

x: Exam angle: date of the separate High Court (1 Jan 2019), seat (Amaravati), first Chief Justice "in Vijayawada".
The Andhra State High Court was established at
Guntur
on 5 July 1954.
From 2014 until the establishment of the separate Andhra Pradesh High Court,
Andhra Pradesh and Telangana shared a Common High Court at Hyderabad
Section 31
provided for the separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh and stated that its principal seat would be notified by the President.
Justice C. Praveen Kumar took charge as the first acting Chief Justice on 1 January 2019, and Justice J.K. Maheshwari became the first regular Chief Justice in October 2019.
All three statements are correct: the count rose from 24 to 25, and the separate Andhra Pradesh High Court functions at Amaravati.

secs.t: High Court - establishment, jurisdiction over UTs, retirement age, strength, acting and additional judges

x: Article 230
concerns the extension of the jurisdiction of High Courts to Union Territories and also permits exclusion of such jurisdiction by parliamentary law.
A High Court judge is removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge: an address by both Houses of Parliament, passed by the prescribed special majority, on proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
Under Article 222, the President transfers a High Court judge after consulting the Chief Justice of India; the CJI consults the collegium and the Chief Justices of both High Courts concerned.
Article 223 concerns an acting Chief Justice, Article 224(1) additional judges, Article 224(2) acting judges and Article 224A retired judges sitting in a High Court.
Additional judges may be appointed for a period not exceeding
two years
, generally to meet temporary increases in work or arrears.

secs.t: PIL - other name, pioneering judges, origin, landmark PILs

x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi, enabling a public-spirited citizen to move the court for persons who cannot approach it themselves.
Kapila Hingorani
is known as the ‘Mother of PILs’ because she filed the Hussainara Khatoon case on behalf of undertrial prisoners.
Hussainara Khatoon was decided in 1979, S.P. Gupta in 1981, M.C. Mehta environmental cases followed, and Vishaka was decided in 1997.
Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
Justices
O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.

secs.t: Judicial review - Articles 13, 32, 137, 226; polity it symbolises; source country

x: Article 13
provides that laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void, including pre-Constitution laws to the extent of inconsistency.
The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 extends to enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose, making it wider in scope than Article 32.
Article 136
confers the Supreme Court’s special leave jurisdiction, while Articles 132 to 135 deal with specified appellate matters.
Article 227
confers on High Courts the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within their territorial jurisdiction, subject to constitutional limitations.
The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure.

secs.t: Judicial activism - origin, activism vs overreach

x: The term ‘judicial activism’ was coined in 1947 by
Arthur Schlesinger Jr
., an American historian.
Judicial overreach occurs when courts enter the executive or legislative domain, thereby straining separation of powers.
Judicial activism has been associated with concerns such as violation of separation of powers, courts doing executive work, weak enforcement of PIL orders, letter petitions and delays in other cases.
The broad and undefined expression ‘complete justice’ under Article 142 is viewed as capable of bypassing democratic scrutiny when used expansively.
In
Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass
(2007), the Supreme Court cautioned judges not to encroach upon legislative and executive functions.

secs.t: Judicial pendency - cases pending, vacancies, reform tools

x: The
Department of Justice web portal
tracks vacancies in the district judiciary every month.
e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
The scheme provides special funding ratios for specified regions and includes the stated overall and Gram Nyayalaya allocations.
The Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure is monitored on the
Nyaya Vikas Portal

secs.t: Legislative response to judgments - ordinary law vs amendment

x: The legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment.
The First Amendment, enacted in 1951, followed early judicial rulings relating to
land reform and reservation
An ordinary Act cannot replace the basic structure doctrine of the Constitution.
The Madras Bar Association decisions struck down Tribunal Reforms provisions that re-enacted conditions previously rejected by the Court.

secs.t: High Court judges - appointment, transfer, resignation, removal instances, writ and supervisory powers, contempt

x: The President appoints High Court Judges after consulting the CJI and the Governor; in the case of a puisne Judge, the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is also consulted.
Justice Soumitra Sen of the Calcutta High Court resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal.
The motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan involved 107 MPs, and the inquiry report concerning Yashwant Varma was to be tabled despite his resignation.
Fair criticism and accurate reporting
are recognised exceptions or safeguards; wilful disobedience, obstruction and scandalising conduct may constitute contempt.
The
Third Judges Case
, arising from the Presidential Reference under Article 143 in 1998, expanded the Supreme Court collegium to the CJI and four senior-most judges.
The First Judges Case established executive primacy; the Second equated consultation with concurrence; the Third expanded the collegium; and the Fourth struck down the NJAC framework.

secs.t: Subordinate judiciary - Article 233, AIJS, Lok Adalats, Gram Nyayalayas, mobile courts

x: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court, and the seven-year advocacy requirement applies to a person from outside the judicial service.
Article 235
vests control over district and subordinate courts in the High Court, including matters such as postings, promotions and leave.
The debate balances uniform merit-based recruitment against concerns relating to State and High Court control and the importance of local languages.
A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of Judicial Magistrate First Class rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level.

All four pairs are correctly matched: Articles 233, 234 and 235 deal respectively with District Judges, other judicial officers and High Court control; Articles 236–237 concern definitions and extension to magistrates.

secs.t: High Courts in India - total number, newest, common High Courts, benches

x: The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over Maharashtra, Goa and the Union Territory of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

The Northern Council has the listed northern States, Delhi and UTs; the Central Council has Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh; the Eastern and Western combinations correspond to i and ii respectively.

secs.t: Common and new High Courts, UTs - who establishes them, Article 241, UT amendment

x: Article 231
empowers Parliament by law to establish a common High Court for two or more States or for States and a Union Territory.
Article 241 authorises Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a Union Territory or declare a court there to be a High Court.
A new High Court is created under a law made by Parliament and brought into being through a Presidential notification.

secs.t: Article → subject match

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2023 matched 137-review, 226-HC writs, 13-void laws, 32-SC writs.

Article 13 concerns laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights; Article 32 provides Supreme Court writs; Article 137 permits Supreme Court review; and Article 226 concerns High Court writs for Fundamental Rights and other purposes.
Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer certain cases to itself.

secs.t: Overcoming a judgment - options before government and legislature

x: A constitutional amendment, a valid law removing the basis of the judgment, and a review petition under Article 137 are available remedies; a curative petition may be the last judicial resort.
The legislature may alter the legal basis on which a judgment rests through a valid law, but it cannot simply declare the judicial decision invalid.

secs.t: Judicial review as a symbol of which government and its theory

x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government.

secs.t: Actions of Governor and President - reviewability

x: The 38th Amendment (1975) made the satisfaction under Articles 123, 213 and 352 non-justiciable; the 44th Amendment (1978) reversed that position.

Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations.

secs.t: Meaning and origin - countries, source

x: Judicial review
is the power of courts to test the constitutional validity of laws and executive actions and invalidate those that are ultra vires.
Marbury v. Madison
(1803), decided under Chief Justice John Marshall, is regarded as the landmark case establishing judicial review in the United States.
Sir Edward Coke’s resistance to King James I is cited as an early historical root of the idea that judicial authority can control the exercise of governmental power.

secs.t: Limits - political questions, restraint, procedure established by law

x: Indian review under ‘procedure established by law’ traditionally focuses on legal validity and procedure, while American due process includes procedural and substantive fairness.
The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
Courts generally exercise restraint in purely political and policy matters, while retaining the power to examine unconstitutional or capricious action.

secs.t: Judicial activism as a new feature - stages in India

x: The sequence is: post-Emergency activism in the mid-1970s, expansion of Article 21 from 1979 to the 1980s, governance cases from the 1990s onward, and Puttaswamy in 2017.
The later stage included
governance and accountability
interventions such as the CVC case, 2G case, coal block cancellation, the Jharkhand Assembly case and directions concerning candidates’ affidavits.

secs.t: Doctrines and remedies evolved by the Supreme Court - genuine vs others

x: Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
The Basic Structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973.
Removal of unnecessary handcuffing is associated with protection of prisoners’ dignity and the broader human-rights dimension of judicial activism.

secs.t: Instruments - suo motu, continuing mandamus, guidelines, expert committees

x: Continuing mandamus
keeps the matter open so that the court can monitor implementation and compliance over time.
The Vishaka Guidelines of 1997 addressed workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation and operated until the POSH Act, 2013.
Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice, including interim remedies in situations involving legislative delay and institutional deadlock.

secs.t: Activism cases

x: Olga Tellis (1985) recognised the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers as part of the protection afforded by Article 21.
The M. C. Mehta cases from the 1980s onward produced extensive environmental directions and also generated debate about judicial policy-making.
The Vishaka judgment was delivered in 1997 and laid down guidelines concerning sexual harassment at the workplace before the POSH Act, 2013.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Judicial activism has democratised access to justice and promoted executive accountability, but it can also blur separation of powers and contribute to overburdened courts.
The High Court moved from Guntur in 1954 to Hyderabad in 1956, became part of the common High Court arrangement in 2014, and shifted to Amaravati in 2019.
A criticism of fast-track courts is that they may increase the speed of disposal without increasing the number of judges, thereby not fully addressing structural capacity problems.

rows.title: Tribunals - Articles 323A and 323B; administrative and specialised tribunals; tribunal reforms
sub: Group-II M1-B-41: Tribunals under Articles 323A and 323B; administrative adjudication

secs.t: Central Administrative Tribunal - legal basis, members, jurisdiction, when set up, appeals

x: CAT has its main Bench at New Delhi and 18 outlying Benches, and its jurisdiction includes specified Central and All-India service matters, civilian defence employees and notified PSUs, but excludes armed forces personnel.
Following L. Chandra Kumar (1997), CAT decisions are subject to review by the
High Court through a Division Bench
, with a further appeal to the Supreme Court where applicable.
CAT has original jurisdiction over service disputes of Central civil servants, All-India Services officers and civilian defence employees.
The earlier S.P. Sampath Kumar case of 1987 also upheld judicial review in the context of tribunals.

secs.t: Specialised tribunals - parent Act and benches

x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT and also deals with appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and appeals from the Competition Commission of India.
There are 22 CGIT-cum-Labour Courts under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947; Mumbai and Kolkata also act as National Tribunals, and EPF appeals have been heard by them since the Finance Act, 2017.

secs.t: Articles 323A vs 323B - subjects, who establishes, 42nd Amendment

x: Article 323A covers recruitment and service conditions of public servants across the listed levels and permits Parliament alone to establish such tribunals.
Article 323B includes taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, elections, rent and tenancy, along with other specified subjects.
The insertion of Articles 323A and 323B by the 42nd Amendment is associated with the
Swaran Singh Committee

secs.t: L. Chandra Kumar case - High Court review of tribunal decisions

x: Both statements are true, and the basic-structure status of judicial review explains why tribunals cannot replace the constitutional review jurisdiction of the High Courts and Supreme Court.
L. Chandra Kumar struck down the exclusion clauses in Articles 323A(2)(d) and 323B(3)(d), holding that judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is part of the basic structure.

secs.t: Tribunals Reforms Act 2021 - abolished tribunals, tenure and age; the 2026 replacement

x: The
Film Certification Appellate Tribunal
was among the appellate tribunals abolished under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021.
The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
The Lok Sabha passed the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 by
voice vote
on 10 August 2026.
In the 2021 Madras Bar Association case, provisions of the
Tribunals Reforms Ordinance
were struck down because they defied earlier judicial rulings.

secs.t: State Administrative Tribunals - APAT establishment and abolition history

x: A State Administrative Tribunal is set up by the Central Government
at the request of the concerned State Government
The 32nd Amendment inserted the constitutional basis under
Article 371D
for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh to deal with public-service grievances.
The Article 371D tribunal was intended to adjudicate grievances relating to public services in Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: Administrative adjudication - quasi-judicial bodies, merits, criticisms

x: A tribunal is quasi-judicial: it is neither purely executive nor a regular court, but occupies an intermediate position between the two.
Tribunals are valued for applying principles of natural justice rather than being bound by the full procedural requirements of the Civil Procedure Code.
A major criticism is that parent ministries, which may be litigants before tribunals, also administer them, creating concerns about executive control and independence.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Although tribunals provide specialised adjudication, their decisions remain subject to the judicial-review jurisdiction of High Courts.
The Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges for the West Bengal roll disputes.
The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in 1985; the Godavari, Krishna-II and Vansadhara water tribunals are associated with 1969, 2004 and 2010 respectively.
