rows.title: Federal structure of India - features of federalism and unitary bias; Seventh Schedule (three lists), residuary powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-1: Nature of the Indian Constitution - federal, quasi-federal and unitary characterisations
Group-II M1-B-69: Unitary features of the Indian Constitution
Group-II M1-B-70: Federal features of the Indian Constitution; the nature of Indian federalism

secs.t: Subject → List (social security, opium, High Courts, mineral-right taxes, education, police, forests, cruelty to animals, panchayats, prisons)

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 matched High Courts → Union, mineral-right taxes → State, education → Concurrent; social security → Concurrent; defence/atomic energy → Union.
Education, forests, and protection of wild animals and birds are
Concurrent List
subjects under Entries 25, 17A and 17B respectively.
Education and forests
were moved to the Concurrent List by the Forty-second Constitutional Amendment.
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on
1 July 2024
, replacing the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act respectively.
Coordination and determination of standards in institutions for higher education is a Union List subject under Entry 66.

secs.t: Federal vs unitary features - statement-based identification

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - Governor, Central Services, CAG and Emergency powers all "violate federal principles" (answer: A, B, C and D).
Exam angle: assertion-reason - A: India is quasi-federal; R: residuary powers/emergency powers lie with the Centre.
Exam angle: "not a federal feature" answers are
Office of the Governor
and
CAG
. "Allocation of financial resources" is not a prominent federal feature.
Quasi-federal means federal in form but possessing a pronounced or strong unitary bias.
An emergency can substantially centralise the constitutional system and make it operate in a unitary manner without a formal constitutional amendment.
The federal scheme and emergency provisions were borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935; the strong Centre reflects the Canadian model; and the Concurrent List was borrowed from Australia.
Article 3 enables Parliament to alter the boundaries or names of States, demonstrating the strength of the Union and the unitary bias in the federal structure.
Changes affecting the representation of States in Parliament fall within the federal provisions requiring ratification by at least half of the State legislatures under the proviso to Article 368(2).
Most provisions can be amended by Parliament through the applicable special or simple majority, while specified federal provisions require ratification by at least half of the States.

secs.t: Descriptions of Indian federalism → scholar

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - "federation with a centralising tendency" =
Ivor Jennings
; APP MCQ - "quasi-federal" =
K.C. Wheare
Exam angle: one-line "Who described India as..." items, or scholar-quote matching.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar
stated that the Constitution is federal in normal times but becomes unitary during emergencies.
Carl Friedrich
made this observation about the distinctive civilisational and continental character of India.

Ivor Jennings described India as a federation with a strong centralising tendency; Granville Austin used the expression cooperative federalism; Morris Jones used bargaining federalism; and Paul Appleby called it extremely federal.
Ambedkar emphasised that India was not formed by an agreement among States, that States had no right to secede, and that the system could be unitary or federal according to time and circumstances.

secs.t: Residuary powers - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2025 - "Art. 248 = residuary" and "Parliament has exclusive power over items in no list" →
both correct
Article 248
deals with residuary legislative powers and gives Parliament exclusive power over matters not included in the State or Concurrent Lists, including residuary taxes.
The
One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
, inserted the GST-related constitutional provisions, including the qualification of Article 248 by Article 246A.

secs.t: Seventh Schedule - three lists, number of entries, key entry numbers

x: The order of precedence is Union List over Concurrent List over State List.
The Concurrent List contains subjects on which both the Union and the States may legislate.
Inserted or omitted entries can make the total count differ from the last visible entry number.

secs.t: Federal and unitary countries - examples

x: Sri Lanka is identified as a unitary country, not a federal country.
The United Kingdom is presented as a unitary country in which Parliament holds all law-making power.
Germany and Canada are federal countries, whereas China and Japan are unitary countries.

secs.t: Subjects transferred from State to Concurrent List → 42nd Amendment

x: Concurrent List entries permit Union legislation, and examples cited include farm laws through Entry 33 and education-related measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.

All four subjects listed—forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice excluding the Supreme Court and High Courts—were shifted to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment.

secs.t: Indestructible union of destructible states - no right to secede, Article 3

x: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States into the Union, particularly territories not already part of India.
The expression reflects the constitutional idea of an indestructible Union of destructible States.
B.
R. Ambedkar
explained that India is called a Union because it is indestructible and no State has the right to secede.
Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new States and alter the area, boundaries or names of existing States.
Ambedkar gave two principal reasons: the Indian Union was not formed by an agreement among States, and no State has the right to secede from it.
India is regarded as an integral whole, with division into States made for administrative convenience.

secs.t: Switching between federal and unitary modes - emergency, Art. 249, Art. 356

x: Exam angle: the President can
reduce or cancel
fund transfers, but "
increase
the transfer" is the wrong statement. Modifying the distribution of finances and giving directions to States are correct consequences.
Exam angle: "internal disturbance" is no longer a ground. "Art. 311 - Financial Emergency" is the mismatch; Financial Emergency is
Art. 360
A National Emergency must be approved by both Houses within one month by the prescribed special majority and may continue through successive six-month approvals.
Continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year requires that a National Emergency is in operation and that the Election Commission certifies the difficulty of holding elections in the State.
Part XVIII, comprising Articles 352 to 360, enables the federal system to operate in a unitary manner during emergencies without a formal constitutional amendment.
The ability to shift between federal and unitary modes without a formal constitutional amendment is regarded as
a unique feature of the Indian constitutional system
Article 352 concerns war, external aggression or armed rebellion; Article 356 concerns failure of constitutional machinery; and Article 360 concerns financial stability or credit.
Articles 249, 312 and 67(b) respectively deal with State List legislation in the national interest, creation of All-India Services and initiation of the Vice-President’s removal.

secs.t: Supreme Court characterisations of Indian federalism

x: In
State of West Bengal v Union of India
(1962), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution was not truly federal and that States were not sovereign.
Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the cited constitutional cases directly support the conclusion that federalism forms part of the basic structure.

secs.t: Centrally controlled institutions - Governor's office, All-India and central services, audit, elections - critique as violating federal principles

x: All India Services such as the IAS, IPS and IFoS are recruited through the UPSC and serve the States as well as the Union.
The Comptroller and Auditor General audits both Union and State accounts.
India has a single integrated judiciary, and the Centre appoints High Court judges.

secs.t: Unitary government - characteristics, merits and demerits

x: A unitary government does not constitutionally divide sovereign powers between the Centre and local units.
Uniform laws, quick decisions and a strong response to crises are merits of a unitary system.
Over-centralisation and neglect of local needs are important disadvantages of a unitary system.
India has a federal structure but includes several centralising features, resulting in a strong Union.

secs.t: Representation of states in Rajya Sabha - basis compared with equal representation

x: Rajya Sabha seats are allocated to States on the basis of population and are listed in the Fourth Schedule.
Uttar Pradesh has 31 seats in the Rajya Sabha under the population-based allocation system.
Rajya Sabha representation is based broadly on population rather than equal State representation.

secs.t: Federalism - definition, distinction from other systems, source of India's federal scheme → Act

x: Federalism involves constitutionally divided powers between the Union and State governments, each supreme in its assigned sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
A confederation is a loose league of sovereign States, generally retaining the right to secede.
While the Government of India Act, 1935 provided the source of India’s federal scheme, the strong Centre was particularly modelled on
Canada

secs.t: Nature of Indian federalism - essential federal feature, right of states to secede, national-integration design, federal-unitary debate

x: The absence of a right to secede and the strength of the Union produce a
centripetal bias
, drawing the constituent units towards the Union rather than away from it.
The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States.
Indian federalism is commonly described as quasi-federal or as federal in structure with unitary features.

secs.t: India vs USA federal systems - common and differing features (citizenship, lists, judiciary)

x: India is a holding-together federation in which a large country distributes power among units to preserve unity.
India has the Union, State and Concurrent Lists, and residuary powers belong to the Centre.
India has a single integrated judiciary, whereas the USA maintains
separate federal and State court systems
Indian States generally do not possess separate constitutions; the former Jammu and Kashmir was an exception.

secs.t: Federal practice over time - phases of centralisation and decentralisation by decade

x: The Rajamannar Committee was set up in 1969 during the phase from 1967 to 1977, when non-Congress State governments led to greater Centre-State confrontation.
The Sarkaria Commission was appointed in 1983, falling within the 1977-1989 phase.
From 2014 onward, NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 and GST was introduced in 2017, within the framework described as cooperative-competitive federalism.

secs.t: Holding-together vs coming-together federations

x: Switzerland
is a coming-together federation in which independent States or units pool sovereignty while retaining equal power.
All four statements correctly describe the two types of federation and their examples.
India's federation is described as formed by “disintegration”, meaning division of power within a large country.

secs.t: Asymmetric federalism - Article 370 (former), Article 371 series, Fifth and Sixth Schedules

x: Article 370 provided Jammu and Kashmir with a separate constitution and flag.
Article 370 provided the special arrangements, which were made inoperative in August 2019; the Supreme Court upheld the action in December 2023.
The special provisions referred to in the Article 371 series extend from Article 371 to Article 371J.
The Sixth Schedule provides for autonomous district councils in
Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The suggested measures included a narrower Concurrent List, a stronger Inter-State Council and reform of Governors;
complete abolition of the Concurrent List
was not stated as a proposed measure.
Fiscal transfer concerns, delays by Governors and ‘double engine’ politics were cited as weakening the federal spirit.
The resolution referred to
vertical fiscal imbalance, cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool, and matching shares in Centrally Sponsored Schemes
The Committee examined
Union-State relations
, and its first part was tabled by Tamil Nadu in the context of seeking a more federal Constitution.
The debate connected possible election deferrals with prolonged President’s Rule and the limits associated with Article 356(5), while recalling earlier misuse addressed in the Bommai context.
Reforms concerning fiscal federalism under GST were suggested as part of the broader debate on strengthening the federal balance.
The resolution demanded that Tamil Nadu receive its fair share of
tax devolution
in accordance with fiscal federalism.

rows.title: Centre-State legislative relations - Articles 245-255, doctrine of repugnancy, parliamentary legislation on state list
sub: Group-II M1-B-42: Distribution of legislative powers - Seventh Schedule and Articles 245-255
Group-II M1-B-43: Parliament's power to legislate on State List subjects; residuary powers and repugnancy

secs.t: Parliament legislating on State List → article and condition

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2023 - during an Emergency, State List laws are made by
Parliament
; PYQ 2018 - international agreements =
Art. 253
Exam angle: statement sets asking which situations are valid ("request of two or more states" is valid; a request by one state is not).
A law made under Article 250 continues after the National Emergency but lapses six months after the Emergency ceases, unless otherwise continued under constitutional authority.
Article 253 authorises Parliament to make laws for implementing international treaties, agreements and conventions, even when the subject would otherwise fall within the State sphere.
Subjects not enumerated in the Union, State or Concurrent Lists fall within the residuary field, and residuary legislative powers are vested in
Parliament
Article 249
enables Parliament to legislate on State List matters in the national interest, subject to a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by the prescribed majority.

secs.t: Article 249 resolution - Rajya Sabha majority, duration, extension

x: Every renewal can extend the resolution only for one year at a time.
The resolution may be renewed any number of times, but each renewal is limited to one year.
A law enacted under Article 249 continues for six months after the resolution authorising it lapses, after which it ceases to operate.
An Article 249 resolution does not suspend the State Legislature’s power.

secs.t: Conflict between lists - Article 246, order of precedence

x: Article 246(4) enables Parliament to legislate on any matter for any part of the territory of India not included in a State, including Union Territories.
Article 246A gives both Parliament and State Legislatures power to make GST laws.
Article 246A was introduced by
the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act
, which established the constitutional framework for GST.

secs.t: Residuary legislative power - Article 248, Part XI, Union List Entry 97

x: Article 248 is located in
Part XI
, which deals with relations between the Union and the States and extends from Articles 245 to 263.
The idea of vesting residuary powers in the central legislature was borrowed from
Canada
, a federation with a strong Centre.
The Sarkaria Commission in 1988 recommended moving all residuary powers other than taxation to the Concurrent List.

secs.t: Repugnancy - Article 254, President's assent exception

x: The doctrine of repugnancy is contained in Article 254, which is located in
Part XI
dealing with Union-State relations.
The Governor may reserve a State Bill for the President under Article 254(2), enabling the Presidential-assent exception to operate.
Article 251
provides that laws made by Parliament under Articles 249 and 250 prevail over State laws.

secs.t: Part XI Chapter I - Articles 245-255; Article 255

x: Article 247 empowers Parliament to establish additional courts for the better administration of laws made by Parliament or existing laws relating to matters in the Union List.
A State may impose reasonable restrictions on inter-State trade in the public interest, but a Bill for that purpose requires the President's previous sanction.
Article 253 empowers Parliament to make laws for implementing international treaties, agreements and conventions, notwithstanding the ordinary distribution of legislative subjects.

secs.t: Territorial extent of laws - Article 245

x: Parliament may legislate for the whole or any part of India, and an extra-territorial operation does not by itself invalidate parliamentary legislation.
Regulations made by
the President
for Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament.
The Governor may bar or modify the application of Acts of Parliament in Scheduled Areas.

secs.t: Doctrine of pith and substance applied to list conflicts - cases

x: Harmonious construction
requires apparently overlapping entries to be interpreted together so that both retain operative effect.
The
doctrine of pith and substance
looks to the true nature and character of the law and disregards incidental encroachment on another legislative field.
The doctrine of
colourable legislation
prevents a legislature from achieving indirectly what it lacks power to do directly.

secs.t: Odd one out - item not in a given list

x: Exam angle: a list of four subjects where one belongs to another list.
Fisheries
is a State List subject.

secs.t: Seventh Schedule - three lists, entries originally and now

x: Article 246
gives the constitutional framework for the distribution of legislative subjects in the three lists of the Seventh Schedule.
The Union List has the greatest predominance, followed by the Concurrent List and then the State List.

secs.t: Constitutional basis for central laws on unusual subjects

x: Prevention of cruelty to animals is placed in
Concurrent List Entry 17
, enabling Parliament to enact central legislation on the subject.
Parliament can legislate on the State subject through Articles 249, 250 or 252, among the specified routes.
Article 253
authorises Parliament to legislate for implementing treaties, agreements, conventions and decisions of international bodies, even on State List subjects.

secs.t: Limits on Parliament's legislative competence

x: Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and 356 are the stated constitutional routes permitting Parliament to legislate in fields otherwise within the State List.
Article 245(2) protects Parliamentary laws from invalidity merely because they have extra-territorial operation.
Articles 301 to 303 restrict discriminatory or preferential treatment between States in laws relating to trade and commerce.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India follows the Canadian approach by placing residuary powers with the Centre, contributing to a comparatively strong Union.
Kerala
criticised the measure as an encroachment on State powers relating to Entries 18 and 50 and indicated that it might approach the courts.

The relevant distribution divides the subject between Union List Entry 9, dealing with defence, foreign affairs and security, and Concurrent List Entry 3, dealing with State security and public order.
The Bill sought to restrict the States’ power to tax
mineral rights and mineral-bearing land
, raising concerns about federal encroachment.

rows.title: Distribution of executive powers between the Union and the States
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-44

secs.t: Executive power of the Union - Art. 53 vesting, Art. 73 extent, President as formal head

x: The President's power as Supreme Commander is regulated by law.
The President is the constitutional or formal head.
Article 73 includes rights, authority and jurisdiction arising from treaties or agreements, with executive operation across the whole of India.

secs.t: State executive power - Art. 154 vesting, Art. 162 extent

x: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the
Governor
, who may exercise it directly or through subordinate officers.
Article 162 extends State executive power to matters on which the State Legislature has power to make laws, within the State's territory.
The Governor of Nagaland has special responsibility under Article 371A, and the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh under Article 371H, in relation to law and order.

secs.t: Executive power in Concurrent List subjects - default rule and exceptions

x: The default rule is that executive power over Concurrent List subjects remains with the States.
The exception to the State default arises where the Constitution or a Parliamentary law expressly gives the executive power to the Centre, through the provisos to Articles 73 and 162.
The territorial extent of executive power follows that of
legislative power

secs.t: Entrustment of functions between Union and states - by consent and by law

x: Articles 256 and 257 impose obligations on States, and non-compliance may attract Article 365, which can open the way to action under Article 356.
Article 258(2)
permits Parliament, by law, to confer functions relating to Union matters on a State or its officers without the State's consent.

secs.t: Emergency effects on executive relations - Articles 353, 356, 360

x: Article 353 permits the Union executive to give directions to any State on any matter during a National Emergency.
Under Article 353, the Union's power to issue directions expands during a National Emergency, but State governments continue to exist and are not suspended merely because of the Emergency.
During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may require Money Bills and other Financial Bills of States to be reserved for the President's consideration.

secs.t: Executive heads of Union Territories - administrators, LGs, Delhi (Art. 239AA)

x: The Lieutenant Governor or Administrator exercises executive power in a Union Territory as the representative of the President.
Chandigarh, Lakshadweep, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu are headed by Administrators.
The
69th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991
inserted Article 239AA and provided Delhi with a Legislative Assembly and a Council of Ministers.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The proposed sui generis elected body for Ladakh is intended to possess legislative, executive and financial powers.
The Governor must act on the advice of the State Cabinet while exercising the remission power under Article 161.
The Governor's discretion is not unlimited and the Governor ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers.

rows.title: Centre-State administrative relations - Articles 256-263, all-India services, directions to states
sub: Group-II M1-B-45: Administrative relations - Articles 256-263, all-India services, inter-state council and zonal councils

secs.t: All India Services - Article 312, removal, creation of new services, AIS vs Central Services

x: Exam angle: "AIS officer can be removed only by the Union Government" is the correct statement.
Article 312 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than
two-thirds of the members present and voting
before Parliament can create a new All India Service.
The correct sequence is IAS restructuring in 1947, UPSC replacing the Federal PSC in 1950, insertion of Article 258A in 1956, and creation of IFoS in 1966.

secs.t: Centre's directions to states - Articles 256 and 257; non-compliance → Article 365

x: Article 365
permits the President to hold that a State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution when the State fails to comply with Union directions.

When a State fails to comply with directions issued under a constitutional provision, such as Articles 256 or 257, the President may conclude that the State government cannot be carried on constitutionally, leading to Article 356 action.

secs.t: Delegation of functions - Articles 258 and 258A

x: Article 258(1) empowers the President to entrust Union functions to a State Government or its officers with the consent of the State Government.
Article 258A enables the Governor to entrust functions of the State to the Union or its officers with the consent of the Government of India.
Delegation under these Articles provides flexibility in administration and helps avoid rigidity and deadlock between the Union and the States.

secs.t: Armed forces and central forces deployment in states - consent issue

x: States object because public order and police fall in Entries 1 and 2 of the State List, making deployment a sensitive issue concerning State authority.
The 1966 Administrative Reforms Commission supported deployment “on their request or otherwise,” meaning that a State request was not treated as indispensable.
The 2025 Supreme Court order referred to granting CAPF officers Organised Group A status and reducing IPS deputation.

secs.t: Public Service Commissions for joint states - JSPSC

x: A Joint State Public Service Commission is created through an Act of Parliament, while its members are appointed by the President.
Article 323A was inserted by the
42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
, to provide for administrative tribunals.
The CAT was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, has its principal bench at New Delhi, and is described here as having 18 benches and 69 members.

secs.t: Integrated administrative tools - Zonal Councils, cooperation, grants

x: Article 261 deals with full faith and credit to public acts, records and judicial proceedings throughout India.
Article 307 provides for an authority to carry out the purposes of the constitutional provisions relating to trade, commerce and intercourse within India.
The ARC was established in 1966, initially chaired by Morarji Desai, later by K. Hanumanthaiya, and its study team was headed by M.C. Setalvad in 1969.

secs.t: Zonal Councils and North Eastern Council - statutory basis, chairman, AP's zone

x: The North-Eastern Council is a separate body established under the
North-Eastern Council Act, 1971
, unlike the five Zonal Councils created under the 1956 Act.
A NITI Aayog representative, Chief Secretaries and Development Commissioners serve as advisers without voting rights to the Zonal Councils.
The 2002 amendment added Sikkim and gave the NEC the role of a regional planning body, while the Union Home Minister has served as its ex-officio Chairman since 2018.

secs.t: Full faith and credit to public acts, records and judicial proceedings

x: Article 261 requires
full faith and credit throughout India to public acts, records and judicial proceedings
of the Union and every State.
Article 261(3)
provides that final judgments and orders of civil courts in any part of India may be executed anywhere within India according to law.

secs.t: All-India vs Central vs State services - classify

x: The
Indian Forest Service
, along with the IAS and IPS, is an All-India Service.
IAS and IPS are All-India Services, the Indian Foreign Service is a Central Service, and the State civil service is a State Service.
State police services belong to the State Services category; they are not All-India Services.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: the meeting was held near Mamallapuram on 20 August 2026, chaired by Home Minister Amit Shah, with Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay as vice-chairman.
The Supreme Court-directed Supervisory Committee in the Mullaperiyar matter involves the
National Dam Safety Authority
under the Dam Safety Act, 2021.

rows.title: Centre-State financial relations - Articles 264-293; taxes assigned, grants-in-aid, borrowing powers
sub: Group-II M1-B-46: Financial relations - tax distribution, divisible pool, grants-in-aid, borrowing powers

secs.t: Taxes by levy, collection and appropriation → Article (268, 269, 270); 80th and 101st Amendments

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2018 - taxes levied and collected by Centre but assigned to states =
Art. 269
Exam angle: statements that surcharges under Art. 271 are shared with states (false).

The 80th Amendment implemented the Tenth Finance Commission's Alternative Scheme of Devolution, provided for States' share in gross Union taxes and omitted Article 272 concerning shared Union excise duties.
Before 2000, Article 269 also assigned taxes on stock-exchange transactions other than stamp duty, estate duty, railway fares and newspapers to the States.
Article 270 covers Union List taxes shared as recommended by the Finance Commission, but excludes Articles 268, 269 and 269A taxes, Article 271 surcharges and cesses.

The 80th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2000, effective from 1 April 1996, introduced an alternative scheme of devolution under which all Union taxes were pooled and shared, replacing the earlier arrangement involving 29% of certain taxes.

secs.t: Borrowing powers - Articles 292 and 293

x: The Net Borrowing Ceiling is imposed through
Article 293(3)
, which requires Union consent for further State borrowing when specified Union loans or guarantees remain outstanding.
The Kerala case involved the counting of off-budget borrowings, the operation of Article 293(3), and an original suit before the Supreme Court under Article 131.
The Sixteenth Finance Commission caps the State fiscal deficit at 3% of GSDP and calls for ending off-budget borrowing.
Kerala's 2024 suit under Article 131 challenged
the Net Borrowing Ceiling imposed under Article 293(3)

secs.t: Grants-in-aid - statutory vs discretionary → Article

x: Statutory grants under Article 275 are made on the recommendation of the Finance Commission, not NITI Aayog.
The special grants in lieu of export duty on jute are associated with
Assam, Bihar, West Bengal and Odisha
Article 275 grants are statutory grants, recommended by the Finance Commission and charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

secs.t: Grants vs tax devolution - effect of a shift between them

x: The Fifteenth Finance Commission recommended a
41 percent
share of the divisible pool for the States.
The budget estimate of tax devolution for 2024–25 was
₹12.47 lakh crore
The report of the Sixteenth Finance Commission was tabled on
1 February 2026
Devolution to States in 2024–25 was reported at approximately
₹12.87 lakh crore

secs.t: Profession tax - Article 276 ceiling, amendment

x: Article 276(2) permits profession tax up to
₹2,500 per person per year
The Sixtieth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 raised the profession-tax ceiling under Article 276 from ₹250 to ₹2,500 per annum.

secs.t: Plan transfer formulas - Gadgil, Gadgil-Mukherjee; special category status

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2017 - Gadgil formula =
devolution of funds
Special category States received Central Plan assistance on the favourable basis of
90 percent grant and 10 percent loan
, with the grants treated as a first charge on such assistance.

Special category parameters included difficult terrain, low population density or sizeable tribal population, strategic border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, and non-viable State finances.

secs.t: Part XII (Articles 264-293) - content, state-exclusive taxes, fiscal disputes

x: Articles 266 and 267
deal respectively with the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts, and the Contingency Fund.
Articles 280 and 281 concern the Finance Commission and its recommendations, while Articles 292 and 293 concern Union and State borrowing respectively.
Article 131
confers original jurisdiction on the Supreme Court in disputes involving legal rights between the Union and one or more States or between States.

secs.t: GST and state fiscal autonomy - compensation cess, GST Council voting weights

x: A proposal in the GST Council requires at least
three-fourths of the weighted votes
of the members present and voting.
Crude oil, petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel, natural gas, electricity, alcohol for human consumption and real estate are listed outside GST.
Article 269A concerns IGST, with the revenue going to
the destination State
in accordance with the destination-based character of GST.
All three statements correctly describe the GST Council’s weighted voting system: one-third for the Centre, two-thirds for the States collectively, and a three-fourths majority for decisions.

secs.t: Tax - levying, collecting and appropriating authority

x: Corporation tax is levied and collected by the Union and has been shared with the States since the 80th Constitutional Amendment.
Union property is exempt from State taxation and State property from Union taxation; however, the Centre can tax a State's commercial operations and State-owned companies.

secs.t: Financial relations framework - Part, Articles, emergencies, Consolidated Fund

x: Part XII is titled Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits, and the financial-relations provisions stated here are Articles 268 to 293.
Article 354
empowers the President to modify the distribution of revenues during a National Emergency.
During a Financial Emergency, the Centre may issue directions to States regarding financial propriety and require Money and Financial Bills to be reserved for the President.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The protest concerned the perceived adverse effect of population-heavy or population-based criteria on the devolution share of southern States.
Vertical fiscal imbalance, non-shareable cesses and CSS conditionality are identified criticisms.
Non-shareable cesses, estimated at about 18% of gross tax revenue, reduce the effective devolution to around 31–32%, below the 41% award share.

rows.title: Centre-State relations - the constitutional scheme and areas of friction
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-46

secs.t: National emergency - effects on Centre-State relations (Arts 250, 353, 354)

x: A National Emergency strengthens the Union and makes the constitutional system operate in a unitary or quasi-unitary manner.
The term of the Lok Sabha may be extended by Parliament for one year at a time during a National Emergency, subject to the constitutional limitation concerning the period after the Emergency ends.

secs.t: Union's duty to protect states - Art 355, links to 356 and 365

x: Article 355 requires the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure that the government of each State is carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
The duty imposed on the Union by
Article 355
to protect States and ensure constitutional government provides the constitutional basis connected with Article 356 action.

secs.t: Constitutional scheme - Parts XI and XII, factors shaping relations

x: Part XI contains legislative relations in Articles 245–255 and administrative relations in Articles 256–263 between the Union and the States.
Part XII deals with financial relations, including Articles 268 to 293.
All India Services are a unitary feature because they provide a common administrative structure serving both the Union and the States.

secs.t: Areas of friction - Governor, 356, fiscal transfers, AIS, river waters, central agencies

x: Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, leaving the pool at approximately 81% of gross tax revenue and reducing the shareable base for States.
Article 262 concerns inter-State river-water disputes, Section 6 of the DSPE Act concerns State consent for CBI investigation, and Article 156 concerns the Governor's office.

secs.t: Recent friction issues - GST compensation, borrowing, Governor disputes

x: Recent friction involved delays in dealing with Bills in Tamil Nadu and Kerala and instances where addresses to the Assembly were skipped.
All three statements are correct: non-shareable cesses were about 18% of gross tax revenue, actual devolution was nearer 31–32%, and the 16th Finance Commission retained a 41% share for 2026–31.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh issues - SCS, APRA 2014 assurances, Polavaram funding

x: The cited unmet assurances include the
Kadapa steel plant, Dugarajapatnam port and metro rail
, and were valued at about ₹5 lakh crore by the opposition.
The Budget 2026–27 provision of ₹3,320 crore was for storage up to
41.15 metres
, whereas groups demanded funding for the full 45.72 metres.
The completion target is March 2027, before the 2027 Godavari Pushkaralu, and ₹3,320 crore was provided for storage up to 41.15 metres in Budget 2026-27.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Tamil Nadu Kurian Joseph Committee was associated with the call for a structural reset of federalism.
For Andhra Pradesh, the principal federal grievances are the demand for Special Category Status and implementation of assurances under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act.

rows.title: Emergency provisions - National Emergency (352), President's Rule (356), Financial Emergency (360); S.R. Bommai case

secs.t: President's Rule - Article 356 grounds, approval and extension, consequences, Article 355, misuse

x: Article 365
provides that failure to comply with, or give effect to, Union directions can justify the conclusion that the State government cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution.
Ambedkar hoped that the emergency provision under Article 356 would remain a “
dead letter
” and be used only in exceptional circumstances.

secs.t: President's Rule in AP and other states - first and longest AP spells, states never under it, count by state

x: The first spell ended on 10 December 1973; the second spell began on 1 March 2014, followed by the Chief Minister’s resignation and the formation of Telangana on 2 June 2014.
The High Court considered whether it could use the Article 356 expression that constitutional machinery had broken down, and the Supreme Court stayed the proceedings.

secs.t: Consequences of National Emergency - Centre-state relations, term extension, Articles 358 and 359

x: Exam angle: LENS Jul 2026 MCQ - the statement "Arts 20 and 21 can be suspended under Art. 359" is
wrong
After the 44th Constitutional Amendment, Article 19 is automatically suspended under Article 358 only when the Emergency is proclaimed on the grounds of
war or external aggression
, not armed rebellion.

secs.t: National Emergency - grounds, written cabinet advice, approval, revocation, instances

x: A notice by at least one-tenth of the Lok Sabha members requires a special sitting within
14 days
to consider disapproval of the Emergency.
The 38th Amendment attempted to make the satisfaction non-justiciable; this position was later reversed, and Minerva Mills affirmed that the proclamation is reviewable.
The Allahabad High Court judgment voiding Indira Gandhi’s 1971 election formed the immediate political background to the 1975 Emergency.

secs.t: S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) - bench, principles

x: The proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review, particularly where it is mala fide or founded on irrelevant grounds.
S.R. Bommai established that the floor of the Assembly, rather than the Governor’s personal opinion, is the proper test of majority.
S.R. Bommai recognised secularism as a basic feature and held that a State government acting against it may be
dismissed under Article 356
, subject to constitutional safeguards.

secs.t: Financial Emergency - Article 360 consequences, instances

x: Article 360 applies where the financial stability or credit of
India or any part of its territory is threatened
A proclamation of Financial Emergency must be approved by Parliament within two months by a simple majority.
Article 360 permits the Union to issue directions to States to observe specified
canons of financial propriety

secs.t: Emergency provisions → source country and earlier Act

x: The emergency provisions and the ordinance power under Articles 123 and 213 are both regarded as relics of the Government of India Act, 1935.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The concern about deferred State elections prolonging President’s Rule is linked to the constitutional limitation associated with
Article 356(5)
Article 356
, dealing with failure of constitutional machinery in a State and President’s Rule, is among the most controversial provisions of the Constitution.
The Six-Point Formula was validated by the
32nd Constitutional Amendment Act
, 1973, which inserted Article 371D.

rows.title: Inter-state relations - inter-state council, zonal councils, river-water disputes (Article 262), full faith and credit

secs.t: Inter-State Council - Article 263, who establishes, recommending commission, Inter-Governmental Council, decision mode, Standing Committee

x: Exam angle: Assertion-Reason pairs on Art. 263 and the commission that recommended the Council.

Article 263 contemplates an Inter-State Council for investigating and discussing subjects of common interest between the Union and States or among States, and for making recommendations on such matters.

The Administrative Reforms Commission during 1966–69 and the Rajamannar Committee in 1969 were earlier advocates, while the Sarkaria Commission later recommended the Inter-State Council that was set up in 1990.

secs.t: Zonal Councils - Act, number, chairman, advisory nature, Southern Zonal Council

x: Chief Ministers serve as Vice-Chairmen by annual rotation, and the Councils are deliberative and advisory.
The Southern Zonal Council includes Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala,
Telangana
and Puducherry.
Amit Shah urged the early settlement of southern water disputes and river-linking at the meeting.

secs.t: River water disputes - Article 262, ISRWD Act 1956, tribunals

x: The
Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal
was set up in 1969 for Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.
The Mahadayi Tribunal, set up in 2010, involves
Goa, Karnataka and Maharashtra
Water is included in the State List under Entry 17, but this is subject to Union Entry 56, which concerns regulation and development of inter-State rivers and river valleys.

secs.t: Inter-state trade and commerce - Articles 301-307

x: Exam angle: PYQ 2018 - a bill restricting goods from other states needs the
President's
previous sanction.
A bill imposing reasonable restrictions in the public interest under Article 304(b) requires the
previous sanction of the President
before its introduction in the State Legislature.
An
Inter-State Commerce Commission
is an example of the authority contemplated under Article 307 for carrying out the purposes of Articles 301 to 304.

secs.t: Krishna Water Disputes Tribunals - AP and Telangana share, KRMB and GRMB

x: KWDT-I dates to 1969, KWDT-II to 2004, Sikkim was added to the NEC in 2002, and KRMB and GRMB were set up under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
The post-reorganisation framework includes KRMB, GRMB and an Apex Council, and disputes have involved Board control, projects such as the Rayalaseema Lift and hydel generation.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Zonal Councils are generally regarded as recommendatory bodies, and their effectiveness is criticised as being constrained by inadequate resources.

rows.title: Issues and challenges in Indian federalism - governor's role, GST Council, central agencies, All India Services
sub: Group-II M1-B-64: Need for reforms in Centre-State relations - the case for greater state autonomy

secs.t: Commissions on Centre-State relations - year, chairman, appointing government, odd one out

x: Exam angle: "constituted in 1983 under a retired SC judge" = Sarkaria; order is State first (1969), then Centre (1983, 2007).
The
Rajamannar Committee
, appointed by the Tamil Nadu Government, was the first State-level review of Centre-State relations.
The Rajamannar Committee was constituted in 1969, the Sarkaria Commission in 1983, the NCRWC in 2000 and the Punchhi Commission in 2007.

secs.t: Commission recommendations - Inter-State Council, Article 356, All India Services, Governor

x: The ARC recommended non-partisan Governors and greater delegation of powers and finances to the States.
The Rajamannar Committee recommended abolishing the Planning Commission, eliminating Article 356 and establishing an Inter-State Council under Article 263.

The Punchhi Commission recommended a fixed tenure for Governors, no misuse of discretion, a President-like removal procedure, time-bound disposal of Bills and regular Prime Minister–Chief Minister meetings.

secs.t: Offices and services said to violate the federal principle - All India Services

x: Article 312 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by not less than
two-thirds of the members present and voting
for creation of a new All India Service.
All India Service officers serve the States under immediate State control, while ultimate control rests with the Centre.
All India Services are defended on the grounds that they maintain high standards, promote uniformity and facilitate Centre-State coordination.

secs.t: State autonomy demands - which state

x: State autonomy demands generally sought more powers, greater control over own revenue, less central administrative control and protection of linguistic interests.
The DMK government of Tamil Nadu appointed the
Rajamannar Committee
on Centre-State relations in 1969; its report was submitted in 1971.
The Kurian Joseph Committee was appointed by Tamil Nadu in April 2025 and consciously followed the Rajamannar Committee’s approach to Centre-State relations.

secs.t: Factors shaping Centre-State relations - phases of centralisation

x: The 1950s and early 1960s were marked by Congress rule at both levels and relative calm, although demands for the creation of new States existed.
Congress dominance characterised the 1950s and early 1960s, opposition State governments became prominent from the mid-1960s, and the coalition era began in the 1990s.
GST subsumed several State taxes, whereas cesses and surcharges continue to remain outside the divisible pool.

secs.t: Central agencies - CBI general consent, ED, NIA

x: Withdrawal of general consent means that the CBI must obtain consent separately for each case.
Under the NIA Act, 2008, the NIA can investigate scheduled offences anywhere in India without State consent.
The Enforcement Directorate enforces the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 nationwide, without State consent.

secs.t: Special category status demand - AP and the 14th Finance Commission

x: The 14th Finance Commission used 42% devolution and revenue deficit grants to address fiscal gaps, a principal reason cited for denying SCS.

The Centre offered Andhra Pradesh a special package instead of Special Category Status after the 14th Finance Commission increased devolution to 42 per cent and provided revenue deficit grants to address State gaps.

secs.t: Institutions criticised as against federal principles

x: The Planning Commission was criticised as an extra-constitutional institution that made States ‘suppliants for aid’.
The Governor is appointed by the President, and this Union-linked appointment is criticised as a possible instrument of central interference.
Articles 356, 256, 257 and 365 are all identified in federalism debates as provisions that may enable excessive Union intervention.

secs.t: Arguments for and against greater state autonomy

x: A major argument for greater State autonomy is that States often lack sufficient resources to perform their constitutionally assigned duties.
The resistance to Hindi in Tamil Nadu illustrates the
linguistic and cultural identity
argument for greater State autonomy.
Punjab militancy is cited by those opposing greater autonomy as demonstrating the risks to national unity and the need for a strong coordinating Centre.

secs.t: Reform proposals - residuary powers, Art 356 limits, devolution share

x: Rajamannar recommended deleting Article 356, Sarkaria treated its use as a last resort, and Punchhi proposed the concept of a localised emergency.
The Rajamannar Committee preceded the Sarkaria Commission, which preceded the Punchhi Commission; the Sixteenth Finance Commission’s 2026–31 recommendation is the latest item.
Time-bound cesses, accounting for off-budget borrowing, and stronger State Finance Commissions are reform proposals.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Tamil Nadu Assembly unanimously resolved in favour of
a fair share of tax devolution
for the States.
Cesses, Centrally Sponsored Schemes and GST are cited in debates on centralisation.
The Andhra Pradesh-specific concerns highlighted are the demand for
Special Category Status and Article 371D
The defeat of the 131st Amendment Bill relating to Lok Sabha expansion sharpened
the North–South debate

rows.title: Rajamannar Committee (1969) - appointment and recommendations
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Recommendations - which were and were not made (ISC, 356, AIS, FC, Planning Commission)

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT a Rajamannar recommendation" - look for any option that strengthens the Centre or the Governor.
The committee criticised the Planning Commission as an extra-constitutional body that
alone decided grants to the States
and recommended its abolition.
The committee recommended revitalising the Finance Commission so that States would depend less on the Centre and widening revenue devolution.

secs.t: Terms of reference - why the state set it up

x: Its principal task was to study
Centre-State relations
and recommend measures for greater State autonomy.
The committee held that, despite the federal form of the Constitution, central dominance had turned the States into
administrative units of the Centre
Articles 256, 257 and 365
were identified as provisions that enabled central overreach over the States.

secs.t: Appointing state, year, members

x: Dr. P.V. Rajamannar
, a former Chief Justice of the Madras High Court, chaired the committee.
The committee was set up by the DMK government under
M. Karunanidhi
, who carried forward C.N. Annadurai’s earlier autonomy position.
The view concerned reducing Union control over subjects such as
health and education
P.V. Rajamannar also chaired the
Fourth Finance Commission

secs.t: Recommendations on Governors, Art 356 and AIS

x: The committee wanted central control over the States reduced and did not recommend strengthening the Governor system.
Abolition of the All-India Services was recommended to
reduce central administrative control over State governments

secs.t: Recommendations on residuary powers and Seventh Schedule transfers

x: It recommended moving subjects from the Union and Concurrent Lists to the
State List
to enlarge State autonomy.
Stock exchanges, trade unions, electricity and factories were all included among the subjects proposed for transfer to the State List.
Rajamannar recommended that residuary powers go to the States, while the Sarkaria position concerned the Concurrent List for residuary powers other than taxation.

secs.t: Tamil Nadu Assembly's autonomy resolution

x: The Tamil Nadu Assembly adopted the State autonomy resolution in
April 1974
on the basis of the report.
The DMK slogan is ‘
autonomy for the States, federalism at the Centre

secs.t: Centre's response and later influence

x: Although the Centre took no action, the report placed the issue of State autonomy on the national agenda.
The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 through the influence of the
Sarkaria Commission
, not directly through the Rajamannar Committee.
The correct sequence is Rajamannar (1969), Sarkaria (1983), Punchhi (2007), and Kurian Joseph (April 2025).

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Part I of the Kurian Joseph Committee report was tabled in the Assembly on
16 February 2026
The Rajamannar Committee was the first committee on Centre-State relations appointed by a State.
Its autonomy-oriented ideas influenced later demands such as the Anandpur Sahib Resolution and the West Bengal memorandum.

rows.title: Sarkaria Commission (1983) - recommendations on legislative, administrative and financial relations
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-49

secs.t: Sarkaria Commission - government, year, chairman, members, objective, report

x: The Central Government set up the Sarkaria Commission in June 1983.
Justice Rajinder Singh Sarkaria, a retired Supreme Court judge, chaired the Commission.
The Commission worked from 1983 to 1987, a period of
five years
, and reported in 1988.
The Sarkaria Commission dealt with Centre-State relations; it was not a commission on
police reform

secs.t: Recommendations on the Governor - selection, tenure, CM consultation

x: The
Chief Minister of the State concerned
should be effectively consulted before the Governor is chosen.
The Commission recommended a secure five-year tenure, which should not be cut short except for extremely compelling reasons.
Both statements are true, and the protection from premature termination explains why a secure five-year tenure was recommended.

secs.t: Recommendations on Art 356 - conditions for use, floor test

x: The majority of a government should be determined by a floor test in the Legislative Assembly, not merely by the Governor’s subjective assessment.
The
Punchhi Commission
, constituted in 2010, later endorsed the approach concerning the order of preference in a hung Assembly.
The Bommai Court drew on Sarkaria’s analysis to distinguish proper from improper uses of Article 356.

secs.t: Legislative relations - Concurrent List consultation, residuary powers

x: The Centre should consult the States before legislating on a Concurrent List subject, preferably through an institutionalised process of prior consultation.

secs.t: Administrative relations - All-India Services, central forces

x: Sarkaria recommended strengthening All-India Services and creating more such services, whereas Rajamannar wanted them abolished.
The Centre may deploy Central armed forces in a State even without its request, though consulting the State beforehand is desirable.
The earlier Administrative Reforms Commission supported deployment of Central forces “
on request or otherwise

secs.t: Financial relations - Finance Commission and Planning Commission

x: The Commission recommended that cesses and surcharges be kept to a minimum and made time-bound, with their subsequent merger into the shareable tax pool.

secs.t: Implementation status - recommendations accepted

x: The Inter-State Council, established in 1990 under Article 263, is regarded as the main implemented recommendation of the Sarkaria Commission.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Sarkaria analysis was relied upon in S.R.
Bommai (1994) and Rameshwar Prasad (2006)
The criticism was that Governors could recommend President’s Rule to
promote the political interests of the party in power at the Centre
Tamil Nadu’s Kurian Joseph Committee of 2025 received comparatively little attention, whereas the Sarkaria report was widely debated.

secs.t: Punchhi Commission - appointing government, year, chairman, members, terms of reference

x: Exam angle: "When was it appointed?" Answer 2007, not 2010. Remember the order 1969, 1983, 2007.
The Punchhi Commission reviewed existing Centre-State arrangements in the light of changes since the
Sarkaria Commission
The Commission considered Panchayati Raj, economic reforms, coalition politics and internal security, besides the distribution of legislative and administrative powers.

secs.t: Recommendations on the Governor - tenure, removal and impeachment, role in universities

x: Exam angle: impeachment of the Governor, the 5-year tenure and the chancellor role are Punchhi's. Periodic "rotation of Governors" and "abolish the office" are distractors.
The Punchhi Commission recommended that Governors should not be made Chancellors of universities or given other statutory roles, to avoid day-to-day clashes with State Governments.

secs.t: Inter-State Council recommendations - frequency of meetings and role

x: The Punchhi Commission recommended that the Inter-State Council should meet at least three times a year and function as a working forum for Centre-State and inter-State issues.

secs.t: Recommendations on Articles 355 and 356

x: Exam angle: "The Commission said there is no need to amend Articles 355 and 356" is the
wrong
statement.
The proposed localised emergency would permit the Centre to
take over a specific troubled area, such as a district or part of a district, for a limited period
instead of the whole State.

secs.t: Concurrent List legislation - consultation with states

x: The Commission recommended that the Centre should
reach broad agreement with the States through the Inter-State Council
before legislating on Concurrent List subjects.
The Commission recommended adding a specific Union List entry on
environment, ecology and climate change
The recommendation also reflected the concern that the Collector was overburdened with responsibilities.

secs.t: Financial recommendations - Finance Commission, cesses and surcharges

x: The Commission recommended better coordination between the Finance Commission and the Planning Commission, with their time periods synchronised with the Five Year Plans.
The recommended area-specific strategy for backward regions included infrastructure, health and education spending, and agriculture.
The Punchhi Commission recommended that the
National Water Resources Council
should play a bigger role in water policy.

secs.t: Deployment of central forces - recommendation

x: The recommendation permitted the Centre to deploy central forces suo motu without the State's prior consent for a short period; the State's consent would be obtained afterwards.
The idea goes back to
the First Administrative Reforms Commission
, which recommended deployment of central armed forces either on the State's request or otherwise.

secs.t: Status - report volumes and Centre's acceptance

x: Article 156 continues to provide that the Governor holds office
during the pleasure of the President
Since Article 156 remains unchanged, Governors continue to hold office during the pleasure of the President.
The Tamil Nadu case of 8 April 2025 fixed timelines, but the Presidential Reference opinion of 20 November 2025 held that courts cannot impose fixed timelines or deemed assent.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The treatment of cesses and surcharges affects the distribution of fiscal resources between the Union and the States, which is the same federal-finance issue raised by the Punchhi Commission.
The CDI identifies
bill deadlines, a mandatory Inter-State Council and a cap on cesses
as the Punchhi agenda capable of contributing to cooperative federalism.

sub: Group-II M1-B-71: Cooperative and competitive federalism - NITI Aayog, GST Council and inter-state institutions

secs.t: Cooperative federalism - first recommended by, NITI Aayog's thrust

x: Knowledge and innovation corresponds to innovation-related work; NITI for States covers cooperative and competitive federalism; transformational change concerns transformative policy action; and monitoring and evaluation is associated with DMEO.

The Planning Commission was created by a Cabinet resolution in 1950; the National Development Council by an executive resolution in 1952; and NITI Aayog by a Union Cabinet resolution on 1 January 2015 with advisory status.
NITI Aayog functions as a policy think tank by providing policy inputs, promoting knowledge and innovation, supporting States and pursuing transformational change.

secs.t: Competitive and competitive sub-federalism - meaning, role in development

x: District rankings under the Aspirational Districts Programme are an example of competitive sub-federalism and are presented through the
Champions of Change dashboard
Performance competition and rankings encourage States to improve social and developmental indicators, thereby supporting sustainable development.
The
SDG India Index
, released by NITI Aayog, tracks States and Union Territories on the Sustainable Development Goals and encourages competitive federalism.

secs.t: NITI Aayog sub-groups of Chief Ministers - subjects

x: Exam angle: "Team India Hub" is the hub that leads State engagement.
Digital payments
is the odd one out among the CM sub-groups.
The sub-group on Rationalisation of Centrally Sponsored Schemes was convened by
Shivraj Singh Chouhan
, then Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh.
The Governing Council also includes
ex-officio members, the Vice-Chairperson, full-time members and special invitees

secs.t: State rankings - publisher and AP's rank

x: NITI Aayog releases the Health Index, Fiscal Health Index and SDG India Index, prepares the Export Preparedness Index with the Institute for Competitiveness, and has localised the SDG framework to districts.
Ease of Doing Business under the Business Reform Action Plan is associated with DPIIT, while the SDG India Index, Health Index and Fiscal Health Index are associated with NITI Aayog.

secs.t: Governing Council of NITI Aayog - members, meetings

x: At the eleventh meeting, the Prime Minister spoke on AI safeguards, El Nino and cooperative federalism, while N. Chandrababu Naidu presented Swarna Andhra @2047.
Ashok Kumar Lahiri
became Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog in April 2026, replacing Suman K. Bery.
The listed full-time members are
K.V. Raju, M. Srinivas, Abhay Karandikar, Gobardhan Das and Rajiv Gauba

secs.t: GST Council as a cooperative federalism model

x: The Centre has one-third and the States collectively have two-thirds of the votes in the GST Council, reflecting joint Centre–State decision-making.
The GST Council is generally cited as a model of cooperative federalism, whereas NITI Aayog rankings encourage competitive federalism.
The GST subsumed many local taxes, thereby curtailing several State taxation powers, and compensation disputes emerged between the Centre and States.

secs.t: Inter-state institutions - Inter-State Council, Zonal Councils, river boards, North Eastern Council

x: Article 262(1) empowers Parliament to provide by law for the adjudication of disputes relating to the use, distribution or control of waters of inter-State rivers and river valleys.
A State makes a complaint under
Section 3
of the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, which provides the basis for constituting a tribunal in the prescribed circumstances.

secs.t: Centrally sponsored schemes - rationalisation and state share debate

x: Centrally Sponsored Schemes constitute a large part of Centre-State transfers and require matching contributions from States, while their parameters are decided by the Centre.
A major criticism is that CSS may squeeze State priorities because the Centre determines important programme parameters and States must provide matching contributions.
The suggested measures include revisiting CSS, increasing the role of States in GST design and holding regular Inter-State Council meetings.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Ashok Lahiri
was identified as the new Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog during April-June 2026.
NITI Aayog is an advisory body and does not possess the financial powers that the Planning Commission formerly exercised.
A criticism is that
some States skip Centre-State meetings
, weakening regular intergovernmental coordination.
Andhra Pradesh was showcased for
Real Time Governance and AI-enabled tools such as AWARE

rows.title: Devolution of powers and finances to local levels - Finance Commission and State Finance Commission transfers
sub: Group-II M1-B-99: Finances of local bodies - own revenue, devolution and the State Finance Commission of AP

secs.t: Sources of Panchayat revenue - assigned, shared, grants, own revenue

x: Property tax is a major own-source revenue of Panchayats, and their power to levy taxes, duties, tolls and fees depends on authorisation by the State Legislature under Article 243H.

Assigned taxes are State-levied taxes handed over to Panchayats; shared taxes are shared according to the State Finance Commission; State Consolidated Fund grants relate to Article 243H and SFC recommendations; Union Finance Commission grants arise under Article 280.

secs.t: Finance Commission grants to local bodies - rural/urban share, basic vs performance, totals

x: Exam angle: the 14th FC split is 90:10 for GPs and 80:20 for municipalities (the 2019 question's key); panchayat total
Rs 2,00,292 crore
The Fourteenth Finance Commission used a 90:10 basic-performance ratio for Gram Panchayats, 80:20 for Municipalities, and distributed grants using 2011 population and area in a 90:10 ratio.
The Fifteenth Finance Commission provided ₹2.36 lakh crore for rural local bodies, with tied and untied components in a 60:40 ratio.
The Fifteenth Finance Commission attached performance-linked conditions such as
audited accounts and property-tax floor rates
The 16th Finance Commission for 2026-31 ended revenue deficit grants, while Andhra Pradesh's devolution share rose to 4.217%, from the earlier 4.05%.

secs.t: Vertical and horizontal devolution - divisible pool and criteria weights

x: Exam angle: "highest weight" and "new criterion" questions for each FC.
Vertical fiscal imbalance arises because the Centre controls more buoyant taxes, while States bear major expenditure responsibilities such as health, education, agriculture and police.
Since about 18% of gross tax revenue is collected through cesses and surcharges outside the divisible pool, effective devolution is closer to
The listed horizontal-transfer criteria include population based on the 1971 and 2011 mix, area, forest cover, income distance, demographic performance and GDP contribution.
The relevant criteria are population, area, forest cover, income distance, demographic performance and, now, GDP contribution; their use has generated disputes over horizontal distribution.
Vertical fiscal imbalance arises because the Union controls larger and more buoyant tax bases, including corporate tax, income tax and most GST, while States undertake major public services.

secs.t: Decentralisation concepts - democratic decentralisation vs delegation, what the 73rd Amendment decentralised

x: Democratic decentralisation involves elected local bodies, whereas delegation or deconcentration keeps functions within the administrative bureaucracy; therefore; .
The 73rd Amendment provided constitutional status, a three-tier structure, direct elections, a five-year term and reservation for Panchayati Raj institutions.
The Gadgil Committee recommended direct elections at all three levels, a State Election Commission and taxation powers for Panchayati Raj Institutions.

secs.t: Assigned revenues - seigniorage, surcharge on stamp duty
Scheme grants - RGSA, MGNREGA, Swachh Bharat convergence

x: The Atmanirbhar Panchayat Program and Training of Trainers on own-source revenue are associated with RGSA.
The framework permits States to notify a pause of up to 60 days, uses normative funding and places Gram Panchayat planning at the centre.
Approximately
₹19,561 crore
was mobilised for Andhra Pradesh Urban Local Bodies from AMRUT 2.0, AIIB, UIDF, SBM 2.0 and other sources.

secs.t: Municipal finance reforms - property tax, bonds

x: AMRUT 2.0 rewards progress in property-tax reform and the mobilisation of resources through municipal bonds.
SVAMITVA drone mapping helps create a baseline for rural properties, which can support the development of rural property-tax systems.
Weak accrual accounting and the absence of credit ratings keep most local bodies outside the municipal bond market.

secs.t: Audit of local bodies - CAG, AP State Audit

x: Article 243J concerns the accounts of Panchayats, while Article 243Z concerns the accounts of Municipalities.
CAG Technical Guidance and Support over local-body audits was recommended by the
Eleventh Finance Commission
The second edition of the State Finances report referred to is for
State own tax revenue is stated to be about
47 percent
of State revenue receipts.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The end of revenue-deficit grants has prompted criticism described as the “
tyranny of the base year
Only duly constituted local bodies qualify for the relevant Sixteenth Finance Commission grants, making local elections important; approximately ₹12,150 crore is at stake.
Tied grants may restrict local priority-setting, and the annual urban local-body transfer of about ₹75,000 crore has been viewed as small compared with urban GDP.

rows.title: Challenges in local devolution - funds, functions, functionaries; parallel bodies and capacity gaps
sub: Group-II M1-B-96: Implementation gaps - funds, functions, functionaries, parallel bodies and capacity

secs.t: Capacity building - RGSA, NIRDPR and SIRDs, eGramSwaraj, AuditOnline

x: RGSA was introduced to strengthen Panchayati Raj Institutions and enable them to contribute to the achievement of
Sustainable Development Goals
RGSA promotes convergence with Mission Antyodaya, focuses on 117 aspirational districts and also covers areas outside Part IX.
The revamped RGSA runs from 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2026 and matches the period of the Fifteenth Finance Commission.

secs.t: Committees and reports on local devolution - Local Body Ombudsman, 2nd ARC, V. Ramachandran

x: The Second Administrative Reforms Commission recommended a Local Body Ombudsman in its Sixth Report, titled Local Governance, published in 2007.
The V. Ramachandran Expert Committee examined the use of Panchayats for efficient delivery of public goods and services.
The Roadmap identifies weak 3F devolution, bureaucratic control, tied funds, dependence on grants and reluctance to tax.

secs.t: 3Fs devolution - funds, functions, functionaries

x: Functions are subjects transferred to local bodies, funds are untied money matching those functions, functionaries are staff answerable to the local body, and the Eleventh Schedule contains 29 Panchayat subjects.
Articles 243G and 243W concern devolution of powers and responsibilities, while Articles 243H and 243X concern local taxation and funds; the use of 'may' makes devolution discretionary.

secs.t: Devolution Index - publisher and AP's rank

x: The Devolution Index report is published by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj and is prepared with the Indian Institute of Public Administration.

secs.t: Parallel bodies - DRDAs, user groups, MP/MLA LADS, AP-specific bodies

x: DRDAs, user groups, SHGs and MPLADS/MLA LADS
were identified as arrangements that bypass elected local bodies.
State-appointed parastatals and SPVs may
bypass citizen participation and elected local bodies
by operating outside the regular local-government framework.
Janmabhoomi committees operated during 2014-19, while village and ward secretariats and volunteers were introduced in 2019; both were criticised as parallel to gram panchayats and wards.

secs.t: Own-source revenue of local bodies - property tax, share of GDP, dependence on grants

x: Property tax
is the main own-source revenue of ULBs, although it remains under-assessed and under-collected.
Weak own-source revenue and outdated property registers make local bodies dependent on tied grants.
Weak balance sheets prevent most ULBs from accessing the municipal bond market effectively.
All three statements are correct: the urban share rises to 45%, the division is 80% basic and 20% performance, and 50% of basic grants are tied to sanitation and water.

secs.t: Elected women representatives - proxy (sarpanch pati) and committee

x: Proxy behaviour falls sharply or markedly when women representatives enter a second term, reflecting increased experience and confidence.
The identified remedies include capacity-building, women-friendly Gram Panchayats, exemplary penalties, public swearing-in and women's ombudspersons.
The MoPR advisory committee under
Sushil Kumar
in 2025 proposed exemplary penalties, public swearing-in and women's ombudspersons.

secs.t: Delays in local body elections and SEC autonomy

x: The State Election Commission and the constitutional five-year term, with elections before expiry or within six months of dissolution, made local government a permanent institution after 1993.
The Cabinet decision included 34% BC reservation in rural local bodies, 33⅓% in urban local bodies, and direct elections for Mayors and municipal chairpersons.

secs.t: Delayed elections and non-constitution of SFCs

x: The conditions include properly constituted local bodies, published audited accounts and timely State Finance Commissions.
State Finance Commission reports are often ignored, weakening the fiscal devolution process to local bodies.

secs.t: Bureaucratic control - Collector, special officers

x: Special Officers
were placed in charge of local bodies whose elected terms had lapsed, including the affected bodies in Andhra Pradesh.
Dependence on block offices for
approvals and funds
is a major expression of bureaucratic control over Panchayat functioning.
Balwantrai Mehta made the Collector the Zilla Parishad chairman.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The criticism is that PRIs function mainly as implementing agencies rather than planning units, while parallel bodies such as Janmabhoomi committees and secretariats may further reduce their institutional centrality.
Both the assertion and reason are true, and the grant conditions explain why failure to constitute elected local bodies and related institutions can put Central funds at risk.
