secs.t: NITI bodies and hubs - Governing Council, Regional Councils, hubs → function

x: The Governing Council includes the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers of all States, Chief Ministers of Union Territories with legislatures, Lieutenant Governors of other Union Territories, ex officio members, the Vice-Chairperson, full-time members and special invitees.
NITI Aayog assists States in setting up State Economic and Transformation Units, or SETUs, to prepare
State Vision@2047 plans

secs.t: NITI indices and reports → subject

x: The SDG India Index assesses the progress of States and Union Territories towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
GROW stands for
Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry
NITI Aayog, which succeeded the Planning Commission, is the nodal agency for poverty estimation.
The India Electric Mobility Index is brought out by NITI Aayog with
WRI India

secs.t: Initiatives → purpose (AIM, Aspirational Districts, Aspirational Blocks, WEP)

x: The Aspirational Districts Programme uses convergence, collaboration and competition, supported by the Champions of Change dashboard and monthly delta rankings.
The Aspirational Blocks Programme, launched in January 2023, covers
513 blocks in 329 districts across 27 States and 4 Union Territories
The ADP, launched in January 2018, covered 112 districts, used 49 KPIs, followed five themes and adopted the three Cs—Convergence, Collaboration and Competition.
The programme was launched in January 2023; the stated IYB coverage is 500 blocks in 27 States and 4 Union Territories, while another count records 513 blocks in 329 districts.
Sampoornata Abhiyan 2.0 aims to achieve saturation of key indicators in both the Aspirational Districts and Aspirational Blocks Programmes.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Parliamentary Standing Committee sought
for 2026–27 while criticising the chronic under-use of funds by the Ministry of Planning and NITI Aayog.

All three statements are correct: the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister attended the 11th Governing Council meeting in June 2026, ASR district topped the Basic Infrastructure theme in March 2026, and Andhra Pradesh ranked fifth in EPI 2024.

rows.title: Centralization vs decentralization - concepts, arguments and Indian experience
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-64

secs.t: Concepts - centralisation, deconcentration, delegation, devolution; political, administrative, fiscal

x: Centralisation concentrates decisions at the apex, such as the Union, the State capital or the headquarters of a department.
Deconcentration remains within the same government, delegation involves semi-autonomous bodies, and devolution empowers elected local governments with their own mandate and revenue.
If the transferring authority can withdraw the power at will, the arrangement is delegation rather than devolution.

secs.t: Arguments for and against centralisation in India

x: Nation-building after Partition, along with the requirements of unity and security, was an argument for centralisation.

All three were arguments advanced in favour of centralisation: a single command for planned heavy industry and food security, weak local capacity, and the risk of elite capture by dominant local castes.
Proximity and information enable local bodies to understand local needs.

secs.t: Gandhian vs Nehruvian views on village self-government

x: Gandhi advocated Gram Swaraj, conceived as
a republic of self-sufficient villages with decentralised economic and political power
The Gandhian Plan of 1944, associated with Sriman Narayan Agarwal, sought
self-contained villages, cottage industry, swadeshi, sarvodaya and trusteeship
The Community Development Programme began in 1952 and was top-down, while Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.

secs.t: Ambedkar's view of the village in the Constituent Assembly

x: Ambedkar criticised the village as a seat of caste domination and called it a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism on 4 November 1948.
Ambedkar preferred
the individual, protected by a strong constitutional state
, rather than the village as the basic unit of the republic.

secs.t: Article 40 DPSP - organisation of village panchayats

x: Article 40 directs the State to organise village panchayats and endow them with the powers necessary to function as
units of self-government
Article 40 is in Part IV and is a Directive Principle of State Policy.
Article 40 represented a compromise: panchayats were named as an objective, reflecting the Gandhian position, but the provision was made non-justiciable, accommodating Ambedkar's reservations.

secs.t: Indian experience - planning-era centralisation, then the 73rd and 74th Amendments

x: The 64th Constitutional Amendment Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in July 1989 by the Rajiv Gandhi Government, sought constitutional status for Panchayats, and was defeated in the Rajya Sabha in October 1989 because it did not secure the special majority.
The 64th Bill passed the Lok Sabha in July 1989, was defeated in the Rajya Sabha in October 1989, a fresh Bill followed in 1990, and the 73rd Amendment came into force in 1993.

secs.t: Subsidiarity principle and the three Fs

x: Subsidiarity assigns a function to the lowest competent level and permits movement to a higher level only when the lower level cannot perform it adequately.
The Second Administrative Reforms Commission invoked subsidiarity for
dividing functions between the three tiers of government
Without adequate funds, functions and functionaries, Panchayati Raj Institutions remain implementing agencies instead of becoming effective planning units.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The call for a “structural reset” referred to addressing the increasing centralisation of power and reconsidering the working of federalism in Union-State relations.

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 came into force on 1 April 2026, are linked to the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and Article 253, and have been criticised for centralising matters belonging to local bodies.

rows.title: Democratic decentralisation - meaning, objectives and preconditions
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-64

secs.t: Democratic decentralisation - meaning, the committee that coined it, what PRIs brought

x: Democratic decentralisation means transferring power to elected local bodies so that people participate in decisions affecting them.
The committee recommended a three-tier system, genuine transfer of power and adequate resources.
The recommended three-tier structure consisted of the
Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad
PRIs brought
formal representation of weaker sections
in village governance and were adopted to decentralise democratic power.

secs.t: Objectives of Panchayati Raj - aims, whose cooperation, preconditions

x: The committee found that
local public participation
was indispensable for development to succeed.
The committee recommended no supersession, or that polls should be conducted within six months if supersession occurred.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee observed that development had become bureaucratised—described as “grass without roots”—and called for restoration of the Zila Parishad’s role.

secs.t: Attributes of local self-government

x: Local self-government does not possess
sovereignty or legislative supremacy
Local bodies may have their own funds and taxing powers and enjoy autonomy within State law.
Judicial powers are not a general feature of local self-government; Nyaya Panchayats are separate institutions associated with judicial functions.

secs.t: Gram Swaraj - the Gandhian idea and the Article 40 link

x: Gram Swaraj means
a self-reliant village republic
in the Gandhian conception.
The constitutional trace of Gram Swaraj is found in
Article 40
, a Directive Principle of State Policy concerning village panchayats.
The Abhiyan is implemented by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj, began from 2018–19 and trains PRI members.
The funding pattern is 60:40 generally and 90:10 in the North-Eastern and hill States.

secs.t: Decentralised planning - district planning, Kerala People's Plan Campaign

x: Kerala's People's Plan Campaign began on 17 August 1996, devolved 35–40% of plan outlay to local bodies, and “People's Plan 2.0” is under discussion.

The People's Plan Campaign devolved 35–40% of plan outlay; the Amaravati region covers nine districts and about 44,962 sq km; the NITI Governing Council coordinates policy; and AP has three economic regions.

secs.t: Global models - Scandinavian and British

x: The Scandinavian model is characterised by strong municipalities, delivery of most welfare services and high local taxes; it is treated as a benchmark for fiscal decentralisation.
In the British model, local councils are creatures of Parliament and are subject to the ultra vires rule; the model also uses a committee system.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Sashakt Panchayat Netri Abhiyan
is associated with strengthening women’s leadership in Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The Economic Survey 2025–26 stresses PRI own-source revenue, e-GramSwaraj and SabhaSaar; SabhaSaar is described as an AI tool for preparing Gram Sabha minutes.
The report referred to
low participation in Gram Sabha meetings
and was associated with LENSD.

rows.title: Evolution of Panchayati Raj - Community Development Programme, Balwant Rai Mehta, Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao and L.M. Singhvi committees
sub: Group-II M1-B-85: Community Development Programme 1952 and the National Extension Service - working and failure
Group-II M1-B-86: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee - recommendations and the three-tier structure
Group-II M1-B-87: Panchayati Raj, 1959-1977 - phases of ascendancy and decline
Group-II M1-B-88: Ashok Mehta Committee - recommendations and the two-tier proposal
Group-II M1-B-89: G.V.K. Rao Committee and L.M. Singhvi Committee
Group-II M1-B-90: 64th and 65th Amendment Bills (1989) and the road to constitutional status

secs.t: Committees → year, government, chronological order, subject

x: Democratic decentralisation
was the central idea associated with the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee, along with the recommendation of a three-tier system.
The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj structure, including the Mandal Panchayat, for the revival of Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee was appointed in 1986 by the Rajiv Gandhi Government to prepare a concept paper on reviving Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The Thungon Committee of 1988 dealt with constitutional recognition, a three-tier structure and a five-year term for Panchayati Raj Institutions.

Balwant Rai Mehta recommended genuine transfer and resources; Ashok Mehta emphasised the district as the first point; G.V.K. Rao sought restoration of the Zila Parishad’s role; and L.M. Singhvi recommended constitutional status.
Uttar Pradesh provided for them under the 1947 Act, Bihar used the Gram Kachahari model, and L.M. Singhvi recommended Nyaya Panchayats for clusters of villages.
G.V.K. Rao used the expression “
grass without roots
” to describe the weakened condition of Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The Thungon sub-committee recommended constitutional recognition, three tiers, a fixed five-year term and several other institutional safeguards, including a State Finance Commission.

secs.t: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee - report, recommendations, non-recommendations

x: Exam angle: "two-tier" and "direct elections to both village panchayat and Zila Parishad" are false. "All planning and development activities entrusted to these bodies" and "Collector as ZP chairman" are true. Keyed answer: c and d. Nyaya Panchayat is NOT one of the three tiers.
The committee was appointed to examine the working of the Community Development Programme launched in 1952 and the National Extension Service launched in 1953, and to suggest improvements.
Under the recommended three-tier structure, the Gram Panchayat operated at village level, the Panchayat Samiti at block level and the Zila Parishad at district level.
The Panchayat Samiti was recommended as the executive body, whereas the Zila Parishad was assigned advisory, coordinating and supervisory functions.
The committee envisaged three organically linked tiers—Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishad—with the higher tiers connected through indirect elections.

secs.t: Committee → distinctive recommendation

x: Exam angle: APPSC (2023, 2025) asked Ashok Mehta = "
two-tier system with four years of term
The
Ashok Mehta Committee
recommended a two-tier structure comprising the Zila Parishad and Mandal Panchayat, with the Mandal Panchayat covering about 15,000 to 20,000 people.
The
Ashok Mehta Committee
recommended that elections should be held within six months if a Panchayati Raj Institution was superseded.

Balwant Rai Mehta proposed the District Collector as chairman of the Zila Parishad, but the Balwant Rai Mehta, First ARC, Ashok Mehta and G.V.K. Rao bodies are identified as cutting the Collector’s development role.

secs.t: Community Development Programme - launch, objectives, components, NES

x: Exam angle: year asked directly (1952, not 1950/1957/1959); "aim = public participation" is the keyed option.
The programme was viewed as a step towards implementing Article 40 of the Constitution, which directs the State to organise village panchayats.
The expected functions included helping implement land reforms, organising voluntary labour for community work and setting up cooperatives.
The National Extension Service, launched in 1953, functioned as the
extension arm
supporting the Community Development Programme.

secs.t: Grow More Food Inquiry Committee and early rural programmes → person

x: The Committee found the campaign too narrow and recommended an integrated village-development approach supported by
a nationwide extension organisation
The correct associations are Gurgaon experiment–F.L. Brayne, Sriniketan–Rabindranath Tagore, Marthandam–Spencer Hatch and Baroda–V.T. Krishnamachari.
Sevagram was associated with Mahatma Gandhi, Etawah with Albert Mayer, Nilokheri with S.K. Dey and Marthandam with Spencer Hatch.
Nilokheri was associated with S.K. Dey and developed as a refugee settlement in East Punjab in 1948; the area is now in Haryana.
The correct order is Gurgaon experiment (1920), Sriniketan (1921), Sevagram (1930s) and Etawah Pilot Project (1948).

secs.t: Constitutional status attempts - 64th Amendment Bill, failure, origin of the 73rd

x: Opponents feared that the 64th Bill would
centralise power and bypass the States
in matters relating to Panchayati Raj.
The
P.V. Narasimha Rao
Government during 1991–92 dropped the controversial portions and enacted the revised proposal as the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
The Singhvi, Thungon and Gadgil lines of thinking contributed to the 73rd Amendment, particularly in relation to constitutional status, regular elections and reservation.

secs.t: AP Panchayati Raj laws and the Mandal Praja Parishad reform

x: Andhra Pradesh, the second State to adopt the system, introduced three-tier Panchayati Raj at Shadnagar on
1 November 1959
In 1985, N.T. Rama Rao abolished the hereditary village officer Patel-Patwari system and introduced the Mandal system.
The AP Panchayat Samithis and Zilla Parishads Act, 1959 brought in the three-tier Panchayati Raj structure in Andhra Pradesh.
The 1986 reform under the NTR Government replaced block-level Panchayat Samithis with smaller Mandal Praja Parishads, reflecting the mandal idea associated with the Ashok Mehta approach.
Ward members and the Sarpanch are directly elected; the Gram Panchayat has a five-year term and the minimum contesting age is 21 years.

secs.t: National Extension Service - year and relation to CDP

x: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee reviewed both the Community Development Programme and the National Extension Service in
January 1957

secs.t: Rural programmes in chronological order

x: The Food for Work programme is associated with 1977.
The IADP was introduced as a pilot programme in seven districts.

secs.t: Social education component - its programme

x: Social education under the Community Development Programme included adult literacy, community centres, and youth and women's clubs.

secs.t: Persons associated with community development → role

x: S.K. Dey was associated with Nilokheri and the Union Ministry of Community Development; Albert Mayer with the Etawah Pilot Project; V.T. Krishnamachari chaired the Grow More Food Inquiry Committee; and Jawaharlal Nehru launched the CDP and inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur.
Jawaharlal Nehru
launched the Community Development Programme in 1952 and inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.

secs.t: Organisation - block, BDO, Village Level Worker

x: A Village Level Worker or Gram Sevak served as a
multipurpose extension worker for a group of villages
In the Maharashtra-Gujarat pattern, the Zila Parishad was dominant and the
district
functioned as the planning unit.
The sequence was Ascendancy (1959-1964), Stagnation (1965-1969), Decline (1969-1983), and Revival (1983 onwards).
The decline phase extended from 1969 to 1983, following the periods of ascendancy and stagnation.

secs.t: Evaluation of CDP → reviewing committee, reasons for failure

x: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was appointed in
January 1957
and submitted its report in November 1957.
The Committee attributed the failure of the programme to inadequate public participation and recommended democratic decentralisation through elected local bodies.
The recommended remedy was democratic decentralisation through elected three-tier local bodies, which later came to be known as Panchayati Raj.

secs.t: Origin of the name 'Panchayati Raj' and its 'architect'

x: The term is credited in this context to M.K. Gandhi’s promotion of Gram Swaraj, which placed villages at the centre of governance.
Balwant Rai Mehta
is popularly called the architect or father of Panchayati Raj because of his Committee’s recommendations on democratic decentralisation.

secs.t: National Development Council's approval

x: The NDC did not insist on one rigid pattern for all States; however, the basic principles of Panchayati Raj were to be the same everywhere.

secs.t: FIRST and second states - dates, whole-state vs partial adoption

x: Exam angle: "first state" = Rajasthan. "First implemented across the entire state in 1959" = Andhra Pradesh.
By the mid-1960s,
most States had established Panchayati Raj Institutions

secs.t: Plan periods and PRIs - which plan phase revived them

x: The
Sixth Five Year Plan
, associated with the Janata Government’s 1978-1983 plan, gave Panchayati Raj a new lease of life but was dropped after 1980 and did not become an official Plan of India.
The Fifth Plan Working Group on Panchayati Raj, constituted in 1972, was chaired by
N. Ramakrishnayya

secs.t: Nyaya Panchayats under state laws

x: Nyaya Panchayats were established under the laws of some States to try petty civil and criminal cases.

secs.t: Phase of decline - causes identified by reviewing committees

x: Development work became bureaucratised and was increasingly cut off from Panchayati Raj Institutions, weakening their role.
Poor finances, irregular elections and supersession, and weak devolution of functions and staff were identified as causes.
The Daya Choubey Committee of 1976 reviewed
Community Development and Panchayati Raj
The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended that supersession should not continue beyond
six months

secs.t: Santhanam Committee - PR finances and elections

x: The K. Santhanam Committee examined Panchayati Raj finances in 1963 and Panchayati Raj elections in 1965.

secs.t: Ashok Mehta Committee - government, PM, year, tiers, term

x: The Committee proposed replacing the three-tier structure with a two-tier system and recommended a four-year term.
The Ashok Mehta Committee recommended Mandal Panchayats at the lower level and Zila Parishads at the district level.
The Zila Parishad was the district-level executive body; the Mandal Panchayat covered a group of villages; the report came in August 1978; and the committee was appointed in December 1977.

secs.t: Constitutional status, nyaya panchayats, taxation, social audit

x: Compulsory taxation powers were recommended so that Panchayati Raj Institutions could raise their own money and become financially capable.
The Committee proposed regular social audit by a district-level agency together with a committee of legislators.

secs.t: Unit of decentralisation, lower tier, political parties, elections

x: Exam angle (UPPSC 2023, key "only (1)"): "three-tier replaced by two-tier" is correct. The second statement, about the block, is the trap: Ashok Mehta made the
district
, not the block, the unit.

The Committee recommended a Minister for Panchayati Raj in the State cabinet, election management involving the State's Chief Electoral Officer and the Chief Election Commissioner, and SC/ST reservation according to population.

secs.t: Fate of the recommendations - political reasons

x: The Janata government fell before completing its term
, and consequently the Centre took no action on the recommendations.
Panchayats formed after 1977 on the lines of the Ashok Mehta recommendations are referred to as
Second Generation Panchayats

secs.t: Odd one out - PR vs other committees

x: Balwant Rai Mehta, Ashok Mehta and G.V.K. Rao were associated with Panchayati Raj inquiries.
The Administrative Reforms Commissions were associated with administrative reforms.
Although its name may suggest a statistical body outside the Panchayati Raj field, the V.R. Rao Committee was associated with
Panchayat Statistics
and was a Panchayati Raj committee.

secs.t: G.V.K. Rao Committee - appointing body, year, district-level recommendations

x: The G.V.K. Rao Committee was set up in 1985 by the
Planning Commission
to review administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation.
The Committee observed that development administration had become bureaucratised and disconnected from Panchayati Raj Institutions, describing PRIs as “grass without roots.”.
G.V.K. Rao examined the administrative set-up for rural development, whereas L.M. Singhvi focused on revitalising Panchayati Raj Institutions as instruments of democracy.

secs.t: Thungon and Gadgil - recommendations on constitutional status

x: The Thungon sub-committee proposed that supersession of a Panchayati Raj body should not exceed
six months
The Gadgil Committee was set up by the
Congress party
in 1988 and its recommendations fed into the draft constitutional amendment proposals.
Both sets of recommendations supported constitutional recognition, a three-tier structure, a five-year term and State-level financial arrangements such as a State Finance Commission.

secs.t: Opposition criticism - states' objections

x: Critics argued that the proposals were centralising because they could enable the Centre to deal directly with local bodies over the heads of the States.
Local Government is a subject in the
State List
, which formed the basis of the States' objection to greater direct Central involvement with local bodies.

secs.t: National Front government's bill - scope and fate

x: The V.P. Singh-led National Front Government introduced fresh bills, including a revised Nagarpalika Bill, in September 1990.
The bills introduced by the V.P. Singh Government were never passed and lapsed upon the dissolution of the Lok Sabha.

secs.t: Narasimha Rao government's bills - introduction, Joint Committee, passage

x: The P.V. Narasimha Rao Government removed the controversial provisions, introduced modified bills in September 1991, and referred them to a Joint Parliamentary Committee.
The National Front bills lapsed after the dissolution of the Lok Sabha; modified bills were introduced in September 1991, referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, and passed in December 1992.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Panchayati Raj evolved from rural development schemes, particularly the Community Development Programme, towards constitutionalised local self-government under Part IX.
The Community Development Programme was
India's first major post-Independence rural development programme
and laid the groundwork for a third tier of government.
Andhra Pradesh implemented the three-tier Balwant Rai Mehta model on 1 November 1959 under Chief Minister N. Sanjiva Reddy's government.
The first elections in Andhra Pradesh witnessed
village and caste clashes
, demonstrating the social tensions accompanying the introduction of local political institutions.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee favoured a Collector-chaired Zilla Parishad.
The Firka Development Scheme was introduced in
the Madras Presidency in 1946
and covered areas that include present-day Andhra regions.
The Ashok Mehta Committee was significant for being the first to seek constitutional recognition and party-based elections for Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The
L.M. Singhvi, Thungon and Gadgil
Committees collectively contributed to the blueprint of the 73rd Amendment, including constitutional status, election and financial institutions, tenure and reservation.
The Constitution (64th Amendment) Bill was the first attempt to confer constitutional status on Panchayati Raj Institutions.
The 1992 constitutional changes transformed Panchayati Raj from a largely policy-based arrangement into a constitutionally protected and justiciable system, creating obligations for the States.
The 1989 Bill failed in the Rajya Sabha, while the 1991 initiative under P. V. Narasimha Rao resulted in the 73rd Amendment and gave effect to Article 40.
Andhra Pradesh uses the
Mandal Parishad
as its intermediate tier, unlike the Panchayat Samiti terminology used in most States.

rows.title: 73rd Amendment - Part IX, Eleventh Schedule, three-tier structure, Gram Sabha, reservations, State Election Commission
sub: Group-II M1-B-91: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act - Part IX, structure, Gram Sabha and the Eleventh Schedule
Group-II M1-B-92: 73rd Amendment - reservations, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission
Group-II M1-B-95: Implementation of the 73rd and 74th Amendments - achievements across states

secs.t: Features of the 73rd Amendment - compulsory vs voluntary, non-features, significance

x: Exam angle: "is/are correct" sets mixing both columns (APPSC-G2 2025 answered "All of the above" for the mandatory list).
The 73rd Amendment came into force on
24 April 1993
, observed as National Panchayati Raj Day.
The 73rd Amendment inserted Part IX, comprising Articles 243 to 243O, and the Eleventh Schedule containing 29 subjects.
The intermediate tier is optional below the 20-lakh population threshold, and chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly.
The correct sequence is Article 243F (disqualifications), Article 243E (duration), Article 243G (powers and functions), and Article 243I (State Finance Commission).
24 April marks the commencement of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, and is observed as National Panchayati Raj Day.

secs.t: Articles 243 to 243O → content

x: Exam angle: "Article → subject" matching; 243G is the Article the Eleventh Schedule hangs on.
Article 243A concerns the Gram Sabha, Article 243B the constitution of Panchayats, Article 243C their composition and chairpersons, and Article 243D reservations.
Article 243M concerns exempted areas, Article 243N permits existing laws to continue for up to one year, Article 243O bars court interference in electoral matters, and Article 243J concerns audit.

secs.t: Eleventh Schedule - number of subjects, identify subjects

x: Exam angle: "18 functional items were placed with Panchayats" is FALSE (18 = Twelfth Schedule).
Article
concerns the powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats, with reference to the subjects in the Eleventh Schedule.

Animal husbandry, dairying and poultry relate to rural production and allied activity; social and farm forestry concerns forestry; minor forest produce concerns forest produce; and small-scale industries concern village and small industries.
Welfare of weaker sections, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
, is an Eleventh Schedule subject.
The sequence is rural housing, drinking water, fuel and fodder, followed by roads and related means of communication.

secs.t: Tier structure and membership - population exemption, age, elections, tenure, dissolution

x: Article 243F prescribes
21 years
as the minimum age for membership of a Panchayat.
Article 243C leaves the method of choosing the village chairperson to State law and provides indirect election of intermediate and district chairpersons by and from elected members.
The reconstituted Panchayat continues only for the remainder of the original term, not for a fresh five-year period.
The cited figures are approximately
15,000 or more Gram Panchayats, 588 mandals and 13 Zilla Parishads

secs.t: Gram Sabha - definition, composition, functions, People's Plan Campaign, PESA powers

x: Article 243(b) defines the Gram Sabha as the body of persons registered in the electoral rolls of a village within the Panchayat area.
PESA gives Gram Sabhas powers over minor forest produce, village markets and liquor, and protection of traditions and community resources; it does not give them control over the Union Budget.
In PESA areas, the Gram Sabha is regarded as supreme at the village level, protects traditions and may settle disputes according to customary practices.
PESA extends Part IX, with modifications, to Fifth Schedule Areas and promotes tribal self-rule.

secs.t: States and areas exempted from Part IX and the 74th Amendment; extension through PESA

x: Parliament may extend Part IX to Fifth Schedule Scheduled Areas with modifications, and PESA performs this function.
Article 243ZC
provides the parallel exemption provision for Part IXA, which deals with municipalities and was introduced through the 74th Amendment framework.
The absence of SC reservation in Arunachal Pradesh does not mean that Part IX is wholly inapplicable there.

secs.t: Reservation for women in PRIs - constitutional minimum, States providing 50%

x: Article 243D(4)
provides reservation of not less than one-third of the offices of chairpersons in Panchayats for women.
Bihar
was the first State mentioned as having raised reservation for women in local bodies to 50 per cent, in 2006.
Of 24.41 lakh elected Panchayat representatives, 12.14 lakh were women, constituting
49.75 per cent
The Sashakt Panchayat Netri Abhiyan is intended to
train women elected representatives

secs.t: Constitutional status to PRIs - amendment, commencement, National Panchayati Raj Day

x: Exam angle: A-R item "73rd is a landmark... because it brought PRIs under the justiciable part" - both true, R explains A.
The 73rd Amendment concerns
rural Panchayati Raj Institutions
, whereas the 74th Amendment concerns urban local bodies.
The assertion and reason are both true.

secs.t: Qualifications to contest (Article 243F)

x: Article 243F refers to disqualification under the law for elections to the State Legislature or under a law made by the State Legislature.

secs.t: Term, dissolution and fresh elections (Article 243E)

x: A Panchayat constituted after an early dissolution continues only for the remainder of the period for which the dissolved Panchayat would have continued.

secs.t: State Finance Commission - Article 243I

x: Karnataka's Fifth State Finance Commission requested that
5 per cent
of urban GST revenue be transferred to Urban Local Bodies.
Part VI of the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 gives effect to
Article 243I
relating to the State Finance Commission.
The Governor lays the State Finance Commission report before the State Legislature together with a memorandum explaining the action taken on its recommendations.
The Union Finance Commission recommends measures to augment a State's Consolidated Fund for supplementing local-body resources, drawing on State Finance Commission recommendations.

The Central Finance Commission may recommend measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations.
A State Finance Commission recommends fiscal devolution, grants-in-aid and measures to improve local finances; it does not appoint the Governor.

secs.t: OBC reservation in local bodies - K. Krishna Murthy and Vikas Kishanrao Gawali

x: K. Krishna Murthy upheld the provisions contained in
Articles 243D(6) and 243T(6)
, while distinguishing political backwardness from social and educational backwardness.
The case clarified that political representation in local bodies involves a distinct constitutional consideration from social and educational backwardness.
The decisions refer to the general ceiling that the aggregate vertical reservation for SCs, STs and OBCs should not ordinarily exceed
50 per cent

secs.t: Names of the intermediate tier across states

x: Anchalik Panchayat is the name used for the intermediate tier in Assam.
All four pairs are correctly matched.
Mandal Praja Parishad is associated with Andhra Pradesh.

secs.t: FIRST state to enact a conformity Act

x: The Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act, 1994, was enacted on
21 April 1994
as the State's conformity law.

secs.t: Devolution Index - MoPR index, state rankings, AP's rank

x: The
Panchayat Advancement Index
is the newer composite, multi-domain index used to assess Panchayat performance against localised Sustainable Development Goals.
The Panchayat Advancement Index is composite and multi-domain, measures localised SDGs, and covers more than 2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats.

secs.t: Model states - Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra, West Bengal

x: Kerala's People's Plan Campaign was launched in 1996.
The campaign devolved a large share of plan funds and encouraged planning from Gram Sabhas upwards.
West Bengal
is associated with the pioneering three-tier system under its 1973 Act, followed by elections in June 1978.
The material states that pradhans held unusual financial powers; therefore; .

secs.t: e-Governance for PRIs - e-GramSwaraj, SVAMITVA, Meri Panchayat

x: Approximately
2.54 lakh
Gram Panchayats had uploaded their Gram Panchayat Development Plans on e-GramSwaraj for FY 2025–26.
SVAMITVA uses drone mapping to support the
preparation of Records of Rights
in rural inhabited areas.
SabhaSaar uses artificial intelligence for preparing Gram Sabha minutes and had reached approximately one lakh Gram Panchayats by November 2025.

secs.t: National Panchayat Awards - categories, AP winners

x: The
Nanaji Deshmukh Sarvottam Panchayat Satat Vikas Puraskar
is the holistic category.
Kuppam mandal received the third Nanaji Deshmukh Puraskar in 2025, accompanied by ₹1.5 crore.
Chittoor District Panchayat Resource Centre received the first Panchayat Capacity Building Institution Award in 2026, carrying ₹1 crore.
Kanipakam Gram Panchayat in Irala received the second Atmanirbhar Panchayat Special Award in 2026, carrying ₹75 lakh.

secs.t: Urban reforms - AMRUT, Smart Cities Mission, municipal bonds

x: Drone mapping for rural Records of Rights
is associated with SVAMITVA, not AMRUT 2.0.
The Urban Infrastructure Development Fund was announced in Budget 2023–24 and is routed through the
National Housing Bank
Only a few large cities have issued municipal bonds because weak municipal balance sheets often prevent them from securing investment-grade ratings.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The stated objective is to convert numerical reservation into
real empowerment
of women leaders.
The 74th Amendment inserted Part IXA, comprising Articles 243P to 243ZG, and the Twelfth Schedule containing 18 subjects.
SabhaSaar is described as the first AI tool for Gram Sabha minutes; it was piloted in Tripura on the Bhashini platform.
The 34 per cent BC quota, together with SC/ST reservations, is required to pass the 50 per cent ceiling associated with Gawali’s ruling or principle.
The
Sashakt Panchayat Netri Abhiyan and Model Women-Friendly Gram Panchayats
are intended to promote substantive women’s leadership and counter token representation.
The Online Water Monitoring System is used to monitor more than 800 water and sewerage projects across 123 urban local bodies.
The Andhra Pradesh structure comprises Gram Panchayats, Mandal Parishads or Mandal Praja Parishads, and Zilla Parishads.

rows.title: 74th Amendment - Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule, types of urban local bodies, ward committees, DPC and MPC
sub: Group-II M1-B-93: 74th Constitutional Amendment Act - Part IXA, types of urban bodies and the Twelfth Schedule
Group-II M1-B-94: 74th Amendment - ward committees, District Planning Committee and Metropolitan Planning Committee

secs.t: 74th Amendment - commencement, Part inserted, provisions included vs not included

x: Exam angle: "came into force on" (1 June 1993) and "which is NOT a mandatory provision" type statements.
Exam angle: the four-option date trap - 24 Apr 1993 (73rd) vs
The 74th Amendment inserted the
Twelfth Schedule
, which contains 18 municipal functions linked to Article 243W.
The 74th Amendment gave urban local bodies constitutional status and required States to establish a uniform municipal framework through conforming laws.
Article 243Q deals with types of municipalities, Article 243R with their composition, Article 243S with Ward Committees and Article 243T with reservation of seats.

secs.t: Twelfth Schedule - 18 subjects

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 asked which one is a municipal Twelfth Schedule function - answer
cattle pounds
Cattle pounds and prevention of cruelty to animals
are Twelfth Schedule subjects.
Libraries and markets and fairs
are listed under the Eleventh Schedule, not the Twelfth Schedule.
Urban and town planning belongs to the Planning group; water supply and fire services are Infrastructure subjects; urban poverty alleviation belongs to the Social group.
Non-conventional energy, small-scale industries and technical and vocational education are Eleventh Schedule subjects.
Urban forestry and protection of the environment and ecology
are included in the Twelfth Schedule.

secs.t: District Planning Committee and Metropolitan Planning Committee

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2018 - "DPC provided by 74th Act; consolidates plans; all members elected" - only the first two are correct.
Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2018 - "provided by the 74th" and "consolidates panchayat and municipal plans" are correct.
An MPC is mandatory for a metropolitan area with a population of ten lakh or more, is provided under Article 243ZE, and such an area may span more than one district.
At least two-thirds of MPC members are elected from the specified municipal and panchayat representatives, with representation based on the urban-rural population ratio.
The DPC considers matters such as spatial planning, resource sharing, integrated infrastructure and environmental issues.
Both statements are true, and the constitutional requirement of at least four-fifths elected members directly explains why the remaining members need not be elected.
DPCs and MPCs are part of Part IXA and were inserted through
the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992

secs.t: FIRST Municipal Corporation - city and year, early municipalities

x: The charter for the Madras Municipal Corporation was issued on
30 December 1687
The Municipal Corporations of Bombay and Calcutta were established in 1726.
The five KAVAL towns were
Kanpur, Agra, Varanasi, Allahabad and Lucknow
The 1989 Municipalities Bill lapsed, while the Bill introduced by P. V. Narasimha Rao in September 1991 resulted in the 74th Amendment and Part IXA.

secs.t: Functionaries → institution matching

x: The
Mayor
, assisted by the Deputy Mayor, presides over the council of a Municipal Corporation.
The
Municipal Commissioner
is the chief executive of a Municipal Corporation and is appointed by the State Government, commonly from the IAS.
Chairman or Chairperson is the designation associated with the Zilla Parishad as well as the Municipal Council and Nagar Panchayat.

secs.t: Part IXA - Articles 243P to 243ZG

x: Article 243Q recognises Nagar Panchayats for transitional areas, Municipal Councils for smaller urban areas and Municipal Corporations for larger urban areas.
Article 243ZF deals with the continuance of existing laws for a specified period, while Article 243ZG bars court interference in electoral matters relating to municipalities.
The Governor may specify the type of urban area by public notification after considering population, density, revenue, non-agricultural employment and economic importance.

secs.t: Membership - minimum age, disqualifications, SEC role

x: Article 243ZA places the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of municipal elections under the
State Election Commission
, the same constitutional authority associated with Article 243K.
The clarification stated that only
Rajya Sabha members and Members of the Legislative Council
registered as voters in the concerned urban local body could vote in such mayoral polls.

secs.t: Types of urban local bodies

x: The eight listed types are Municipal Corporation, Municipality or Municipal Council, Notified Area Committee, Town Area Committee, Cantonment Board, Township, Port Trust and Special Purpose Agency.
The three principal authorities of a Municipal Corporation are the Council headed by the Mayor, the Standing Committees and the Commissioner.
A statutory town has a local body notified under law, while a census town is identified through population, occupational and density criteria.

secs.t: AP urban local bodies - Corporations and municipal laws

x: Exam angle: "how many" questions, where the answer changes with the year.
Andhra Pradesh has 123 urban local bodies:
17 Municipal Corporations, 79 Municipalities and 27 Nagar Panchayats
The State Election Commission notified ward-wise photo rolls for 41 urban local bodies, including 12 Municipal Corporations.
Polls are proposed in 100 of 123 ULBs; the others are delayed by court cases, and 33.33 percent reservation has been provided for BCs in ULBs.
The APSES 2024–25 figures recorded
17 Municipal Corporations and 79 Municipalities
within the total of 123 Urban Local Bodies.
The notified rolls cover 12 Corporations and 29 Municipalities or Nagar Panchayats, together making 41 Urban Local Bodies.

secs.t: Qualifications to contest (Article 243V)

x: Article 243V requires a minimum age of 21 years for municipal membership, not 25 years.

secs.t: Term, SEC and SFC for municipalities

x: A municipal election must be held before expiry of the five-year term or, in the case of dissolution,
within six months of dissolution
, subject to the constitutional qualification relating to the remaining period.
A municipality continues for five years from the date appointed for its
first meeting
, unless dissolved earlier according to law.

secs.t: Composition - direct elections, nominated persons, ex officio members, reservation, chairperson

x: State law may provide for the representation of
persons having special knowledge or experience in municipal administration
, but such nominated persons do not have voting rights in municipal meetings.
Rajya Sabha members and Members of the Legislative Council registered as electors within the municipal area may be included in the municipal composition.
The reservation framework under Article 243T mirrors the reservation provisions for Panchayats under
Article 243D

secs.t: Industrial townships - provision

x: Where municipal services are being provided by an industrial establishment, the Governor may specify the area as an industrial township and a municipality need not be constituted there.

secs.t: Wards committees - Article 243S

x: Article 243S makes Wards Committees mandatory in municipalities having a population of
three lakh or more
Wards Committees may cover one or more wards, while State law determines their composition and territorial area; the ward councillor sits on the relevant committee.

secs.t: Working of DPCs - states where functional, Kerala model

x: District Planning Committees remain weak in most States, and operationalising them continues to be listed among the mandates of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.
The Andhra Pradesh District Plan and Development Committee is chaired by the District Collector and includes MPs, MLAs and municipal chairmen.
Kerala's DPC integrates plans prepared through the
People's Plan Campaign

secs.t: Area Sabha and community participation law (Model Nagara Raj Bill)

x: An Area Sabha consists of all voters in a polling-booth area and is situated below the Wards Committee.
The Community Participation Law was a mandatory reform under the Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (
JNNURM
The Model Nagara Raj Bill associated with community participation and Area Sabhas dates to 2008.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Cabinet approved direct election of Mayors and municipal or Nagar Panchayat chairpersons, replacing the indirect system.
The stated risk was the loss of approximately
Rs 12,150 crore
in Central funds if polls slipped beyond October.
All three statements reflect the criticism: ULBs spend less than 1 per cent of GDP, employ about 10 per cent of the public workforce, and are described as the 'stepchild' of federalism.
Property tax
is the key own-source revenue of Urban Local Bodies, but it is chronically under-collected.
Only Rajya Sabha members and Members of Legislative Councils registered as voters in the concerned ULB may vote as ex-officio members in these elections.

rows.title: PESA Act 1996; Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas and tribal self-governance
sub: Group-II M1-B-100: PESA Act 1996 and self-governance in the scheduled areas of Andhra Pradesh
Group-II S3-33: Constitutional provisions for Scheduled Tribes - Articles 244, 275, 338A; Fifth and Sixth Schedules

secs.t: Sixth Schedule - Article, states, Autonomous District/Regional Councils

x: Exam angle: G2 2025 statement set - the Sixth Schedule is NOT applied "wherever STs exceed 40%"; the key was "None" correct. GS 2019: Nagaland is not in the Sixth Schedule.
An Autonomous District Council can have up to 30 members, including four Governor-nominated members; the others are elected by adult franchise and elected members serve five years.
The legislative powers of District Councils cover land, forests, canal water, shifting cultivation, village administration, inheritance, marriage and social customs, subject to the Governor's assent.
District Councils may assess land revenue and levy specified taxes, and the tribal areas receive grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India under Article 275(1).

secs.t: Fifth Schedule - Article, declaration, Governor's regulations, TAC

x: Exam angle: "Governor is NOT authorised to direct that an Act does not apply" is the false statement. Regulations are issued by the
Governor
. TAC size is
up to 20
Exam angle: TAC size "up to 20" (G2 2017 - answer key was left blank; the Constitution says not more than 20).

The Governor may make regulations for peace and good government in a Scheduled Area, including regulation of tribal land transfer and money-lending, subject to the prescribed consultation and Presidential assent.
A Tribes Advisory Council may have up to 20 members, about three-fourths of whom are ST MLAs, and the President may direct its constitution in a State with STs but no Scheduled Areas.

secs.t: Fifth vs Sixth Schedule

x: The President declares a Scheduled Area under the Fifth Schedule, while the Governor organises districts under the Sixth Schedule framework.
Under the Fifth Schedule, the Union's executive power extends to giving directions to the State regarding Scheduled Areas.
Both statements are true, and the concentration of Scheduled Tribes in contiguous areas explains why the Constitution provides area-based protection through the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.

secs.t: PESA Act 1996 - committee, states, Gram Sabha powers

x: PESA assigns these functions to Gram Sabhas and Panchayats, including regulation of intoxicants, control of money-lending, management of village markets and local plans including Tribal Sub-Plans.
PESA provides that Scheduled Tribes shall have
at least 50 per cent of the seats
in Panchayats in Scheduled Areas, while reservation is also related to population proportions.

PESA first establishes community-oriented local governance, requires consultation before land acquisition, requires a recommendation before the minor-mineral lease, and the lease follows that recommendation stage.
PESA requires consultation before land acquisition and resettlement, while a Gram Sabha recommendation is mandatory before prospecting licences or mining leases for minor minerals.
PESA operationalises
Article 243M(4)(b)
by extending Part IX relating to Panchayats to Fifth Schedule Areas, subject to exceptions.

secs.t: Effect of Scheduled Area status - land transfer, mining cases

x: In the 2013 Niyamgiri or Orissa Mining Corporation case, Gram Sabhas were to decide whether bauxite mining affected
religious and forest rights
Both statements are true, and the Fifth Schedule's power to make regulations for peace and good government explains the Governor's role in restricting land transfers.
PESA is concerned with extending Panchayati Raj and tribal self-governance to Fifth Schedule Areas; the autonomous-region framework belongs to the Sixth Schedule.

secs.t: Scheduled Areas in Andhra Pradesh - districts, ITDAs, AP PESA Rules

x: All four statements are correct: the map was redrawn in 2025 with 28 districts, including new Polavaram and Markapuram, and the reorganisation created a need to realign land-transfer adjudicating authorities.
Scheduled Areas cover 16,267.63 square kilometres, approximately 10.15 percent, include 3,512 villages and are inhabited by about 12.9 lakh STs; seven ITDAs cover 76 mandals.
Multi-specialty hospitals were sanctioned at
Seethampeta, Parvathipuram, Rampachodavaram, Buttaigudem and Dornala
, at a total sanctioned cost of Rs 482 crore.

secs.t: Implementation gaps

x: More than
40 per cent
of elected representatives in PESA panchayats could not explain what a Gram Sabha is.
Tana Bhagats in Jharkhand stated that PESA consent was not taken for the Bharatmala highway.
The suggested reform is to merge the consent requirements under PESA, FRA 2006 and LARR 2013 into one binding Gram Sabha clearance.

secs.t: PESA states - covered and not covered

x: PESA concerns Fifth Schedule areas; the four named north-eastern States are Sixth Schedule States, while Tamil Nadu is listed as having no Scheduled Areas.
The ten States are
Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan
Nine of the ten Fifth Schedule States have framed PESA rules; Odisha has only draft rules.

secs.t: AP PESA Rules 2011 - notification and implementation

x: All three statements are correct: 2,038 notified PESA Gram Sabhas are being strengthened, 19 model Gram Panchayats cover 43 Gram Sabhas, and the PESA Mahotsav was held in Visakhapatnam for the Act's 30th anniversary.
The Andhra Pradesh PESA Rules were notified in 2011, following the PESA Act of 1996 and the AP amending Act of 1998.

secs.t: Forest Rights Act 2006 link and Samatha judgment

x: The corresponding areas are 5,78,560 acres for individual claims, 6,23,678 acres for community claims, 4,54,706 acres for individual titles and 5,26,454 acres for community titles.
Scheduled Tribe farmers holding Recognition of Forest Rights (RoFR) are covered under
NTR Rythu Bharosa
All four numbers correspond to the APSES 2024–25 data: 2,85,087 individual claims, 3,294 community claims, 2,26,651 individual titles and 1,822 community titles.

secs.t: Article 342 - notification of STs; religion

x: The President specifies the Scheduled Tribes for a State or Union Territory after consultation with the Governor of the concerned State, through the Constitutional Scheduled Tribes Order, 1950.
The Kalelkar Commission observed that tribes may belong to
any religion
, supporting the religion-neutral character of Scheduled Tribe status.
The traits include primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact and backwardness.

secs.t: Article 338A - National Commission for Scheduled Tribes

x: The Commission focuses on minor forest produce, mineral and water rights, and rehabilitation of displaced tribals.
The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes requisitioned reports on Forest Rights Act implementation from the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Fifth Schedule framework involves the Governor, Tribal Advisory Councils and PESA, while the Sixth Schedule provides autonomous district councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
AP's Scheduled Areas correspond to the old Agency tracts, AP is among the ten Fifth Schedule States, and Araku is an ST Lok Sabha seat.
A post-Maoism policy discussion has emphasised the need to implement PESA in earnest rather than abandon its Gram Sabha-centred framework.

rows.title: Panchayati Raj and urban bodies in Andhra Pradesh - structure, elections, finances, performance
sub: Group-II M1-B-97: Panchayati Raj in Andhra Pradesh - structure, elections, powers and finances
Group-II M1-B-98: Urban local bodies in Andhra Pradesh - municipalities, corporations and their functioning

secs.t: Gram Panchayat working - meetings, execution, functions, Marriage Officer

x: Exam angle: "Who convenes / who implements / who is Marriage Officer" - the answer is the Secretary, not the Sarpanch.
The Sarpanch is the elected political head of the Gram Panchayat, whereas the Panchayat Secretary is the executive functionary responsible for administration.
Sanitation, drinking water, drains, street lighting, village roads and burial grounds are obligatory functions.

secs.t: AP State Election Commission

x: Exam angle: statement pairs on "appointed by Governor for 5 years" + "status of HC judge" - both correct.
The State Election Commissioner enjoys protection comparable to that of a
High Court judge
in matters of removal.
The order concerned photo electoral rolls for
MPTC and ZPTC elections
, which are local-body elections.
Article 243K provides the constitutional basis for the State Election Commission in relation to Panchayat elections; Article 243ZA relates to municipal elections.
The State Election Commission supervises, directs and controls electoral rolls and local-body elections, including republication of Gram Panchayat rolls.

secs.t: AP municipal laws - Acts, Amendment Bills, Mayor election mode

x: The 33.33 per cent BC quota is implemented under the Andhra Pradesh Municipal Corporations Act, 1994 and the Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965.
A companion Bill removed the two-child bar on contesting panchayat elections in November 2024.
The Third Amendment Bill, 2026 adds a Uniform Mutation Fee on title transfers recorded in municipal records.
The Cabinet approved direct election of
Mayors of Corporations and Chairpersons of Municipalities and Nagar Panchayats

secs.t: AP Panchayat Raj Act 1994 - three tiers

x: Part II deals with Gram Panchayats, Part III with Mandal Parishads, Part IV with Zilla Parishads and Part VI with the Finance Commission.
ZPTC members are directly elected, but the Zilla Parishad Chairperson is elected
indirectly from among the ZPTC members
The minimum age for contesting Panchayati Raj elections is
21 years
, consistent with the floor under Article 243F.

secs.t: Evolution of PRIs in AP - order, first Acts, Mandal system, committees

x: Andhra Pradesh introduced the three-tier Panchayati Raj system on 1 November 1959 under Chief Minister Neelam Sanjiva Reddy, with Kasu Brahmananda Reddy holding the Local Bodies portfolio.

Balwant Rai Mehta is linked with the Panchayat Samiti–Zilla Parishad relationship; Ashok Mehta with the two-tier and party-participation model; G. V. K. Rao with the ‘grass without roots’ observation; and L. M. Singhvi with constitutional recognition and Gram Sabha.

secs.t: AP State Finance Commission and local body finances

x: The
Governor
constitutes a State Finance Commission under Articles 243I and 243Y.
The 16th Finance Commission operates for 2026–31, and Andhra Pradesh Rural Local Bodies are allocated Rs 16,627 crore.
The 14th and 15th Finance Commission grants prioritised
drinking water and sanitation
The Atmanirbhar Panchayat Program is a challenge for revenue-generating projects under the
Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan
of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj.

secs.t: Village/Ward Secretariat system and volunteers

x: Ward Secretariats and the Volunteer system operate under the
Municipal Administration Department
as service-delivery mechanisms.
The system was launched on
2 October 2019
, with a secretariat intended for each village or ward cluster.
The 2024–25 outcome target was to improve the quality and accountability of urban services through Ward Secretariat and Volunteer Systems across all ULBs.

secs.t: Gram Panchayat functions - obligatory vs discretionary

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked which is an "essential function" - burial grounds.
Maintaining burial grounds
is an obligatory or essential function of a Gram Panchayat.

secs.t: AP tier reforms - Panchayat Samithis to Mandal Praja Parishads

x: In 1986, during the N.T. Rama Rao Government, Panchayat Samithis were replaced by Mandal Praja Parishads and Zilla Parishads were renamed Zilla Praja Parishads.

secs.t: Elections - unanimous-election incentives, recent polls

x: The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet approved
34 percent
reservation for Backward Classes in rural local bodies on 18 August 2026.
All four statements are correct: ULB terms ended on 15 March 2026, panchayat terms on 4 April 2026, MPPs/ZPPs were due by 23 September 2026, and Special Officers were administering the bodies.

secs.t: AP Municipalities Act - commencement, grades, nagar panchayats

x: The grades of municipalities are determined by
annual income
The recognised grades are Special Grade, Selection Grade, Grade I, Grade II and Grade III.
A
Nagar Panchayat
is constituted for an area transitioning from rural to urban character under Article 243Q.
Population, population density, revenue for local administration and the percentage of non-agricultural employment are considered in classifying areas.

secs.t: Urban e-governance projects - purpose

x: Mee Seva is a single-window counter for government citizen services in Andhra Pradesh and has operated since 2011.
e-Panchayat is a Ministry of Panchayati Raj Mission Mode Project for digitising Panchayat planning, budgeting and service delivery through the e-Gram Swaraj portal.
Digitised bill processing reduced the time for payments from approximately 20–25 days to
about one week

secs.t: Urban development authorities - APCRDA, VMRDA and others

x: Urban Development Authorities are special-purpose functional agencies, established by State Act or executive resolution, autonomous and not subordinate to ULBs.
Urban Development Authorities are not subordinate to ULBs; their separate and autonomous functioning can fragment urban governance.
The three-level uniform mechanism extends across
Nagar Panchayats, municipalities, corporations and Urban Development Authorities

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Incomplete devolution of the three Fs—
Funds, Functions and Functionaries
—limits Panchayati Raj Institutions and leaves them mainly as implementing agencies.
Bokkasam Palem in Srikalahasti mandal of Tirupati stood first in the women-friendly panchayat category, while Sringavaram topped governance.
Sringavaram in Visakhapatnam topped the
governance
category in the Deendayal Upadhyay Panchayat Satat Vikas awards.
The 74th Amendment constitutionalised urban local government through Part IX-A, Articles 243P–243ZG and 18 Twelfth Schedule subjects.

rows.title: Public policy - meaning, types, policy cycle (formulation, implementation, evaluation), policy instruments
sub: Group-II S3-30: Public policy and the welfare state in India - evolution and approach

secs.t: Definitions of public policy → thinker

x: Thomas Dye
defined public policy as whatever governments choose to do or not to do, thereby treating governmental inaction also as policy.
James Anderson defined public policy as
a purposive course of action followed by an actor or set of actors in dealing with a problem
Public policy is a systematic state course of action addressing public issues, pursuing development goals and regulating behaviour; it bridges political intent and administrative action.

secs.t: Types of policy - Lowi classification

x: Distributive policies spread benefits to specific groups while their costs are generally borne by the wider public; farm input subsidies and PM-KISAN illustrate this type.
Redistributive policies
transfer resources from one group to another, as in land reforms and progressive income taxation.
Constitutive
policies create or reorganise institutions and rules; setting up NITI Aayog and delimitation illustrate this category.

secs.t: Policy cycle stages

x: Adoption
is the stage at which the legislature or executive debates, amends and formally adopts the policy.
Implementation translates an adopted policy into action through planning, allocation of resources, coordination and, where necessary, new regulations or programmes.
Termination or revision deals with ineffective policies and allows policy learning to feed back into agenda setting.

secs.t: Policy models → proponent

x: Herbert Simon is associated with the
rational-comprehensive model
and its critique based on bounded rationality and satisficing.
Charles Lindblom
developed incrementalism, famously described as the “science of muddling through,” in 1959.
Amitai Etzioni
is the proponent of the mixed-scanning model.
David Easton’s systems model represents policy-making through inputs, conversion, outputs and feedback.

secs.t: Policy instruments

x: The stated regulatory illustration permits registration of only e-three-wheelers and N1 trucks from 1 January 2027 and e-two-wheelers from 1 April 2028.
Tax rates, subsidies, DBT-based subsidy reform, PLI incentives and public borrowing are listed as fiscal policy instruments under this category.
Information instruments
influence public action through disclosure, communication and campaigns; proactive disclosure under Section 4 of the RTI Act is an example.

secs.t: Implementation approaches

x: The top-down approach emphasises central direction and faithful execution, while the bottom-up approach recognises that front-line officials shape actual outcomes.
Pressman and Wildavsky’s “Implementation,” published in 1973, showed how chains of clearances can derail programmes.
Michael Lipsky
developed the concept of street-level bureaucracy in 1980, referring to front-line officials who shape policy outcomes.

secs.t: Policy evaluation

x: DMEO is the apex M&E office under NITI Aayog; it evaluates Central schemes on its own initiative or at a ministry’s request, advises States and supports evidence-based policy.
The Draft National Health Research Policy 2026 uses the
ICMR Impact of Research and Innovation Scale
to assess research contributions to public policy and practice.

secs.t: Policy failure and implementation gap

x: The bypassing of citizens by
parastatals and Special Purpose Vehicles
is identified as a cause of implementation gaps.
Phased implementation with milestones, real-time monitoring and public outcome tracking is prescribed as a remedy for implementation gaps.
Swarna Andhra Vision 2047 is cited as an example of multi-phase execution combined with performance evaluation.

secs.t: Social welfare services and social development programmes - Social Policy/Justice/Defence/Welfare

x: Social welfare services target vulnerable groups such as
disabled persons, destitute children and widows

Social policy is the overall framework for social well-being; social justice removes inequalities; social welfare serves vulnerable sections; and social defence involves rehabilitation in deviant or vulnerable situations.
Article 38 concerns social order and reduction of inequalities, while Article 46 concerns the interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections.

secs.t: Social legislation - aims, types, examples

x: Social legislation protects vulnerable groups and establishes minimum floors for a dignified life.
The shift signifies State intervention to protect vulnerable parties and ensure minimum standards of fairness.
Protective legislation prevents exploitation, regulatory legislation governs conduct and relations, and enabling legislation creates entitlements.
The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 is an example of regulatory legislation.

secs.t: Welfare ministries → renaming and bifurcation history

x: The
SC, Tribal and Minority divisions
moved from the Ministry of Home Affairs into the reorganised welfare structure.
The Ministry of Minority Affairs and the Ministry of Women and Child Development became separate ministries
during 2006–07.
The present departments include Social Justice and Empowerment and Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (Divyangjan).

secs.t: Evolution of welfare approach - Five Year Plan phases

x: State-led planned development characterised the 1950s–70s, welfare shifted towards development in the Sixth Plan, empowerment marked the Eighth–Ninth Plans, and rights-based laws emerged in the 2000s.
The Sixth Plan marked a shift from welfare towards development, particularly in relation to women.
New welfarism is described as targeted and technology-driven, relying on DBT benefits rather than primarily on legal rights.

secs.t: Rights-based entitlements - RTI, NREGA, NFSA, RTE

x: The Right to Information framework provides information within
30 days
in the stated entitlement summary.
The RTE Act, 2009 provides free schooling for children aged
6–14 years
under Article 21A.
Civil society
played an important role in helping to win these rights-based entitlements.
The emphasis has subsequently shifted towards
cash transfers

secs.t: Delivery reforms - DBT, JAM trinity, social audit (AP model)

x: DBT and JAM can reduce ghost beneficiaries and remove middlemen from benefit delivery.
People lacking digital access may be excluded from technology-driven benefit delivery.
Section 17 of MGNREGA provides for social audit by the
Gram Sabha
Andhra Pradesh pioneered statewide NREGS social audits in 2006, and the independent Society for Social Audit, Accountability and Transparency was established in 2009.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The index gives weights of
to transport electrification, charging and research and development, respectively.
The index is intended to reinforce
evidence-based policymaking
by providing an analytical basis for decisions on electric mobility.
The shift toward outcome-based governance is linked with Action Taken Reports (ATRs) and evaluations by the Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO).

rows.title: Actors in policy-making - executive, legislature, judiciary, bureaucracy, media, civil society, think tanks

secs.t: Media - agenda setting, public opinion, image-building, free press and new media

x: Public awareness and media coverage
are identified as important drivers through which issues are pushed onto the policy agenda.
AI-driven foreign information manipulation can exploit social fault lines by using synthetic media and algorithmic polarisation.
Mass media shape political images through the ideology of the outlet and the manner in which news is selected and presented.

secs.t: Legislature - law-making, committees, options against a Supreme Court decision

x: Parliament is the chief law-making body, but the Cabinet determines the substance and timing of bills, while the bureaucracy generally drafts them.
Without a Rajya Sabha majority, a government may have to concede or negotiate, as illustrated by the rejection of the Prevention of Terrorism Bill, 2002, in the Rajya Sabha.

secs.t: Executive - Cabinet, PMO, Cabinet Secretariat, NITI Aayog

x: The noted criticisms include delays, bureaucratic influence, overlapping mandates, political considerations and secrecy, even though the Cabinet and Cabinet Committees take key decisions.
The Cabinet Secretariat is headed by the Cabinet Secretary, works directly under the Prime Minister and administers the Transaction of Business Rules.
The Chief Minister of
Andhra Pradesh
ordered a two-month review cycle for ₹50,999 crore of Amaravati contracts, drawing on the Centre's PRAGATI model.

secs.t: Judiciary - activism, PIL, court guidelines acting as law

x: Vishaka dealt with workplace sexual harassment, Prakash Singh with police reforms, and T.S.R. Subramanian with civil-services safeguards.
T.S.R. Subramanian was associated with
Civil Services Boards, fixed tenure for civil servants and written instructions from political executives
Upendra Baxi's typology includes ideological, epistemic, management, legitimation and democratic fears.
The orders concerning an NCERT Class 8 chapter on “
corruption in judiciary
” were described by an MP as judicial overreach.

secs.t: Bureaucracy - advice, drafting, implementation discretion

x: The permanent executive includes personnel from All-India Services, State services, local bodies and public sector undertakings, assisting ministers in policy formulation and implementation.
Although bureaucracy assists ministers in formulating and implementing policies, it remains bound by policy approved by the legislature.
Vigilance, conduct rules, the CAG, CVC and Lokpal are accountability tools for bureaucracy.

secs.t: Civil society and pressure groups - campaigns that produced laws

x: The MKSS movement led to the RTI Act, 2005; Right to Work/NAC advocacy was associated with MGNREGA, 2005; and the Right to Food campaign contributed to the National Food Security Act, 2013.
The relevant sequence is PUCL v. Union of India in 2001, followed by the RTI Act and MGNREGA in 2005, and then the National Food Security Act in 2013.

secs.t: Think tanks and expert bodies → type

x: NITI Aayog, along with DMEO, is classified as a Government think tank or expert body.
The Syama Prasad Mookerjee Research Foundation is linked with the BJP, whereas the Rajiv Gandhi Foundation is linked with the Congress.
Policy labs, hackathons and idea competitions
are identified as newer channels for policy innovation and expert participation.

secs.t: Political parties and manifestos in agenda setting

x: Political party manifesto promises can enter the policy agenda and become government policies after the party assumes power.
The 33.33% BC quota in Andhra Pradesh urban local bodies was an NDA 2024 poll promise and was subsequently implemented through G.O. Rt.
Andhra Pradesh began publishing Action Taken Reports from 22 June 2026 against seven sectoral white papers, enabling public tracking of manifesto delivery.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Accountability concerns include delays by Governors and Speakers in deciding assent and Tenth Schedule matters, along with an RTI backlog and fewer committee referrals.
PIL is criticised when it is misused for publicity or political purposes rather than for a genuine public cause or protection of rights.
Sri Lanka's proposed 22nd Amendment would raise the retirement age of Supreme Court judges from 65 to 67, prompting debate concerning judicial independence.

rows.title: Governance and good governance - meaning, dimensions, World Bank/UNDP indicators

secs.t: Centre for Good Governance, Andhra Pradesh

x: The CGG is a governance-reform think tank that advises the government on administrative reforms, e-governance, research and training.
The Centre for Good Governance was established in collaboration with
DFID of the United Kingdom and the World Bank

secs.t: Governance and good governance - originating body/thinker

x: The World Bank defines governance as
the manner in which power is exercised in managing a country's economic and social resources for development
UNDP describes governance as the exercise of
economic, political and administrative authority
to manage a country's affairs at all levels.
Democracy aids development by encouraging
citizen participation and accountability

secs.t: Good governance characteristics - UN/UNDP list

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT a feature" - look for centralisation, secrecy, discretion or majoritarian rule as the odd one out.
Ethos means service, ethics means honesty and integrity, equity means empathy for weaker sections, and efficiency means speedy delivery using ICT.
Good governance requires transparency, accountability and equity or inclusiveness; secrecy, unchecked discretion and majoritarian rule are contrary to these principles.

secs.t: World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators

x: The WGI cover more than 200 countries since 1996 and include Government Effectiveness and Rule of Law among their six dimensions.
The
Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances
, or DARPG, is India's nodal department for the WGI.
India was described as having moderate government effectiveness and rule of law, while political stability was low compared with global averages.

secs.t: Good Governance Index (DARPG)

x: The GGI is a uniform tool intended to rank
states, Union Territories and districts
The GGI is intended to be revised
every two years
; the latest edition mentioned is 2021.
Foreign affairs and diplomacy
is not one of the ten GGI sectors.
The NCGG was established by upgrading the
National Institute of Administrative Research
associated with LBSNAA.

secs.t: Second ARC reports on ethics and citizen-centric administration

x: The 4th Report, titled “Ethics in Governance,” was published in 2007 and covered codes of ethics, anti-corruption bodies and ethics in legislatures.
All four subjects were covered in the 12th Report, “Citizen Centric Administration - The Heart of Governance,” published in 2009.
People's participation
is identified as the most foundational tool for implementing good governance; other tools include RTI, Sevottam, Citizen Charters and e-governance.

secs.t: Governance indices → publisher

x: The Public Affairs Index is published by the Public Affairs Centre, BRAP rankings by DPIIT, the SDG India Index by NITI Aayog, and the Good Governance Index by DARPG.
The Governance Readiness Assessment Index (GRAI) is listed with the Good Governance Index under
DARPG
The National MPI is associated with NITI Aayog, UNDP and OPHI and uses
12 indicators

secs.t: Universal angles

x: India showcased
CPGRAMS and the Samadhan Didi AI grievance chatbot
to Malaysia in August 2026.
All three statements are correct: Mana Mitra offers 500-plus services, received Rs 100 crore for RTGS in the 2026–27 Budget, and aims to reach 1,000 services.
WGI and V-Dem are contested because perception-based indices rely substantially on expert opinion, which can affect their objectivity and comparability.

rows.title: E-governance - models, types of interaction, National e-Governance Plan, Digital India and governance outcomes

secs.t: AP e-governance initiatives - purpose and developer

x: e-Pragati aims at
faceless, paperless and cashless governance
, with additional citizen services integrated into the platform.

All four statements are correct. e-Pragati is based on the Seva model, integrates the four listed service areas, added 45 services in February 2026, and advances faceless, paperless and cashless governance.
The Real Time Governance Society uses Artificial Intelligence, Big Data, GIS, IoT and real-time dashboards.

secs.t: E-governance awards and conferences - NCeG host city, national awards

x: The National Awards for e-Governance were instituted by
DARPG under the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
The theme of the 28th NCeG in 2025 was “
Viksit Bharat: Civil Service & Digital Transformation
The 29th NCeG in Jaipur adopted the Jaipur Declaration on DPI, AI-enabled governance, cybersecurity and data governance.

secs.t: National digital platforms - expansion and purpose

x: UMANG is a single application providing multiple government services through web, SMS and IVR channels.
DigiLocker is a cloud locker for documents and certificates and is a key Digital India initiative.
The material associates CSCs with approximately
5.1 lakh
village-level service outlets where grievances can be filed.
The dates and institutional association identify BHIM, PRAGATI, Dial.Gov and e-Taal respectively.

secs.t: E-governance interaction types - G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E

x: G2B means Government to Business interaction; MCA portal, GSTN and e-Procurement are examples.
G2G concerns inter-government interaction, while G2E concerns government services for its employees.
Online birth, income and caste certificates are Government-to-Citizen services, or
G2C

secs.t: Models of e-governance - theorist

x: Critical flow
channels critical information to a targeted audience, such as corruption data sent to an ombudsman.
Comparative analysis
involves learning from best practices elsewhere.
E-advocacy or mobilisation and lobbying uses online civil-society networks to influence decisions.
Interactive service
is the two-way G2C model involving activities such as filing, payments and feedback.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A Singapore delegation reviewed
RTGS
in Andhra Pradesh.
The subject of the speech was ‘
Technology, governance and the future
E-governance is associated with citizen engagement, better service delivery, fewer face-to-face contacts and audit trails.
Andhra Pradesh declared 2026 the '
Technology-Driven Decision Making
Year'.
