rows.title: Kinship - descent, lineage, clan, kinship terminology; North-South Indian kinship contrast
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Kinship types - consanguineal vs affinal, degrees (primary, secondary, tertiary), family scenarios

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2025. Ravindra-Seema's children are Krishna and Madhavi; Madhavi-Harish's daughter is Jyothi.
Krishna-Jyothi
(maternal uncle-niece) is consanguineous. Ravindra-Seema, Madhavi-Harish and Krishna-Harish are affinal.
Consanguineal kinship is based on blood relations, such as parent-child and uncle-nephew relationships.
Radcliffe-Brown defined kinship as
a system of dynamic relations regulated by social usage

secs.t: Descent rules - patrilineal, matrilineal, bilateral, double descent, Indian examples

x: Patrilineal descent is found among the
Kondhs, Santhals and Bhils
, while Khasi, Garo and Nair are examples of matrilineal communities.
Bilateral or cognatic descent gives equal recognition to descent through both the paternal and maternal sides.
Double or bilineal descent
transmits different attributes through different parents.
Satavahana rulers used matronymics, but the monarchy itself was patriarchal.

secs.t: Descent groups - lineage, clan, gotra, phratry, moiety

x: A
lineage
is a unilineal descent group whose members trace descent from a known ancestor and which is exogamous.
A moiety is one of the two descent-based halves into which a society is divided.
Gotra is an exogamous Hindu clan, and the same-gotra bar dates from
the Later Vedic period

secs.t: Kinship terminology - classificatory vs descriptive, who proposed the distinction

x: L. H. Morgan
proposed the classificatory-descriptive distinction in Systems of Consanguinity and Affinity (1871).
A classificatory term uses one word for several categories of kin, such as different kinds of uncle.
Kinship terms may be classified by structure or use, and Kapadia connected them with marriage and inheritance rules.

secs.t: Kinship usages - avoidance, joking, teknonymy, avunculate, amitate, couvade

x: Avoidance
refers to socially prescribed restraint between particular relatives, including a daughter-in-law and father-in-law.
A
joking relationship
permits socially sanctioned teasing between specified relatives, such as a man and his wife’s younger sister.
Amitate
denotes the special role of the father’s sister and is associated with patrilineal societies.
Couvade is the practice in which the husband imitates or observes his wife’s pregnancy-related taboos.

secs.t: North-South kinship contrast - Karve's zones, preferred marriage rules

x: North Indian kinship is characterised by gotra and village exogamy and sasan or sapinda marriage prohibitions.
South Indian kinship
includes marriage with the elder sister’s daughter, father’s sister’s daughter or mother’s brother’s daughter, along with a principle of symmetry.
Pauline Kolenda
’s Regional Variations in Hindu Kinship, published in 1968, built upon Karve’s work.

secs.t: Ritual kinship - godparenthood, fictive kin, ritual brother/sister bonds

x: Fictive kinship consists of socially assumed ties between persons who are not related by birth or marriage.
Godparenthood, dharam bhai or behen relationships and rakhi ties are examples of ritual or fictive kinship.
Buddhist monks’ use of kin terms for fellow monks represents a spiritual family and is an example of fictive kinship.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kinship rules shape marriage choice, inheritance patterns and the form of households.
Karve is regarded as the ‘Mother of Indian Kinship Studies’ because she was the first to map Indian kinship systematically.
Morgan’s work dates to 1871, Karve’s work to 1953, Kolenda’s work to 1968, and the end of Marumakkathayam to 1975.

src: Sources: CDX (Indian Society Part 1 pp.17-20, 26; Part 2 pp.7-9); APP (Society > Kinship: Definition and Types, Approaches, North India, South India, North-South Comparison); CDI (Block01 Vedic); UPSC (Ancient History pp.69-70); APHQ 2011 Q71

rows.title: Caste - features, theories of origin, varna-jati distinction
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Theories and period of origin → proponent, stage of history when caste emerged

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2007 asked when caste "began" as a new social organisation (after the Vedic period / Mauryan / Gupta / after Gupta). The printed key is garbled in your bank. Your notes date the crystallisation to the
Later Vedic
age.
The Early Vedic period lacked rigid varna divisions, the Purusha Sukta is considered a late addition, and hereditary four-fold divisions crystallised in the Later Vedic period.

secs.t: Jajmani system - inter-caste dependence, who studied it, regional equivalents

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2020 matched the pairs above (answer 1-3-4-2).
The Jajmani system was a socio-economic and ritual arrangement in which the landholding jajman received hereditary services from kamin castes.
The system was not based entirely on state-paid cash wages; it involved hereditary services and traditional forms of exchange, including barter.

secs.t: Caste - features lists by scholars (Ghurye; hierarchy, endogamy, occupation, commensality)

x: Ghurye identified lack of
free choice of occupation
, not free choice of occupation, as a feature of caste.
G.S. Ghurye’s Caste and Race in India was published in 1932.
Ascription by birth is a central feature of caste.
Caste has a vertical dimension expressed through ranking and a horizontal dimension expressed through grouping into separate communities.

secs.t: Varna model vs jati - Vedic source, number of jatis, relationship

x: Jati consists of numerous local and regional groups, not exactly four groups.
Varna is the idealised four-fold scheme, while jati refers to the numerous concrete and regionally varied caste groups.
Each varna is subdivided into jatis
The 1931 Census recorded 4,147 castes.
The term caste is derived from the Portuguese
casta
, meaning race or breed.

secs.t: Caste - definitions and books (Ketkar, Risley, Bougle, Dumont)

x: Risley described caste in terms of families sharing a common name, claiming descent from a mythical ancestor and following the same hereditary calling.
Louis Dumont
analysed caste through the opposition of purity and impurity in Homo Hierarchicus, published in 1966.
Martindale and Monachesi emphasised that caste obligations and privileges are
fixed by birth and sanctioned by religion

secs.t: Purity-pollution and cultural traits of caste

x: McKim Marriott explained caste interaction and ranking through the exchange of coded substances, including food, water and services.
Universal inter-caste commensality
is contrary to the commensal taboos associated with caste.
Dipankar Gupta argued that castes are discrete communities and that social difference is not necessarily the same as hierarchy.

secs.t: Caste among non-Hindus - Muslims, Christians, Sikhs

x: In the noted classification, Ashraf refers to nobles or upper-caste converts, Ajlaf to commoners or lower-caste converts, and Arzal to
Dalit converts
Mazhabi Sikhs
are identified as the largest Scheduled Caste component among the Sikh groups mentioned.
All three statements are correct: the 1950 Order initially covered Hindus, Sikhs were included in 1956, and Buddhists were included in 1990.

secs.t: Tribe-caste continuum - concept and scholars (F.G. Bailey, Surajit Sinha)

x: F.G. Bailey
treated tribe and caste as the two poles of a social continuum in *Tribe, Caste and Nation* (1960).

Bailey is associated with the tribe-caste continuum; Sinha with secondary state formation; Bose with *The Hindu Method of Tribal Absorption*; and Ghurye with the description of tribes as ‘backward Hindus’.
Xaxa and Elwin
contested Ghurye’s characterization of tribes as ‘backward Hindus’.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The 2009 genetic study referred to in the analysis found that most Indians descend from
two
ancestral populations.
The argument is that caste creates biological differences rather than simply inheriting pre-existing biological differences.
The Satavahanas organised the eighteen professions; the Kakatiya era is called the ‘Age of Shudras’; and Brahmins were classified as Vaidiki or Niyogi.

rows.title: Caste in modern India - dominant caste, sanskritisation, caste associations, caste and politics
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Caste and politics - vote banks, caste parties, politicisation of caste (Rajni Kothari)

x: Exam angle: RPSC 2013 A-R. Castes are being politicised, and casteism in politics is increasing. Both are true,
but R is not the explanation
Christophe Jaffrelot
authored *India's Silent Revolution*, which discusses the political rise of lower castes.
The conflict has increasingly shifted from ritual status to competition for political power, while casteism in politics has also increased.

secs.t: Dominant caste - originator, criteria, village of study, historical dominant castes

x: The concept of dominant caste is associated with sociologist
M.N. Srinivas
The traditional criteria are sizeable arable land, numerical strength and high ritual status.
Later additions include Western education, administrative jobs and urban income.

secs.t: Caste status mobility - sanskritisation, upward claims (census petitions)

x: Sanskritisation involves adoption of rituals, vegetarianism and the sacred thread associated with twice-born castes.
The colonial Census, beginning in 1871, ranked castes; groups consequently formed associations and petitioned for higher status.
Marathas, Jats, Yadavs, Thevars and Nairs have been associated with claims of warrior or Kshatriya status.
In medieval Andhra, these groups were Kshatriyaised through the
Nayankara system

secs.t: Caste associations - meaning, examples, Rudolph and Rudolph

x: Marathas, Gujjars and Patels have all been cited as groups seeking OBC status.
Lloyd Rudolph and Susanne Rudolph authored *The Modernity of Tradition*, published in 1967.
The Rudolphs viewed caste associations as agents of
democratisation
, citing groups such as the Nadars and Vanniyars of Tamil Nadu.
The expression 'bullock capitalists' is associated with
Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph

secs.t: Changes in caste - education, urbanisation, reservation, land reforms

x: Urbanisation and industrialisation weaken food taboos and promote mixing across castes, but they do not completely abolish caste identity.
Reservation and the Mandal process reinforced caste identity; OBCs were computed at 52 percent or more in the cited context.
Gramdan failed in the heartlands because dominant landowning castes impeded the redistributionary process.

secs.t: Dominant castes of Andhra Pradesh - landholding castes and their political role

x: Reddys, Kammas, Velamas and Kapus rose as martial and agrarian castes in Andhra Pradesh.
The
Kayasthas
were described as an administrative elite, whereas the other listed groups were identified primarily as martial and agrarian castes.
The Justice Party rested on intermediate-caste mobilisation involving
Kammas, Reddys and Naidus
The EWS Welfare Department clubs the Reddy, Kamma, Kapu, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vysya and EBC corporations.

secs.t: Caste census debates - SECC 2011, Bihar survey, AP BC enumeration

x: All four statements are correct: approval came on 30 April 2025, the exercise is projected as the first digital Census and first caste count since 1931, and Population Enumeration is due in February 2027.
The Centre dropped OBC lists on the ground that they represented classes rather than castes; the Opposition sought that the questionnaire be scrapped.

secs.t: Scholars and books on caste in modern India (Srinivas, Béteille, Dipankar Gupta, Jan Breman)

x: M.N. Srinivas
developed the concepts of Sanskritisation and dominant caste in the study of social change in India.
André Béteille
authored Caste, Class and Power, published in 1965.
André Béteille is associated with the idea of
dispersed inequality
Jan Breman wrote Patronage and Exploitation, which deals with hali bonded labour in south Gujarat.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The debate includes the choice between an open column and a pre-coded caste list, the risk of social fragmentation, and the possible use of data for sub-categorisation and consideration of the 50% cap.

All three statements correctly describe the caste-organised welfare structure cited for Andhra Pradesh: BC groups are divided into A–E, the SC share is 17.08 percent, and corporations exist for forward castes.

rows.title: Tribe - definition, classification, distribution and characteristics
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Scheduled Tribe definition and criteria - Art. 366(25), Art. 342, Lokur criteria

x: Marshall Sahlins described a tribe as
a segmental organisation of equivalent, unspecialised multi-family groups, clans or bands
The criteria are primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact with the community at large and backwardness.
Under Article 342(1), the President specifies the Scheduled Tribes for each State or Union Territory after consulting the Governor in the case of a State.

secs.t: PVTGs - criteria, numbers, states, AP list

x: The 12 listed groups include Chenchu, Konda Savaras and Bodo Gadaba, but
Konda Reddis
is not in that specific list of 12 undivided Andhra Pradesh groups.
PM-JANMAN covers all 75 PVTGs, operates from 2023-24 to 2027-28, has an outlay of ₹15,000 crore and includes the listed basic-services and livelihood interventions.
Chenchu, Bodo Gadaba, Gutob Gadaba and Dongria Khond
are all included in the 12-member undivided Andhra Pradesh list given for PVTGs.

secs.t: Denotified and nomadic tribes - Criminal Tribes Act, repeal, replacement

x: The Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 branded approximately 200 communities as ‘hereditary criminals’.
The Act was amended in 1924 and repealed on 31 August 1952 following the All India Criminal Tribes Inquiry Committee report.
Nomadic tribes do not have permanent settlements; pastoralists, hunters and entertainers are among the groups included in this description.

secs.t: Books on Indian tribes → author

x: Exam angle: MPPSC 2025 matched Russell-Hiralal / Raizada / Naik / Elwin.
‘The Baiga’ and ‘A Philosophy for NEFA’ were written by
Verrier Elwin

The correct associations are The Bhils: A Study—T.B. Naik; Tribal Development in M.P.—Ajit Raizada; The Scheduled Tribes—G.S. Ghurye; and The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces—R.V. Russell and Hira Lal.

secs.t: Classification and characteristics - racial, linguistic, economic; totemism; dormitories

x: Austro-Asiatic includes Santhal, Munda, Khasi and Shompen; Dravidian includes Gond, Oraon, Khond and Kui; Tibeto-Burman includes Nyishi and other north-eastern tribes.
The economic categories include food-gatherers and hunters, shifting cultivators, settled agriculturists, artisans, pastoralists and industrial labour.
Totemism
refers to a clan’s mystic bond with an animal or plant totem that is revered and not killed.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: According to the cited Census 2011 data, 64.83% of Andhra Pradesh’s Scheduled Tribes were
marginal holders
The Banchhada are listed as Scheduled Castes in
Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
, despite their earlier description as a ‘criminal tribe’.
The Nicobar tribal council alleged pressure on the Shompen in connection with the
Great Nicobar project

rows.title: Ethnicity - concept, ethnic identity and ethnic movements in India
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Ethnic movements and militant outfits → region + demand, and state operations

x: Exam angle: code names of operations (Blue Star, APPSC 2025) and "ULFA belongs to" (Assam).
ULFA was formed in Assam in April 1979 and demanded
a sovereign Assam for ethnic Assamese
The Gorkhaland movement in the Darjeeling hills was associated with the Gorkha National Liberation Front led by Subhash Ghising.

secs.t: Ethnic conflicts → communities, causes, accords (Manipur, Assam, Tripura)

x: The Assam Accord was signed in 1985 with AASU and AAGSP and fixed 24 March 1971 as the cut-off date for detecting foreigners.
The Bodo settlement process included the 1993, 2003 and 2020 accords, leading respectively to the Bodoland Autonomous Council, BTC and BTR, with the listed organisations involved at different stages.

secs.t: Ethnicity and ethnic group - definitions, markers

x: An ethnic group consists of people who identify with one another through common language or dialect, history, society, culture or nation.
India’s linguistic diversity includes more than 19,500 returned languages and dialects, 121 languages, 270 mother tongues and 22 Scheduled Languages.
The conflict approach views groups as interest groups competing unequally, with South Africa and Sri Lankan Tamils cited as examples.

secs.t: Ethnic identity - primordialist vs instrumentalist vs constructivist

x: Primordialism views ethnic identity as given by birth and rooted in deep primordial attachments.
Paul Brass
is associated with the instrumentalist approach, which argues that elites mobilise identity for power and resources.
Rajni Kothari and Christophe Jaffrelot are associated with instrumentalist discussions, while Barth and Anderson are associated with constructivist perspectives.

secs.t: Ethnic groups of India - North-East groups, linguistic groups, ethnic minorities

x: The ‘iyu-ena’ taboo on killing tigers is associated with the
Idu Mishmi
community of Arunachal Pradesh.
Longpi pottery is a distinctive marker associated with the
Tangkhul Naga
community of Manipur.
The linguistic stocks listed are
Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic and Tibeto-Burman
The
Apatani
are noted for practising wet-rice cultivation in the Ziro Valley without animals or machines.

secs.t: Language groups and linguistic identity - linguistic states, Potti Sriramulu, Andhra State

x: Fazl Ali headed the States Reorganisation Commission, which was constituted in 1953; the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 led to the formation of Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956.
Potti Sriramulu died in December 1952, the Commission was constituted in 1953, Andhra State was formed in October 1953, and Andhra Pradesh in November 1956.

secs.t: Ethnic Muslim minority groups and 'national minority' - concept

x: Arnold Rose describes a minority as a group set apart by race, nationality, religion or language that sees itself, and is seen by others, as different, with negative connotations.
Giddens identifies disadvantage, group solidarity and physical or social isolation as features associated with minorities;
constitutional sovereignty
is not included.
Jains
were included among the notified national minorities in 2014; the list also contains Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists and Parsis.

secs.t: State response - Sixth Schedule councils, Art. 371, statehood

x: Article 371A concerns Nagaland, 371B Assam, 371C Manipur and 371D Andhra Pradesh in relation to public employment and education.
The stated response includes statehood, the Inner Line Permit, AFSPA, peace accords and MDoNER.
The application of Parliamentary and State legislation is subject to the prescribed authority: the Governor in Assam and the President in Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Regionalism may aid democratisation, illustrated by the Tripura ADC, but may also feed secessionism such as Greater Nagalim and vote-bank politics.
Greater Nagalim
is associated with secessionist pressures connected with Naga aspirations.
Tronglaobi is identified with
Bishnupur
district; the reported incident was followed by shutdowns in 12 districts.
The Centre provided rice valued at
₹10 crore
for approximately 40,000 refugees and displaced people in Mizoram.

rows.title: Processes of social change - sanskritisation, westernisation, modernisation, secularisation
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Factors and sources of social change

x: Modern education, legislation, behaviour-change communication and social movements are all identified as sources or illustrations of social change.
The Green Revolution is associated with the
Third Plan
in the classification of planning as a factor of social change.
State policy, reform movements, Sanskritisation and Westernisation are all identified as contributing to change among Dalits.

secs.t: Diffusion processes - acculturation, diffusion, assimilation

x: Assimilation
occurs when a minority merges fully into the wider society and loses its distinct identity.
The German-Austrian school, associated with Graebner and Schmidt, developed the idea of
culture circles
Mackay
is associated with the interpretation that the Indus civilisation involved migration from Mesopotamia.
The sequence presented is Mackay's migration interpretation, Wheeler's diffusion-of-ideas interpretation and Marshall's indigenous-evolution position.

secs.t: Sanskritisation - originator, book, definition, reference groups, de-sanskritisation

x: Sanskritisation is the adoption by a low caste or tribe of the customs, rituals and way of life of a higher, often twice-born, caste to claim higher status.
Sanskritisation brings positional change for a group within the existing social structure; it does not by itself bring structural change.
De-sanskritisation involves rejecting Sanskritic norms and asserting one's own identity, as illustrated by the non-Brahmin or Dravidian movement.

secs.t: Modernisation - scholars, books, indicators

x: For Daniel Lerner, empathy is associated with
psychic mobility
, an aspect of modernisation.
Daniel Lerner discussed these stages and the idea of empathy in
The Passing of Traditional Society
, published in 1958.
Rationality, scientific temper, industrialisation, urbanisation, literacy, mass media and democratic participation are all listed as indicators of modernisation.

secs.t: Cultural lag - originator, material vs non-material culture

x: W.F. Ogburn
propounded the concept of cultural lag in Social Change, published in 1922.
Ogburn held that material culture, particularly technology, changes faster, while beliefs, norms and other non-material elements lag behind.
Religion, law and tradition are identified as lagging factors.
The example illustrates
cultural lag
because technological change is faster than the adjustment of social norms.

secs.t: Westernisation - originator, levels, difference from modernisation

x: Srinivas identified technology, institutions, ideology and values as levels at which the effects of British rule produced Westernisation.
Srinivas preferred to treat Westernisation as ethically neutral, whereas modernisation is commonly value-loaded through the idea of progress.
Srinivas observed that urbanisation and education can alter authority patterns within families without necessarily ending the
joint family

secs.t: Secularisation - sociological meaning vs constitutional secularism

x: Constitutional secularism is associated here with Articles 25 to 28, concerning freedom of religion and the state's relationship with religious practice.
Sociological secularisation and constitutional secularism are distinct, and constitutional secularism does not require the exclusive removal of religion from public life.
Srinivas listed secularisation together with Sanskritisation, Westernisation and dominant caste.

secs.t: Theories of social change - proponents

x: Spengler wrote about the decline of the West, Toynbee proposed challenge and response, Sorokin distinguished sensate and ideational cultures, and Pareto explained the circulation of elites.
Elliot Smith, Perry and Boas
are identified with the diffusion theory of social change.
Karl Marx, Ralf Dahrendorf and Lewis Coser
are associated with the conflict theory of social change.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan uses
community outreach and street plays
as tools of behavioural change.
Sanskritisation may provide mobility to a caste but leaves the hierarchy intact; the Westernisation-modernisation debate concerns value-neutrality.
The criticism is that Sanskritisation may enable mobility for a caste but does not remove the broader caste hierarchy.

rows.title: Social stratification and mobility in India
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Social stratification - bases and characteristics

x: Exam angle: "which is NOT a basis" type questions; Green's definition; Varna vs Jati.
Social stratification is the hierarchical ranking of groups according to unequal
wealth, prestige and power
Class stratification rests on achievement-related and economic factors such as
education, wealth, occupation and business ownership
Harappan society shows differentiation, including the distinction between citadel and lower town, but not a rigid caste system.

secs.t: Theories of stratification → theorist

x: Davis and Moore argued that unequal rewards help attract scarce talent to positions considered functionally important.
Melvin Tumin
criticised the functionalist view, arguing that stratification can waste talent and reproduce inequality across generations.
Beteille observed that land ownership and political authority had moved away from the old ritual hierarchy, showing that caste, class and power may diverge.

secs.t: Caste vs class - closed vs open systems

x: The Jajmani system has weakened, and caste dominance increasingly rests on secular factors such as economic and political power.
Ashraf, Ajlaf and Arzal are status categories found among
Muslims
, illustrating that stratification is not confined to Hindus.
In urban India, class-based considerations in marriage alliances increasingly include
education, occupation and wealth
alongside caste.

secs.t: Social mobility types

x: Horizontal mobility
means a change of position without movement up or down the social hierarchy, such as moving between similar clerical jobs.
Sanskritisation is the process by which lower castes imitate the rituals and lifestyle of higher castes to seek upward social mobility.

Vertical mobility is movement up or down; horizontal mobility is movement at the same level; inter-generational mobility occurs between parents and children; structural mobility results from occupational restructuring.

secs.t: Agrarian class structure - Daniel Thorner, Andre Beteille

x: Mazdoors are poor tenants, sharecroppers and landless labourers who work on other people’s land.
Thorner’s classification is based on the nature of land rights and the type of income derived from agriculture.
Studies in Agrarian Social Structure
is associated with Andre Beteille.
A dominant caste combines
numerical strength, sizeable arable land and fairly high ritual rank

secs.t: Middle class and new classes in India

x: Macaulay's Minute of 1835
promoted English education, which contributed to the emergence of an English-educated middle class that later participated in the freedom struggle.
The cited projection places India's middle class at 61 per cent by 2047, while the OECD expects it to become the world's largest by 2035, overtaking China's.
The 2026 NEET paper leak
was cited as an event that shook the middle class's trust in professional qualifications as a pathway to mobility.

secs.t: Mobility through reservation, education, migration

x: Better education is associated with better employment opportunities and higher social standing, thereby enabling upward mobility in the emerging class system.
Reservation promoted group mobility and broadened the urban middle class by bringing backward classes and Dalits into new educational and occupational positions.
The shift from toddy tapping to tailoring and cottage industries illustrates
occupational mobility
among the Ezhavas.

secs.t: Dalit and OBC mobility patterns

x: The Mandal Commission estimated OBCs at over 52 per cent of the population and used 11 indicators: four social, four economic and three educational.
The three avenues identified for Dalit change are state policy, reform movements, and Sanskritisation or Westernisation.
Dominant peasant castes such as Marathas, Gujjars and Patels have demanded OBC status in pursuit of
greater life chances

secs.t: Terms - status inconsistency, status group, life chances

x: Status inconsistency is associated with Gerhard Lenski and means differing rankings across dimensions.
Status inconsistency
occurs when a person occupies different ranks on different dimensions, such as wealth, caste and occupation.
Weber described a status group as people sharing a lifestyle and social honour.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The horizontal category consists of young voters from different caste groups who share concerns over jobs and examinations, cutting across vertical caste loyalties.
The estimate places the decline in poverty from 21.9 per cent in 2011–12 to
2.3 per cent in 2023–24
Kshatriyaisation may provide mobility and enhanced status claims, but the criticism is that it reproduces the hierarchical structure rather than eliminating it.

rows.title: Rural, urban and tribal society in India - features and interlinkages
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Rural community - elements, 'village republics', village studies, little community

x: Exam angle: "Which is NOT an element/feature"; village → scholar matching.
Charles Metcalfe
described Indian villages as ‘little republics’, referring to their character as relatively self-reliant units.
S.C. Dube
studied Shamirpet near Hyderabad and presented the study in Indian Village, published in 1955.
McKim Marriott used universalisation and parochialisation to describe
the two-way flow between Great and Little traditions

secs.t: Rural-urban continuum - folk-urban continuum, village vs town vs city

x: The folk-urban continuum treats settlements as lying along a gradual continuum from folk to urban forms rather than in two completely separate categories.
Villages are mainly agricultural, small and sparse, relatively homogeneous, based on primary face-to-face relations and governed largely through informal social control.
The Registrar General of India is stated to retain the criteria for Census 2027 despite objections from
the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

secs.t: Urban society - features, urbanism as a way of life, trends (Census 2011)

x: Urbanism refers to the social, cultural and behavioural dimensions of urban life, whereas urbanisation denotes the process through which population shifts towards urban areas.
Satellite and built-up data using DEGURBA placed India’s urbanisation at about
in 2015, more than double the Census figure of 31%.
For 2026–31, the 16th Finance Commission raised the ULB share of local-body grants from 36% to 45%, recognising projected urbanisation of 41% by 2031.

secs.t: Urbanisation processes - primary vs secondary (Redfield and Singer), orthogenetic vs heterogenetic

x: Primary urbanisation is orthogenetic: folk culture is carried forward into a Great Tradition, producing cities of moral order such as cultural or temple centres.
A heterogenetic process involves new modes of thought clashing with or replacing older cultures, not the exclusive continuity of folk culture.
Milton Singer
studied Hinduism in urban Madras and, in When a Great Tradition Modernizes, highlighted continuity between tradition and modernity.

secs.t: Urban problems - slums, housing, pollution, crime; link to industrialisation

x: Rapid urbanisation may weaken social control and produce maladjustment, crime, environmental degradation and alienation; it does not universally strengthen traditional social control.
The Economic Survey 2025-26 perspective treats informality as a structural outcome of rapid urbanisation that should be integrated rather than eradicated.
Low-income workers often prefer informal housing near jobs because formal affordable housing on the urban periphery may not have adequate connectivity.

secs.t: Tribal society - features vs peasant society, tribal-rural transitions

x: N.K. Bose is associated with the Hindu method of tribal absorption; Surajit Sinha with tribe-caste continuum and secondary state formation; and T.K. Oommen with tribal autonomy movements.
All four statements are correct: the ST decadal growth rate was 23.66%, the all-India rate was 17.69%, the ST sex ratio was 990 against 940 overall, and 705 ST groups were recorded.

secs.t: Migration linkages - rural-urban migration, footloose labour, informal labour

x: Monsoon failure and rural unemployment
push people away from rural areas towards urban employment opportunities.
About 35% of rural households lack quality healthcare within 5 km, and migration can leave ageing parents behind.
Jan Breman’s Footloose Labour (1996) describes circular migrant workers who move between seasonal, casual and informal employment.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh - rural/urban/tribal shares and urban centres

x: Scheduled Areas covered 16,267.63 square kilometres, approximately 10.15% of Andhra Pradesh, and included 3,512 villages.
The cited Scheduled Areas include villages in
Parvathipuram Manyam, Vizianagaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Anakapalli and Eluru
districts.
About
12.9 lakh
tribals live in the Scheduled Areas, compared with 27.39 lakh Scheduled Tribes in the State as a whole.
The cited spatial imbalance is approximately 47% urban in Visakhapatnam against 16% in Srikakulam, corresponding broadly to the 13-district figures.
The Rurban cluster scheme covers 359 Andhra Pradesh panchayats, Amaravati is associated with HRIDAY, and the skill hubs are associated with APSSDC.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
told the parliamentary panel headed by TDP MP Magunta Sreenivasulu Reddy that the Census Town definition is outdated.
Although the Census Town definition was criticised as outdated, the Registrar General of India is retaining it for Census 2027.
The rural-urban binary may leave rapidly urbanising areas under panchayats with limited fiscal power, creating a governance mismatch.

rows.title: Casteism - meaning, causes, manifestations and remedial measures
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Casteism - definitions and difference from caste as an institution

x: Kaka Kalelkar described casteism as “
an overriding, blind and supreme group loyalty
” that ignores justice, fair play and universal brotherhood.

Caste is a hereditary and endogamous group; casteism produces discrimination and vote-bank politics; caste as a social structure relates to Ghurye’s features; and casteism may use caste for political, economic or social gain.

secs.t: Causes - endogamy, caste consciousness, political mobilisation, economic competition, limits of urban anonymity

x: The estimate states that only
about 5 per cent
of Indian marriages are inter-caste, indicating the continuing strength of endogamy.
Urban migration does not automatically eliminate caste prejudice; migrants may carry it into cities.
Caste-based vote banks and caste politics have increased, and caste associations may act as pressure groups in electoral politics.

secs.t: Manifestations - caste voting, caste panchayats, honour killings, job and housing discrimination

x: Manifestations include refusal of tenants by upper-caste landlords, workplace discrimination and caste-based matrimonial sites.
The 2026 Regulations covered discrimination against SC, ST and OBC members, were stayed interim by the Supreme Court, and the case arose from student suicides in Abeda Salim Tadvi v. Union of India.

secs.t: Caste and elections - caste arithmetic, caste parties, Andhra Pradesh caste politics

x: Rajni Kothari argued that politics does not merely use caste but also politicises it, thereby transforming caste into a political resource.
In Tamil Nadu,
Gounders, Mukkulathors and Vanniyars
used caste solidarity to enter the legislature, illustrating caste arithmetic.
The Justice Party era mobilised
Reddys, Kammas, Kapus and Velamas
against Brahmin dominance.

secs.t: Remedial measures - inter-caste marriage incentive, education, legal action

x: The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 provide penal safeguards against untouchability and atrocities.
The allocation mentioned for the Ambedkar Overseas Vidya Nidhi for SC students abroad was
₹36 crore
The
SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989
addresses atrocities against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

secs.t: Thinkers against caste → works and statements (Ambedkar, Periyar, Phule, Jashuva)

x: Periyar led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925, supported self-respect marriages without Brahmin priests and was jailed during the Vaikom Satyagraha in 1924.
Gurram Jashuva
was associated with the title 'Ubhaya Bhasha Praveena' and is regarded as a pioneer of Telugu Dalit literature.
AP reformer
Raghupati Venkataratnam Naidu
organised Saha Pankti Bhojanam as an initiative promoting inter-caste dining.

secs.t: Caste panchayats and khap diktats - Supreme Court directions (Shakti Vahini case)

x: In Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court held that khap or caste-panchayat interference in the marriage of consenting adults is illegal.
Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) included directions concerning safe houses in every district and police protection for couples facing caste-panchayat interference.
Tamil Nadu announced a safe house in each district for inter-caste couples in line with the directions associated with
Shakti Vahini v. Union of India

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The reported purification ritual took place at
Haldwani
in Uttarakhand and was criticised as an instance of untouchability after Kharge's rally was attacked.
The debate is whether caste enumeration would ossify caste identities or instead expose existing inequities for corrective policy.
The AP angle includes the political dominance of intermediate castes such as Reddy, Kamma and Kapu, along with Dalit assertion after Karamchedu.

rows.title: Communalism - meaning, causes, forms and growth in India
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Communalism - definitions → scholar

x: Exam angle: definition → scholar matching (asked in APPSC-G2 2025).
T.K. Oommen identified six dimensions ranging from assimilationist to secessionist, while Asghar Ali Engineer is a leading scholar of communalism and communal harmony.
In India, communalism is commonly understood as religious differences between groups that generate tension and rioting, often when one group promotes its interests at the expense of others.

secs.t: Stages of communalism - Bipan Chandra's three stages

x: Communal nationalism
is the first stage, in which followers of one religion are believed to share common political and economic interests while remaining nationalist in outlook.
Extreme communalism treats community interests as mutually antagonistic and is expressed through fear, hatred and violence; .
After the 1937 elections, the Muslim League adopted extreme communalism based on
fear, hatred and violence

secs.t: Causes - historical, political, economic, media, colonial policy

x: The recording of caste and religion in the first census of
is identified as a historical or colonial factor contributing to communalism.
Fake news and hate messages on social media, along with media amplification of communal narratives, can intensify communal tensions.
The Arya Samaj promoted Shuddhi and Sangathan, while Muslim organisations promoted Tabligh and Tanzim in the 1920s.

secs.t: Growth in colonial India - Lord Minto, Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha

x: The Aga Khan led the Simla Deputation to Lord Minto, which demanded separate electorates, and the Muslim League was founded at Dacca with Nawab Salimullah associated with its establishment.
Lord Minto
is called the Father of the Communal Electorate because the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909 introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

secs.t: Communal Award and two-nation theory - authors and events

x: Syed Ahmad Khan
is regarded as the ideological father of the Two-Nation Theory, particularly in connection with the Hindi-Urdu controversy and his advice to Muslims to stay out of the Congress.

Syed Ahmad Khan is associated with the ideological basis of the Two-Nation Theory, Iqbal with the proposal for a consolidated Muslim state, Jinnah with the Fourteen Points, and Ramsay MacDonald with the Communal Award.

secs.t: Forms of communalism - political, economic, social, separatist, retaliatory (Oommen's six dimensions)

x: Assimilationist communalism involves the absorption of smaller religious groups into a larger one, as illustrated by claims that STs, Jains, Sikhs and Buddhists are Hindus.
Retaliatory communalism attempts to harm members of other communities and may produce riots and cycles of revenge.
The political, economic and social forms respectively concern electoral mobilisation, competition over opportunities and resources, and prejudice or social distance.

secs.t: Religious fundamentalism and communalism - distinction

x: Religious fundamentalism is mainly doctrinal, emphasising a return to fundamentals and literal scripture.
Fundamentalism can exist without inter-group conflict; therefore; .
Both statements are true, and the mobilisation of one community against others explains why communalism necessarily has an “us versus them” or relational character.

secs.t: Communalism and secularism - constitutional safeguards against communal politics

x: An appeal for votes on the ground of religion is treated as a corrupt practice under
Section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951
The
Religious Institutions (Prevention of Misuse) Act, 1988
bars the use of religious institutions or places for political or communal purposes.
The Shah Bano case was treated in the cited APPSC-General Studies key as a development contributing to
the spirit of communal harmony

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Kerala Chief Minister
V.D. Satheesan
called for unity against communalism and linked the Haldwani “purification” controversy with secular values on 16 August 2026.
The Muslim League was formed in 1906, the first legal separate electorate was introduced by the 1909 Act, “Secular” was added in 1976, and S.R. Bommai was decided in 1994.

rows.title: Communal violence - major episodes, consequences and remedies
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Inquiry commissions → matter probed

x: Exam angle: commission → matter matching.
The
Liberhan Commission
investigated the demolition of the disputed structure at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992.
The Ranganath Misra Commission of 1985 examined the 1984 anti-Sikh riots in the context of the Punjab Accord.
The Wadhwa Commission examined the murder of missionary Graham Staines in Odisha in 1999, whereas the Jain Commission examined the conspiracy behind Rajiv Gandhi’s assassination.

secs.t: Major communal riots → year + state

x: The Direct Action Day and Noakhali violence occurred in 1946 in
Bengal, including Calcutta and Noakhali
The aftermath of the Babri demolition involved
Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh, Mumbai and other places
during 1992–93.
The Godhra train burning involved 59 people, mostly kar sevaks, occurred on 27 February 2002, and was investigated by an SC-appointed SIT.

secs.t: Consequences - ghettoisation, displacement, loss of trust, polarisation

x: Communal violence can undermine the rule of law by producing insecurity, instability and loss of faith in the police and courts, especially when guilty persons are not brought to book.
Communal violence can cause polarisation, weaken social capital, threaten unity in diversity, and harm India’s global image and the diaspora.

secs.t: Remedies - Communal Violence Bill (draft), National Integration Council, peace committees

x: The National Foundation for Communal Harmony
supports child victims of violence and promotes inter-faith dialogue
All four are recognised measures: peace committees, responsible media conduct, curbing extremist outfits and the MHA Guidelines for Communal Harmony covering prevention, containment and response.
Home Guards were first raised in December 1946 to assist the police in controlling civil disturbance and communal riots.

secs.t: Role of police and administration - Sachar Committee, police reforms

x: The Sachar Committee found that Muslims lagged in education and employment and were under-represented in public employment, including the police.
The judgment mandated bodies such as the State Security Commission, Police Establishment Board and Police Complaints Authority, along with separation of investigation from law and order.
In Tehseen Poonawalla (2018), the Supreme Court directed the appointment of nodal officers in every district to prevent mob violence and hate crimes.

secs.t: Hate speech and communal violence - Law Commission reports, IPC/BNS provisions

x: Prakash Singh is associated with police reforms; Tehseen Poonawalla with nodal officers; Ramji Lal Modi with Section 295A; and Pravasi Bhalai Sangathan with the request to define hate speech.

Promoting enmity is covered by IPC Section 153A and BNS Section 196; deliberate acts outraging religious feelings by IPC Section 295A and BNS Section 299; and statements conducing to public mischief by IPC Section 505 and BNS Section 353.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh - communal incidents and peace-building (Hyderabad old city history)

x: The Mecca Masjid blast on 18 May 2007 was followed by
tension and police firing
Mecca Masjid was completed in 1693, the Rameeza Bee-related disturbances occurred in 1978, old-city riots occurred again in 1990, and the blast took place in 2007.
Mecca Masjid was completed by
Aurangzeb
in 1693, after its construction had been begun by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1614.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: A Muzaffarnagar court allowed withdrawal of a 2013 riot case against 25 people, including former Union Minister Sanjeev Balyan.
The 37 accused were acquitted for
lack of proof
Low conviction rates and case withdrawals are criticised for weakening deterrence against communal violence.
The draft communal violence law has been attacked as
one-sided

rows.title: Regionalism - meaning, causes, forms and sons-of-the-soil movements
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Domicile-based job reservation laws - private-sector local quotas and court rulings

x: Exam angle: APPSC-G2 2025 asked which state's 75% private-sector local quota was struck down by the High Court -
Haryana
The AP Employment of Local Candidates in the Industries/Factories Act, 2019, was identified as the first such State law and provided a 75% quota for locals in private industrial jobs.

secs.t: Causes - uneven development, cultural identity, language, historical memory, neglect, migration

x: Exam angle: UPPSC 2008 - uneven development, fear of losing cultural identity and political prominence are all causes (answer: "all the above").
Bombay and West Bengal together held
of capital in 1948, a figure used to illustrate regional economic inequality.
The sons-of-the-soil sentiment becomes strongest where migrants and local educated youth compete for middle-class employment.

secs.t: Regionalism - meaning, positive vs negative regionalism

x: Supra-state regionalism involves several States sharing interests, inter-state regionalism involves conflicts between States, and intra-state regionalism concerns a region within a State seeking recognition.
Hostility to migrants
is a negative consequence associated with parochialism, including the activities of organisations such as Shiv Sena and MNS.
The Tripura Tribal Autonomous District Council illustrates
intergroup solidarity
as a positive dimension of regionalism.

secs.t: Forms - separate statehood, autonomy, inter-state disputes, sons-of-the-soil

x: Dravida Nadu represents secessionism, Telangana represents a demand for a separate State within the Union, and NCT of Delhi represents full Statehood demands for Union Territories.
Maharashtra–Karnataka and Assam–Mizoram are boundary disputes, Cauvery is a river dispute, and Chandigarh is a capital dispute.
Assam–Nagaland is a boundary dispute, while Parwanoo is associated with Haryana–Himachal Pradesh and Sarchu with Ladakh–Himachal Pradesh.

secs.t: Sons-of-the-soil movements → state

x: All four statements are correct: the MNS targeted North Indians in 2008, and the Assam Movement ran from 1979 to 1985 around illegal immigration, with later clashes involving Bodos and Bengali-speaking Muslims.
The Mulki rules provided a
preference for local residents in jobs in Hyderabad/Telangana
and contributed to the agitations of 1969 and 1972–73.

secs.t: Linguistic reorganisation - Dhar Commission, JVP Committee, SRC

x: The Dhar Commission was set up in 1948, followed by the Visalandhra Mahasabha in 1949, Swami Sitaram's fast in 1951 and the States Reorganisation Commission in December 1953.
The Dhar Commission preceded the 1949 Visalandhra Mahasabha, Swami Sitaram fasted in 1951, and the second Visalandhra Mahasabha met at Hyderabad on 13–14 June 1954.

secs.t: Regional parties - rise and role in federal politics

x: Both statements are true, and the exploitation of regional sentiment for votes explains why it can become a negative feature of regional-party politics.
The listed measures include the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, the National Integration Council, Articles 44 and 51A, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and the Eighth Schedule.
Articles 44 and 51A
are mentioned among the governmental and constitutional measures intended to contain regionalism.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: All three statements are correct: the MHA panel was set up under former Deputy NSA Pankaj Kumar Singh to draft a permanent solution, with concerns centred on the Siliguri Corridor.
The Ministry of Home Affairs set up a panel under
Pankaj Kumar Singh
to examine the Gorkhaland statehood demand.
The Bill revived debate over the 1971 seat freeze and regional equity, especially the representation of southern States.

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Capital city debate - Amaravati, three-capitals laws and their repeal

x: Exam angle: APPSC-GS 2023 asked for the bill behind the three capitals -
APCRDA (Repeal) Bill, 2020
. APPSC-GS 2022 asked when the Decentralisation Act 2020 was dropped -
YSRCP criticised large spending on Amaravati as harmful to north coastal districts and drought-prone Rayalaseema; the coalition feared that the three-capitals plan could be revived in 2029.

secs.t: Regions of AP - Coastal Andhra, North Andhra (Uttarandhra), Rayalaseema

x: Guntur, Prakasam and Nellore were placed in Coastal Andhra, not North Andhra.
Zone II comprised
East Godavari, West Godavari and Krishna
All four statements are correct in the stated six-zone arrangement.

secs.t: Committees on regional imbalance → mandate

x: The Bhargava Committee of 1969 assessed the Telangana surplus funds that had allegedly been diverted to other regions.
The Srikrishna Committee submitted its report in December 2010 and presented
six
options on the Telangana/united Andhra Pradesh question.
The 8-Point Formula of 1969 itself set up a high-level committee under a judge and a special committee on Telangana surpluses.

secs.t: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 - backward districts package, special category status

x: The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 took effect on the appointed day,
2 June 2014
Hyderabad was to serve as the common capital for up to ten years, not permanently.
Sections 46(2)-(3) provide for a special development package for backward areas, while Section 94 provides tax incentives.
The backward districts package was designed on the
KBK/Bundelkhand model

secs.t: Regional disparity indicators - irrigation, per capita income, literacy

x: The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet tracked
₹8.55 lakh crore
of investment aimed at generating jobs in North Andhra and Rayalaseema.
JSW steel in Kadapa, the Kia plant, Royal Enfield in Tirupati and renewable parks are all associated with Rayalaseema’s emergence as an industrial hub.
A Space City near Sriharikota
has been proposed, alongside defence units and renewable parks, in the broader regional-development context.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The agreement-based safeguards of the Sri Bagh Pact of 1937 and the Gentlemen’s Agreement of 1956 are criticised for institutionalising sub-regional fault lines; poor implementation fed subsequent agitations.
The Sri Bagh Pact dates to 1937, the Gentlemen’s Agreement to 1956, the Special Category Status promise to February 2014, and the Reorganisation Act took effect on 2 June 2014.

rows.title: Youth unrest and agitation - causes, forms, student movements and remedies
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Youth unrest - meaning and causes

x: Youth unrest refers to collective frustration among young people when society's norms seem ineffective or harmful.
Shared dissatisfaction, public attention and a desire for change are signs of youth unrest;
complete acceptance of existing conditions
is not.
Resource mobilisation theory gives greater importance to tactics and leadership than to grievances alone.

secs.t: Forms - agitations, protests, radicalisation, drug abuse, violence

x: An agitation seeking examination postponement is an example of
persuasive agitation
Resistance agitation
is directed against rules such as compulsory attendance.
Naga, Assam and Khalistan agitations are cited as regional or secessionist youth agitations.
The Dalit Panthers emerged in
1972 in Maharashtra
and are associated with militancy.
A newer pattern is leaderless digital protest conducted through encrypted applications.

secs.t: Student movements in India → state + issue

x: The JP movement of 1974 was associated with student agitations in
Bihar
and was led by Jayaprakash Narayan.
AASU's movement in Assam from 1979 to 1985 opposed illegal migrants and culminated in the Assam Accord of 1985.
The Patidar movement occurred in 2015, the Jallikattu movement in 2016–17, and the Anna Hazare movement is included among the other movements.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh youth and student agitations - Jai Andhra, Visakha Ukku, SCS

x: The Jai Andhra agitation occurred in 1972–73 after the Supreme Court upheld the Mulki Rules and demanded a separate Andhra; it ended with the Six-Point Formula in 1973.
The Special Category Status demand arose after 2014, with students and youth seeking the status promised at bifurcation.
YSRCP student and youth wings protested statewide over alleged
Mega DSC recruitment
irregularities on 29 July 2026.

secs.t: National Youth Policy 2014 - youth age group, priority areas

x: The National Youth Policy 2014 defines youth as persons aged
15–29 years
The vision of NYP 2014 is to help youth reach their full potential and thereby help India find its rightful place among nations.
The National Youth Policy 2014 has
5 objectives and 11 priority areas
Entrepreneurship, community engagement and participation in politics and governance are priority areas.

secs.t: Remedies and programmes - NYKS, NSS, Skill India, youth parliament

x: MY Bharat was launched on 31 October 2023 and replaced
NYKS
under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
Anger-management education, guidance from parents and teachers, and responsive administration are identified remedies.
The last non-statutory National Commission for Youth functioned during
; a Bill seeks a constitutional National Commission for Youth.

secs.t: Youth unemployment data - PLFS youth unemployment rate

x: For youth aged 15–29 years, the reported unemployment rates were 13.0% for males and 12.5% for females.
The ILO 2026 figures cited are a 12.4% youth unemployment rate, about 67 million unemployed youth and a 20% NEET rate.
Global youth unemployment was reported at 27.4% for women and 13.1% for men.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NEET paper leak protests began at
Jantar Mantar
and subsequently spread across the country.
The protests started at Jantar Mantar, spread nationwide, and SFI, AISF and other organisations demanded the Education Minister's resignation.
The ministerial resignation followed on
5 August 2026
, after the protests and demands for resignation reported on 24 July 2026.
The comparative account refers to youth-led protests in
Bangladesh, Nepal and Kenya

sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Suicide - NCRB ADSI report, farmer suicide causes, top states, types (Durkheim)

x: Bankruptcy or indebtedness
ranked first among the causes of farmer suicides in ADSI 2015, followed by farming-related issues.
Egoistic suicide is associated with too little integration, altruistic with too much integration, anomic with too little regulation, and fatalistic with too much regulation.
Durkheim described
anomic
suicide as arising from too little regulation, particularly during crisis or sudden change.

secs.t: Beggary - state data, Bombay Act, court judgment, SMILE

x: The Bombay Prevention of Begging Act was enacted in 1959 and became a punitive model copied by many States.
SMILE includes a sub-scheme for
comprehensive rehabilitation of persons engaged in begging
and shifts towards rights-based rehabilitation.
The SMILE-Beggary Survey App was launched at the
Chandigarh Chintan Shivir
held from 24 to 26 April 2026.

secs.t: Attempt to suicide in law - IPC 309, Mental Healthcare Act 2017, Tele-MANAS

x: Exam angle: MPPSC 1991 key: suicide, whose attempt is punishable but whose completed act cannot be punished.
P. Rathinam
, decided in 1994, held Section 309 invalid; Gian Kaur in 1996 overruled that position.
The BNS 2023 contains no general offence of attempted suicide; Section 226 covers an attempt made to
coerce a public servant

secs.t: Alcoholism - Article 47, prohibition states, Anti-Arrack Movement

x: Article 47, a Directive Principle, refers to prohibition of
intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health, except for medicinal purposes
Dubagunta Rosamma
led the Anti-Arrack Movement among neo-literate women of the literacy campaign.
The Social Purity Association established by R. Venkataratnam Naidu in 1891 was
a temperance campaign

secs.t: Drug abuse - NDPS Act 1985, Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, National Survey

x: The Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan is implemented by the
National Institute of Social Defence
and focuses, among other areas, on campuses.
The August 2026 youth campaign is being taken forward by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports through MY Bharat.
Alcohol
was the most-used substance, with a reported prevalence of 14.6 per cent, followed by cannabis and opioids.

secs.t: Social Defence - National Institute of Social Defence

x: NISD works under the
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
Social defence covers drug and alcohol abuse, beggary, destitute elderly persons and transgender persons;
regulation of foreign exchange markets
is unrelated.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh - farmer suicide ex gratia, liquor policy changes

x: Chittoor Police
ran “Dharya Sparsa - Operation Flush-Out” against drugs and illegal liquor.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: Andhra Pradesh conducted 463 school and 308 college suicide-prevention programmes during 2023–25.
The approach is moving from punishment, including Section 309 and anti-begging laws, towards health and rehabilitation through measures such as MHCA, SMILE and NMBA.
Emphasis on counselling, medical care and rehabilitation reflects the movement from punishment-oriented measures to a health and rehabilitation approach.

rows.title: Poverty, unemployment and social exclusion as social problems
sub: Group-II only - placed after Group-I B-89

secs.t: Poverty estimation expert groups - year, method, cut-offs

x: The Lakdawala methodology retained the calorie base, used state-specific poverty lines, and applied CPI-AL for rural areas and CPI-IW for urban areas.
The Tendulkar methodology dropped the calorie anchor, used the Modified Mixed Reference Period, applied an urban basket to both rural and urban areas, and included health and education.
NITI Aayog
is the present nodal body for poverty estimation using NSSO data; it succeeded the Planning Commission in this role.

secs.t: Measurement - NSO surveys, activity status, price index, agency

x: The consumption survey is generally conducted about once
every five years
, and MPCE is used in determining the poverty line.
MPCE means
Monthly Per Capita Expenditure
and is used in setting the poverty line through consumption expenditure data.
Female LFPR increased from 23.3 percent to
41.7 percent
, as stated for the relevant periods.

secs.t: Poverty and employment programmes - chronology

x: IRDP was introduced in 1978–80, SGSY in 1999, NREGA in 2005–06 and DAY-NRLM in 2011.
The Integrated Rural Development Programme (
IRDP
), introduced during 1978–80, promoted self-employment through subsidy and credit.
SGSY merged
IRDP, DWCRA and TRYSEM
and adopted an SHG-based approach.
PMEGP, launched in 2008, merged PMRY and REGP and provided credit-linked subsidy through KVIC.

secs.t: MGNREGA - features, renaming, rights-based guarantee, first state scheme

x: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was renamed the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act on
2 October 2009
If work is not provided within
15 days
of demand, an unemployment allowance is due under the stated rights-based guarantee.
The VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025, passed on 18 December 2025, proposed raising the guarantee from 100 to
125 days
and changing the funding pattern.

secs.t: Poverty concepts - absolute vs relative, social indicators, MPI, trends, AP position

x: The National MPI is prepared by NITI Aayog in association with the United Nations Development Programme and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative.
Illiteracy, lack of safe drinking water, poor health and sanitation, and lack of job opportunities are social indicators of poverty.
Cooking fuel, sanitation, electricity and bank accounts are all included among the stated MPI standard-of-living indicators, along with drinking water, housing and assets.

secs.t: Social exclusion - meaning, bases, practices

x: Social exclusion is a process through which people are denied access to facilities, benefits and opportunities available to others.
Untouchability, segregation and denial of access to land, water and jobs are practices of social exclusion.
The stated position is that income does not eliminate caste exclusion; therefore, economic advancement alone is not treated as ending caste-based discrimination.

secs.t: Poverty by social group and state

x: Scheduled Tribes have the highest poverty incidence, followed by Scheduled Castes.
Bihar
recorded the highest multidimensional poverty level in the NITI MPI 2023, at 33.76%.
The figures are 0.4 per cent for rural Himachal Pradesh, 1.9 per cent for urban Tamil Nadu and 25.1 per cent for rural Chhattisgarh.

secs.t: Culture of poverty and informal labour - proponent, unorganised labour, social security gaps

x: The concept of the “culture of poverty” was propounded by
Oscar Lewis
The culture-of-poverty perspective associates poverty with fatalism and patterns that are passed down from one generation to another.
Informal employment accounted for
62.3 per cent
of rural employment in Andhra Pradesh according to the cited APSES estimate.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The MGNREGA framework is described as giving way to the 125-day VB-G RAM G framework.
The cited PLFS 2023–24 figures are 4.1 per cent unemployment for Andhra Pradesh, 3.2 per cent for India and a 47.5 per cent labour-force participation rate for Andhra Pradesh.
The Tendulkar poverty line is criticised for being too low and therefore for understating the extent of poverty.
The cited World Inequality Database assessment indicates that
income inequality is rising

units.title: Rights Issues - Human Rights, Women's Rights, SC/ST Rights, Child Rights

rows.title: Human rights - concept, generations of rights, UDHR, ICCPR and ICESCR; UN human rights machinery

secs.t: UN human rights machinery - Human Rights Council, UPR, OHCHR, treaty bodies, special rapporteurs

x: Exam angle: APPSC 2018 asked the Asia-Pacific seat count (
The UN General Assembly may suspend a Council member for gross and systematic violations through a two-thirds vote.
The UPR is a peer review of the human rights record of every UN member state, conducted under the Human Rights Council.
The Global Alliance for Human Rights used the
Imagine–Dialogue–Act
model in preparation for the UDHR's 80th anniversary in December 2028.

secs.t: Rights newly recognised by the UN General Assembly → year

x: The Right to Development was recognised in 1986; the Right to Water and Sanitation on 28 July 2010; and the Right to a Clean, Healthy and Sustainable Environment on 28 July 2022.
The UN General Assembly recognised the
right to a clean, healthy and sustainable environment
as a universal human right on 28 July 2022.

secs.t: UDHR - date, drafting chair, articles, rights included and not included, Human Rights Day

x: Eleanor Roosevelt
chaired the drafting committee of the UDHR.
The UDHR contains
30 articles covering civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights
The listed UDHR rights include dignity, liberty, equality, life, an adequate standard of living and education.
The UDHR protects privacy under Article 12 and the ICCPR protects it under Article 17.

secs.t: Concept of human rights - dignity, universalism, indivisibility, which entitlements count

x: Human rights are inherent and inalienable rights possessed simply by virtue of being human.
Every Fundamental Right is a human right, but the wider category of human rights is not limited to constitutionally guaranteed Fundamental Rights.
The right to vote is
a statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act
, not a Fundamental Right.

secs.t: Generations of human rights → proponent and rights

x: Karel Vasak
proposed the three-generation classification of human rights in 1977.
The first, second and third generations were mapped respectively to
liberty, equality and fraternity
or solidarity.
First-generation rights are civil and political; second-generation rights are economic, social and cultural; third-generation rights are collective rights such as peace and development.

secs.t: International Bill of Human Rights - components, ICCPR and ICESCR, optional protocols

x: The International Bill of Human Rights consists of the UDHR, the ICCPR, the ICESCR and the optional protocols.
The ICESCR covers work, social security, health and education, with these rights realised progressively.

The First Optional Protocol to the ICCPR provides for individual complaints, the Second Optional Protocol concerns abolition of the death penalty, and the ICESCR Optional Protocol provides a complaints mechanism.

secs.t: Human rights NGOs and awards → focus

x: Amnesty International was founded in London in 1961 and focuses, among other matters, on prisoners of conscience.
The UN Human Rights Prize is given by the UN General Assembly, usually once every five years, and has been awarded since 1968.
Amnesty International
described Afghanistan’s new police law as “a sweeping assault on human rights.”.

secs.t: Core UN human rights treaties → subject and India's ratification status

x: All four statements are correct: India ratified CERD in 1968 and CEDAW in 1993, signed but did not ratify CAT in 1997, and acceded to CRC in 1992.
CMW concerns migrant workers, CRPD concerns persons with disabilities, and CPED concerns enforced disappearance.
The CRPD concerns persons with disabilities and gave rise to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, which raised recognised disabilities from 7 to 21.

secs.t: Paris Principles for national human rights institutions - content, GANHRI accreditation

x: The Paris Principles require independence and autonomy from government and powers to investigate; exclusive dependence on the executive is contrary to these requirements.
The Paris Principles require all four features: a legal mandate, independence, pluralist composition, adequate resources and investigative powers.
GANHRI uses ‘A’ for
fully compliant
institutions and ‘B’ for partly compliant institutions.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The sequence is Magna Carta (1215), the event of 1688, the Declaration of Independence (1776), and the French Revolution (1789).
The Magna Carta of 1215 is regarded as the first human-rights document among the listed instruments.
The chronological order is Magna Carta (1215), UDHR (1948), ICCPR (1966) and CEDAW (1979).

rows.title: Human rights in the Indian Constitution; Protection of Human Rights Act 1993

secs.t: Rights that are both FRs and human rights - Arts 14, 19, 21, 21A, 23, 24, 32 vs UDHR

x: The UDHR was proclaimed on
10 December 1948
, which is observed as Human Rights Day.
Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children aged six to fourteen years and parallels Article 26 of the UDHR.
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour; its principal UDHR parallel is Article 4.

secs.t: Protection of Human Rights Act 1993 - commencement, objective, definitions, NHRC/SHRC constitution

x: Although the Act was enacted later, it was deemed to have come into force from
28 September 1993
, the date of the Ordinance.
The statutory definition covers rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity that are guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in International Covenants and enforceable by Indian courts.

secs.t: Human Rights Courts and Special Public Prosecutors

x: The proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings for offences corresponding to false evidence under IPC Section 193 and insulting a public servant in judicial proceedings under IPC Section 228; the corresponding BNS/BNSS provisions apply from 1 July 2024.
From 1 July 2024, the earlier IPC and procedural references are read with the corresponding provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

secs.t: DPSPs and Fundamental Duties reflecting UDHR and ICESCR

x: The Preamble, DPSPs and Fundamental Duties reflect UDHR principles and human-rights-oriented constitutional values.
Articles 39(a), 39(d), 42 and 43 respectively relate to adequate livelihood, equal pay, humane work conditions with maternity relief, and living wage.
Article 51A(e)
requires citizens to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women.
Article 51 contains all three directives, in addition to encouraging settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

secs.t: International covenants and Indian law - Articles for treaty implementation, CEDAW cases

x: In Vishaka (1997), the Supreme Court relied on the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (
CEDAW
) to frame workplace-harassment guidelines.
The principles associated with public interest litigation enabled courts to rely on international conventions in Guruvayur Devaswom (2003).
The NCPCR was set up in 2007 and works in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (
UNCRC

secs.t: Human rights of specific groups - prisoners, manual scavengers, bonded labour

x: Imprisonment does not erase a person's human rights; restrictions must have a lawful basis and prison administration remains subject to constitutional scrutiny.
The 2013 Act bans employment involving cleaning insanitary latrines, sewers and septic tanks without protective gear.
Article 23
prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other similar forms of forced labour, including bonded labour.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The Global Alliance for Human Rights targets progress before the 80th anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in December 2028.
India has not accepted the ICCPR individual-complaint mechanism through the First Optional Protocol, and advice of the NHRC is non-binding.

rows.title: NHRC and SHRCs - composition, powers, functions and limitations
sub: Group-II M1-B-53: National Human Rights Commission - composition, powers, functions and limitations
Group-II M1-B-54: State Human Rights Commissions and the Human Rights Courts

secs.t: NHRC appointment, term and removal

x: Exam angle: "appointed by" = President.
Appointment of a sitting Supreme Court Judge or a sitting High Court Chief Justice requires consultation with the
Chief Justice of India
A Chairperson or member of the NHRC resigns by writing addressed to the
President of India
Insolvency, outside paid employment and conviction for an offence involving moral turpitude are specified grounds of removal.
For proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the President refers the matter to the Supreme Court, whose inquiry precedes removal.

secs.t: NHRC composition - chairperson before/after 2019, members, deemed members, selection committee

x: Exam angle: "Member is not eligible for re-appointment" is the WRONG statement; after office, chairperson/members are ineligible for further government employment.
The Chairpersons of the NCM, NCSC, NCST and NCW, along with those of the NCBC, NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities, are deemed members.

All four changes are reflected in the post-2019 framework: expanded Chairperson eligibility, three human-rights experts with at least one woman, removal of the earlier five-year reappointment limit, and a three-year-or-70 term.

secs.t: NHRC status and history - statutory basis, year, first and present Chairpersons

x: Exam angle: "NHRC is a constitutional body" and "established in 1994" are both false; "constituted in 1993" is correct.
The NHRC was established in conformity with the
Paris Principles
relating to national institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights.
The Ordinance was promulgated on 28 September 1993, the NHRC was constituted on 12 October 1993, and the Act received assent in January 1994.

secs.t: NHRC and SHRC functions and powers - civil court, suo motu, jail visits, NGOs

x: The 2006 amendment enabled the NHRC to visit jails and detention places without prior intimation to the State Government.
All four are recognised functions of the NHRC: review of safeguards, study of treaties, consideration of inhibiting factors such as terrorism, and encouragement of NGOs.
The Commission’s civil-court powers include summoning persons, examining them on oath, requiring documents, and requisitioning public records.

secs.t: SHRC - chairperson eligibility, appointment, selection committee, acting chairperson, consultation

x: The Chairperson is appointed by the Governor and can be removed only by the President, on the same grounds applicable to the NHRC.
The 2006 amendment reduced the Commission’s strength from five to three: the Chairperson, one judicial member and one person with human-rights knowledge or experience.
Functions relating to a Union Territory may be conferred on an SHRC; however, Delhi continues to remain within the NHRC’s jurisdiction.
The SHRC submits its annual report to the State Government, which lays it before the State Legislature along with a memorandum of action taken.

secs.t: Limitations - time bar, armed forces, purview, non-binding, sub judice

x: The Allahabad High Court held that the NHRC was exceeding its mandate by directing an EOW probe into
558 aided madrasas
An inquiry begins with a complaint or suo motu action, proceeds through inquiry, may result in recommendations, and is followed by the Government’s communication of action taken.
The NHRC’s role concerning the armed forces is limited; it may
seek a report from the Central Government
and act within the statutory framework.

secs.t: Andhra Pradesh State Human Rights Commission - establishment, seat after bifurcation

x: In the Gade Sai Krishna case, the NHRC directed the Andhra Pradesh SHRC, the Director General of Police and the Chief Secretary to report.

secs.t: NHRC annual report → laid before; GANHRI accreditation

x: The NHRC report is sent to the appropriate governments and laid before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum, while an SHRC report is laid before the State Legislature.
GANHRI accreditation depends on conformity with
the Paris Principles
, which concern independence and effectiveness of national human-rights institutions.
The Paris Principles, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993, set standards of independence, pluralism and a broad mandate for national human-rights institutions.

secs.t: Specialised NHRC mandates - bonded labour, custodial deaths, encounter deaths

x: In 1997, the Supreme Court entrusted the NHRC with monitoring the
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
Custodial deaths are to be reported to the NHRC within
24 hours
; post-mortem videography and independent investigation are also associated safeguards.
NHRC guidelines and PUCL v. Maharashtra (2014) require reporting and a magisterial inquiry in cases of encounter deaths.

secs.t: Deemed members - chairpersons of other national commissions

x: Before 2019, the chairpersons of the
National Commissions for Minorities, SCs, STs and Women
were included as deemed members of the NHRC.
The Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities functions under
Section 75(1) of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016

secs.t: Division of functions between NHRC and SHRCs - jurisdiction, UTs

x: An SHRC deals with subjects in the State List and Concurrent List.
The Central Government may confer the human-rights functions of a Union Territory on an SHRC.
Constitution of an SHRC is optional; the State Government may constitute one under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

secs.t: SHRC vs NHRC - overlapping complaints, transfer

x: The arrangement prevents simultaneous inquiry by the SHRC, NHRC or another statutory commission into the same pending matter.
The
2006 amendment
authorised the NHRC to transfer complaints to the concerned SHRC.

secs.t: Universal angles

x: The NHRC sought reports from the AP DGP, Chief Secretary and SHRC
within a week
in connection with the alleged custodial death of Gade Sai Krishna.
Harish Iyer resigned from the NHRC's LGBTQI+ core group, alleging non-consultation on the Transgender Persons Amendment Bill, 2026; the development was reported in March 2026.
The notes identify optional creation, advisory powers and vacancies as weaknesses of SHRCs, and report that SHRCs in the highest-GDP States receive only 80 paise per capita.
